trait.name: Peaceful Aura, Fearsome Presence
entries: Beipiaosaurus is a docile creature, calmly feeding on vegetation in the chilly mountains of Yixian. However, if attacked, Beipiaosaurus will erupt into a frenzy of slashing claws. The first time Beipiaosaurus is attacked, the attacking creature must succeed a {@dc 12} Charisma saving throw or be {@condition frightened} of Beipiaosaurus until the end of their next turn.

trait.name: Slow Metabolism
entries: Beipiaosaurus has advantage on saving throws to prevent the {@condition poisoned} condition. However, if it does become {@condition poisoned}, the duration of that condition is doubled.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Beipiaosaurus chooses the attack action, it may make two Sabre-Clawed Slash attacks.

action.name: Sabre-Clawed Slash
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 3} to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}7 ({@damage 1d6 + 4}) damage.
A creature hit by this attack must succeed a {@dc 10} Constitution saving throw or take {@dice 1d6} additional slashing damage.
{@i "BAY-PEE-OW-SORE-US"} {@b (BEIPAO REPTILE)}

We were followin' a clearin' through the forest, hikin' in single file up the mountainside. Knackered from the walk, we stopped for a moment to catch our collective breath. Mid-swig o' water, I spotted 'em right there, less then 50 ft. away. Three slumped fuzzy creatures sat on their backsides, dozily graspin' at branches with their sickle claws and pullin' leaves off 'em. One of 'em turned its head sluggishly towards me and just carried on chompin' slowly. It didn't care one bit that we were there.
{@i Beipiaosaurus} is a small therizinosaurid from China that sheds light on the phylogenetic relationships of therizinosaurs.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Beipiaosaurus} was a small (8 ft. long) therizinosaurid, a group of unusual theropod dinosaurs that evolved herbivory within an otherwise generally carnivorous group. It had a long neck, small leaf-shaped teeth, a short tail, enlarged gut, and strong forelimbs with large sickle-like claws. {@i Beipiaosaurus} was an early member of the group, distinguished by its small size and relatively large head.

Some {@i Beipiaosaurus} specimens preserve a full body covering of simple quill-like feathers and {@i Beipiaosaurus} is unique among feathered dinosaurs due having secondary coat of more elongate feathers with unbranched filaments. Recent studies suggest that these feathers were brown in colour and were primarily for insulation in the chilly Yixian environment.

{@i Beipiaosaurus'} diet consisted mainly of ferns, early flowering plants, and leaves. However, it is possible that in the early stages of this group's transition into herbivory they supplemented their diet with insects.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Little is known for certain about the behavior of {@i Beipiaosaurus}, but some researchers report that their nests show that they were communal and probably cared for hatchlings, despite the hatchlings being able to feed themselves.

However, many parallels have been drawn between therizinosaurs and sloths (including giant ground sloths) due to their shared herbivorous diet, downy fuzz, enlarged guts, and sickle claws. It is possible that they occupied very similar niches, with {@i Beipiaosaurus} functioning like an agile dinosaur-sloth equivalent. Therizinosaurs were hunted by larger theropods, and {@i Beipiaosaurus'} small size and slow speed would have made it cautious and potentially highly-aggressive when threatened.

We recommend {@i Beipiaosaurus} be played as a relatively relaxed and seemingly sedate animal, that can erupt into an aggressive display of sharp claws if disturbed. Adults should be particularly hostile if in groups or near nesting sites.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: Therizinosaur skulls and teeth are similar to prosauropods, the precursors to sauropods, and they used to be considered a relic lineage of this group, or an unknown form of saurischian. It wasn't until 1993 that they were confidently identified as theropods. Within Theropoda, therizinosaurs are part of the maniraptorans, the group that includes dromaeosaurs, oviraptorosaurs, and modern birds.

trait.name: Altruistic Behaviour
entries: When attacked, a herd of Bolong will tend to flee. However, one will always stay behind to buy time for the others to escape. That Bolong will attack and fight to the death. The other individuals will only fight if they are cornered or cannot escape.

trait.name: Thundering Charge
entries: If Bolong moves at least 20 ft. in a straight line before using its Crushing Bulk attack, that attack deals an additional {@damage 2d6} bludgeoning damage this turn, but also deals {@damage 1d6} bludgeoning damage to Bolong on a successful hit.

trait.name: Defensive Gouge
entries: If Bolong is hit by a melee attack, it may use its reaction to make a single Thumb Gouge attack at the creature that hit it.
{@i "BOW-LONG"} {@b (BO'S DRAGON)}

The blizzard had rolled in pretty hard and we were pushin' through the snow to find some shelter. We decided to move into a denser part of the forest – to get a bit of cover from that piercin' wind. Seems we weren't the only ones with that idea. We came across a herd of lumberin' hadrosaur-lookin' dinosaurs. They were kinda small for that group and were spendin' most of their time on their hind legs, scrapin' away the snow in search of fresh growth. They weren't keen on us takin' up their warm spot in the forest and were honkin' loudly..
{@i Bolong} is one of the most basal members of the Hadrosauroidea, the group that includes the duck-billed dinosaurs, and is a relatively small member of it.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Bolong} was a relatively small hardrosauroid with an estimated length of 13 ft. and weighed approximately 440 lb. Although it shared many of the same features as other members of Hadrosauroidea, such as a beaked snout, robust hindlimbs, much lighter forelimbs, and a long thick tail, {@i Bolong} had much stockier proportions than its relatives. As the earliest branching hadrosauroid, it had features similar to the closely related iguanodontians including the first digit on each forelimb being modified into a thumb spike.

Like all hadrosauroids, {@i Bolong} was a herbivore and, given its low profile, likely fed near to the ground. It had large robust teeth and a modified jaw, specialised for chewing. This, combined with stomach contents, shows that {@i Bolong} was able to eat hard plants and even decomposing wood.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Hadrosauroids are frequently portrayed as relatively harmless animals that could only flee from danger. However, any modern large herbivore can be extremely dangerous, either because it is naturally aggressive or because it will use its bulk to defend itself. Hadrosauroids had thick, powerful tails which could strike attackers and {@i Bolong} possessed a thumb spike which could be used to fight predators (or other {@i Bolong}). Most hadrosauroids are also thought to have been communal animals, who were likely involved and protective parents, similar to modern cows.
We suggest {@i Bolong} be played as an apparently peaceful grazing animal, but with both the capacity for extreme aggression (especially if protecting young) and sudden panic, fleeing en-mass.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: Hadrosauroids are members of the iguanodontians, a highly successful group of dinosaurs that arose in the Middle Jurassic and thrived until the end Cretaceous extinction. They were a varied group, containing animals such as {@i Iguanodon} ({@b page 132}) and the famous "duck-billed" hadrosaurs, as well as small bipedal animals like {@i Dryosaurus}.

{@i Bolong} provides a better understanding of this group's distribution during the Early Cretaceous. It's presence in China clarifies that a land connection between Asia and western North America + Europe was already established before or during the Barremian (middle of the Early Cretaceous), allowing us to better reconstruct ancient geography.

entries.name: Walking
entries: There has been some debate over whether {@i Bolong} walked on four legs all the time (obligate quadruped) or was capable of walking on two legs as well (facultative biped). Its front legs were relatively short and appear less able to support its body weight compared to other hadrosauroids, yet the foot was short and stocky, similar to those of true quadrupeds. Interestingly the younger animals had proportionally longer limbs, similar to their four-legged relatives. Perhaps juveniles walked on all fours before becoming more bipedal as heavier adults.

trait.name: Arboreal
entries: If Microraptor uses the Dash action, do not increase its flight speed, but instead triple its climb speed. Microraptor also has advantage on Stealth checks while in a wooded or forested environment.

trait.name: Feathered and Evasive.
entries: When making a Dexterity saving throw to take half damage from an attack, spell, or effect, Microraptor instead takes no damage if the saving throw is succeeded.
{@i "MY-CROW-WRAP-TOR"} {@b (SMALL PLUNDERER)}

The ancient forest 'round us was filled with the chirpin' and squawkin' of various dinosaurs, radiatin' from the trees above. Among the foliage, I glimpsed the shimmerin' of iridescent feathers streakin' through the sky. A tiny, but brilliant, four-winged dinosaur soared down from above, landin' on a branch just a few feet away. Remarkable!

{@i Microraptor} is a small, highly specialised member of the Dromaeosauridae. Its most distinctive feature was its well-developed flight feathers on all four limbs, making it the first four-winged dinosaur known. This trait may be present in other dromaeosaurs, but {@i Microraptor} was the first animal with unequivocal evidence of four wings.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Microraptor} was extremely small, one of the smallest non-avian theropods at only 2.5 ft. long, weighing only 1-3 lb., and with a wingspan of about 3 ft. Its long tail ended in a feathery fan, and it possessed long flight feathers on both its forelimbs and hindlimbs. Studies into dinosaur colour suggest that it might have been black with an iridescent sheen like modern starlings.

{@i Microraptor} was a predatory arboreal (tree dwelling) animal, hunting in dense forests. It could fly, although not particularly well by modern bird standards. It likely darted from tree to tree, jumping from one and flapping somewhat awkwardly or gliding to another.

{@i Microraptor} had a non-specialized carnivorous diet, eating whatever it could find. This included insects, small lizards, small mammals, birds, other non-avian dinosaurs, and fish. It is known to have swallowed small prey whole, likely dropping down from branches above, surprising prey.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: The four wings of {@i Microraptor} likely made it a clumsy walker. It spent the vast majority of its time in trees, gliding and flying from branch to branch. It should rarely leave the trees but can be seen by players hunting in the canopy. As a dromaeosaur, {@i Microraptor} was probably relatively intelligent for its size.

We recommend playing this creature as an inquisitive hunter that may follow a party, taking advantage of them distracting prey. This may lead a particularly curious {@i Microraptor} to become relatively docile around the party and may allow an opportunity for a wily party member to tame it.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Microraptor} was a dromaeosaurid but was not closely related to the more famous {@i Velociraptor} ({@b page 183}) or {@i Utahraptor} ({@b page 181}). Instead, it was part of a group of smaller dromaeosaurs currently only known from China. Many of these animals had a similar morphology to {@i Microraptor} and it has been suggested they may also have been able to fly or glide.

entries.name: Fossil Fakes
entries: When the first {@i Microraptor} fossil was discovered between 1997-1999, it was illegally smuggled out of China and amalgamated into a chimera. This is a practice that some unscrupulous fossil dealers undertake to try to increase the value of their fossils. Chimeras and improper fossil collecting methods not only risk the loss of valuable scientific information, but they also give private collectors (even those who act legally and morally) a bad reputation.

The original specimen, informally called "Archaeoraptor", attracted a lot of media attention for its excellent preservation, but controversy quickly arose due to the illegal handling of the fossil and its suspicious 'cobbled-together' appearance. When finally examined, it became apparent that the fossil was actually three distinct animals that were each a new species. The tail-end was eventually described as the remarkable {@i Microraptor}.

trait.name: Predatory Ancestors
entries: Beipiaosaurus retains the nocturnal hunter-killer instincts of its predatory theropod ancestors. At night, Beipiaosaurus gains the following temporary changes:

items: It has darkvision 60 ft.
Its movement speed is 35 ft. and its climb speed is 20 ft.
It has advantage on Perception checks.
It has resistance to non-magical bludgeoning, piercing, and slashing damage.
It has vulnerability to radiant damage.
It has an aversion to bright light.
It loses its "Peaceful Aura, Fearsome Presence" ability.

entries.name: Fossil Fakes
entries: When the first {@i Microraptor} fossil was discovered between 1997-1999, it was illegally smuggled out of China and amalgamated into a chimera. This is a practice that some unscrupulous fossil dealers undertake to try to increase the value of their fossils. Chimeras and improper fossil collecting methods not only risk the loss of valuable scientific information, but they also give private collectors (even those who act legally and morally) a bad reputation.

The original specimen, informally called "Archaeoraptor", attracted a lot of media attention for its excellent preservation, but controversy quickly arose due to the illegal handling of the fossil and its suspicious 'cobbled-together' appearance. When finally examined, it became apparent that the fossil was actually three distinct animals that were each a new species. The tail-end was eventually described as the remarkable {@i Microraptor}.

When fleeing from a threat, it is difficult to make out individual Psittacosaurus among the crowd. So long as there are three or more Psittacosaurus fleeing within 20 ft. of each other, ranged attacks against them are at disadvantage.

{@i "SI-TAC-OH-SORE-US"} {@b (PARROT REPTILE)}

Occasionally, the doldrum of the cold forest would be broken by loud cherpin'. The first time this happened, we moved on quickly to avoid whatever was makin' that racket. The second time, we hung around to see what it was. Turns out it was a huge swarm of quilled, beaked, ceratopsians. There was one big 'un, and dozens of lil' 'uns. They didn't half make a racket, cryin' at the big one for attention as they scurried to keep up. Like a mumma duck and her hatchlin's, 'cept no single mumma laid that many eggs for sure!

{@i Psittacosaurus} is a basal member of the Ceratopsia (horned dinosaurs) and is known from many Early Cretaceous localities, including several from Mongolia, China, Russia, and Thailand. Due to the high number of exceptionally preserved fossils of {@i Psittacosaurus}, it is one of the best understood dinosaurs.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Psittacosaurus} was a 6.5 ft. long bipedal herbivore that lacked the true horn and frills of its more derived ceratopsain relatives. It had a broad head with cheek bones that flared out into triangular keratin-covered points.

Exceptionally preserved specimens have retained the entire exterior of this animal, revealing colour patterned scaly skin, a series of long quills running down the upper surface of its tail, and even a cloaca with dark pigmentation.

{@i Psittacosaurus} was a herbivorous animal, able to scissor off tough leaves with its beak. This, combined with grinding teeth and its short stature, strongly indicates that it was an undergrowth-feeder, devouring fresh plant growth. Wear marks on young {@i Psittacosaurus} teeth indicate that they were precocial and could feed themselves immediately after hatching.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Psittacosaurus} are known to be highly social and gregarious (grouping together), even beyond basic nesting behaviour. They formed large herds of dozens to hundreds of individuals and, despite the young being able to feed themselves, they were still protected by numerous adults. Eggs were laid in clutches of up to 30, and the young formed creche groups made up of individuals of a variety of ages. It is even possible that parental duties may have been shared among the herd to lessen the load.

We recommend that {@i Psittacosaurus} be played as a dinosaurian equivalent to sheep, gathering in huge herds with some individuals maintaining a lookout. Upon spotting a threat, they should be more prone to fleeing, using their numbers to confuse their attackers. They should only stand and fight in desperate situations when unable to flee.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Psittacosaurus} was the most basal member of the Ceratopsia, the horned dinosaurs. This group includes a huge variety of dinosaurs ranging from small bipeds (like {@i Psittacosaurus}) to large-headed quadrupeds in the Leptoceratopsids, and the classic horned giants like {@i Centrosaurus} ({@b page 116}). The group enjoyed great success, surviving right up to the end-Cretaceous extinction.

entries.name: Biostratigraphy
entries: {@i Psittacosaurus} was an exceptionally successful animal. They inhabited huge swathes of Asia in vast herds and persisted for at least 24 million years. This means that their fossils occur in such large numbers across such vast areas and timescales that we are able to use them to reliably date rock formations, based on the species of {@i Psittacosaurus} present (see Biostratigraphy {@b page 16)}. This is almost unheard of for vertebrates and highlights just how successful {@i Psittacosaurus} was.

trait.name: Thick Feathered Coat
entries: Yutyrannus has immunity to cold damage and resistance to non-magical bludgeoning and piercing damage.
If Yutyrannus falls below half health, it loses its resistance to piercing and bludgeoning damage and replaces its immunity to cold damage with resistance to cold damage.

trait.name: Arch-Predator
entries: Yutyrannus cannot be easily swayed from the hunt. It has advantage on Charisma and Wisdom saving throws.

trait.name: Call the Pack (1/day)
entries: As a bonus action, Yutyrannus can let out a gut-wrenching bellow alerting other members of its pack to the conflict.
At the start of the next round, up to two additional Yutyrannus join the combat as allies to this Yutyrannus. They approach from nearby cover and do not have the Call the Pack ability.

If this ability is used by a polymorphed or otherwise shapeshifted humanoid, their friends, family, or party members are considered to be their 'pack' instead, and are made aware of the conflict, regardless of where they are.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Yutyrannus chooses the attack action, it may make one Feathermaw Bite attack and two Feathered Claw attacks.

action.name: Feathermaw Bite
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 11} to hit, reach 10 ft., one target. {@h}19 ({@damage 4d6 + 5}) piercing damage.

If a creature hit by this attack is Medium or smaller, it is {@condition grappled} (escape {@dc 16}). Until this grapple ends, the target is {@condition restrained}, and the Yutyrannus cannot Feathermaw Bite another target.

action.name: Feathered Claw
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 7} to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}10 ({@damage 1d12 + 4}) slashing damage.

action.name: Downy Shoulder Bash
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 11} to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}23 ({@damage 4d8 + 5}) bludgeoning damage.

If Yutyrannus moved at least 30 ft. before using this attack, a creature hit by this attack must succeed a {@dc 16} Strength saving throw or be knocked {@condition prone}. If Yutyrannus knocks a creature {@condition prone} with this attack, it may then make a single Feathered Claw attack against that creature.

legendary.name: Coordinate
entries: Yutyrannus signals its pack with grumbles and tail flicks. On its next turn, Yutyrannus has advantage on attack rolls against any creature that has at least one other Yutyrannus within 10 ft. of it that isn't incapacitated.

legendary.name: Hunt
entries: Yutyrannus searches for its prey. It may make a Perception check. If a hidden creature within 60 ft. has taken damage, Yutyrannus has advantage on this check, specifically for detecting that creature (disregard the additional d20 for all uninjured creatures).
{@i "YOU-TIE-RAN-US"} {@b (FEATHERED TYRANT)}

The silence of the frigid night-time forest was broken by the sound of deep, growlin' breathin'. In the darkness, those topaz eyes pierced the black veil, locked directly with mine. An eerie shiver ran up me back as a second, then third pair appeared.

{@i Yutyrannus} is an early tyrannosauroid. While much smaller than the true giants like {@i Tyrannosaurus} ({@b pages 186 and 195}), it was still a very large predator and is the biggest animal known with direct fossil evidence of feathers.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Yutyrannus} was a sizeable animal, estimated to be about 30 ft. long and weighing 1.5 tonnes. It was more lightly built than its larger cousins, although was still a powerful animal, and retained relatively long arms with three clawed fingers. It also possessed a small but distinctive head crest, accompanied by small, pointy brow horns.

{@i Yutyrannus} was covered in a thick layer of feathers, and these are preserved in some of its fossils. These feathers were undoubtedly used for insulation in the chilly Yixian Formation environment, but also perhaps for camouflage. As the largest predator currently known from Yixian, {@i Yutyrannus} is thought to have preyed on a variety of potential food items including ceratopsians, sauropods, therizinosaurs, hadrosaurs, ankylosaurs, and other theropods. It is presumed to be the arch-predator of the Yixian food chain.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: The first {@i Yutyrannus} fossils found were a near complete adult specimen associated with two smaller {@i Yutyrannus}, with one at least eight years younger than the adult. This association is unlikely to be chance and the assemblage probably represents an adult with its large (but still immature) offspring. The association of these three together suggests that {@i Yutyrannus} reared its young well past the hatchling stage and could indicate that they were group hunters. While still speculation, this hypothesis is supported by research into other large social predators and additional evidence also suggests that some tyrannosaurids probably lived in social or family groups.

We suggest that {@i Yutyrannus} be played as a dominant active predator living in small groups. During colder periods, they should be hunting considerably more to help maintain their energy reserves. Hunting {@i Yutyrannus} should be a deadly threat, able to pursue prey for a long time and potentially coordinate their attacks. When not hunting, they can be resting or be socialising, bickering and playing with each other. Nevertheless, they should opportunistically attack a party if they see them as easy prey.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Yutyrannus} was a tyrannosauroid, a highly diverse group of theropods ranging from 10 ft. long average-sized animals to 40 ft. long giants. They arose in the Middle Jurassic of Asia, and became one of the dominant theropod groups, spreading to modern day North America, across the northern palaeo-continent of Lauraisa. There is currently no record of them from the southern palaeo-continent of Gondwana, excluding perhaps one putative bone from Australia.

{@i Yutyrannus} is the largest dinosaur with preserved feathers, but other larger tyrannosauroids appear to have secondarily lost their full feather coat and replaced them with scales, or perhaps reducing them to a thin covering of small, sparse feathers.

trait.name: Dexterous Aquatic Predator
entries: While submerged in water, the Bahariyan Polycotylid has advantage on Dexterity checks, advantage on Dexterity saving throws, advantage on saving throws to prevent it from being {@condition restrained}, and cannot be knocked {@condition prone}. The Bahariyan Polycotylid can also hold its breath for up to 10 minutes.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If the Bahariyan Polycotylid chooses the attack action, it may make one Swim-by Bite attack and one Paddle Slap attack.

action.name: Swim-by Bite
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 7} to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}13 ({@damage 2d6 + 6}) piercing damage.

action.name: Paddle Slap
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 7} to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}11 ({@damage 2d4 + 6}) bludgeoning damage.

action.name: Stir Mud
entries: If submerged in water, as an action, the Bahariyan Polycotylid can use its paddles to stir up sediment from the riverbed/seabed. For 30 seconds all connected water within 30 ft. becomes clouded with mud, rendering it opaque. A creature submerged in this water is considered {@condition blinded} and heavily obscured.
"POL-E-COH-TEA-LID"

When we approached a small pool, the water was murky and muddy. Practically opaque – couldn't see a thin' through it. The only indication that somethin' was in there were the rollin' splashes in the otherwise calm water. We threw a large pebble in to see if we could spook whatever it was away. The splashes stopped for a bit, then a slick shiny reptilian head poked out of the water to look at us. It almost looked friendly, like a croc crossed with a seal. But the set of nasty pointed teeth interlockin' along its mouth hinted otherwise.

The Bahariyan Polycotylid is a relatively long (>10 ft.) freshwater plesiosaur from the Bahariya Formation, Egypt. We initially included this animal based on its original identification as the cosmopolitan genus {@i Leptocleidus}. However, recent studies noted the lack of leptocleidids in the Bahariya Formation and the reappraisal of these fragmentary specimens to the family Polycotylidae. As the fossil material has not been redescribed since its original study in the 1920s, we will refer to it here as the "Bahariyan Polycotylid".

entries.name: Ecology
entries: Plesiosaurs are relatively morphologically conservative within their group, with streamlined bodies, elongated necks, squat heads, short tails, and four highly modified paddle-like limbs. Polycotylids deviated from this norm however, and had much shorter necks, as well as relatively thin and elongated jaws. This gave them a superficially streamlined crocodile-like appearance, similar to the giant oceanic pliosaurs, which are a group of plesiosaurs adapted to hunt other large marine reptiles. The Bahariyan Polycotylid was, in contrast, much smaller and better suited to life in shallow water. Its occurrence in the Bahariya Formation indicates that it likely ventured into estuaries, freshwater lagoons, and riverways, as well as along the coastal shelf. Its smaller body would have allowed greater mobility in these restricted environments, while its long jaws would have allowed it to easily snap up passing fish or potentially grab small animals from the shoreline.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: While the Bahariyan Polycotylid would have been a prominent predator of fish in the African lagoons and coastal areas, its small size meant it would have been vulnerable to larger aquatic predators. This means it may have been relatively cautious, perhaps using the murky waters as a means of evading attacks or hiding from prey.

We suggest that it be played as a wary animal. Most humanoids should be too large to be considered potential prey, but players entering the water may be considered a disturbance to their feeding or breeding grounds, which could result in an attack – especially if the animal has limited options to escape. If more than one Bahariyan Polycotylid is in the area (especially a mother and large calf), they may attack in a co-ordinated manner, making them much more dangerous to unlucky parties.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: Polycotylids were a globally successful group of plesiosaurs found in deposits throughout the Cretaceous. Their highly modified bodies mean that it is difficult to place them precisely within Plesiosauria, with different phylogenies resolving them in very different positions. The current consensus associates them with similarly highly modified leptocleidids, potentially even as a sibling group.

entries.name: Escaping the Land
entries: For many years, it was theorised that plesiosaurs were capable of limited terrestrial movement. This was largely tied to the idea that they needed to lay eggs on land, like turtles. However, new polycotylid specimens have since demonstrated that they birthed a single, relatively large, infant. The size of their offspring suggests a heavy investment from the parent and could indicate that plesiosaurs continued to nurture their young until maturity. If they did not lay eggs, then it also means that they had little need to come onto land and, given their highly adapted morphology, it is likely that they never willingly left the water.

trait.name: Dexterous Aquatic Predator
entries: While submerged in water, the Bahariyan Polycotylid has advantage on Dexterity checks, advantage on Dexterity saving throws, advantage on saving throws to prevent it from being {@condition restrained}, and cannot be knocked {@condition prone}. The Bahariyan Polycotylid can also hold its breath for up to 10 minutes.

trait.name: Echosnap
entries: The Bahariyan Polycotylid has a blindsight of 40 ft.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If the Bahariyan Polycotylid chooses the attack action, it may make one Swim-by Bite attack and one Paddle Slap attack.

action.name: Swim-by Bite
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 7} to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}13 ({@damage 2d6 + 6}) piercing damage.

action.name: Paddle Slap
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 7} to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}11 ({@damage 2d4 + 6}) bludgeoning damage.

action.name: Stir Mud
entries: If submerged in water, as an action, the Bahariyan Polycotylid can use its paddles to stir up sediment from the riverbed/seabed. For 30 seconds all connected water within 30 ft. becomes clouded with mud, rendering it opaque. A creature submerged in this water is considered {@condition blinded} and heavily obscured.
"POL-E-COH-TEA-LID"

When we approached a small pool, the water was murky and muddy. Practically opaque – couldn't see a thin' through it. The only indication that somethin' was in there were the rollin' splashes in the otherwise calm water. We threw a large pebble in to see if we could spook whatever it was away. The splashes stopped for a bit, then a slick shiny reptilian head poked out of the water to look at us. It almost looked friendly, like a croc crossed with a seal. But the set of nasty pointed teeth interlockin' along its mouth hinted otherwise.

trait.name: Titanic Fighter
entries: Carcharodontosaurus has advantage on attacks against creatures with a size category of Large, Huge, or Gargantuan. Carcharodontosaurus also has resistance to slashing damage.

trait.name: Legendary Resistance (1/day)
entries: If Carcharodontosaurus fails a saving throw, it may choose to succeed it instead.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Carcharodontosaurus chooses the attack action, it may make three Ripping Bite attacks.

action.name: Ripping Bite
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 11} to hit, reach 10 ft., one target. {@h}24 ({@damage 4d8 + 6}) piercing damage.
When a creature is hit by this attack, if it is not already affected by the 'Torn' condition, it gains the 'Torn' condition (see below).

action.name: Condition: Torn
entries: A torn creature has had a large piece of flesh ripped away from its body and is bleeding heavily.

At the start of its turn in combat or every minute outside of combat, the creature must succeed a {@dc 18} Constitution saving throw or take {@damage 3d6} slashing damage. On a successful save they take half as much damage.
This effect persists until one of the following occurs:

items: The creature is healed by at least 25 hit points.
The creature finishes a long rest (do not make saves while resting but begin again if the rest is interrupted).
A {@dc 18} Medicine check is passed on the creature.
A {@spell lesser restoration} spell is cast on the creature.
It dies.

entries: {@i "CAR-CHAR-OH-DON-TOE-SORE-US"} {@b (SHARK TOOTH REPTILE)}

There are some beasts that really do straddle the line between animal and monster. We heard it first – the thunderin' footsteps and gurglin' deep growls. We could feel the sounds deep in our chests. Cowerin' in the undergrowth, we used some subtle magic to mask our scent and a few members of the party whispered prayers to their deities. When we finally glimpsed it through the bushes, we had to hold back our gasps. The towerin' creature was among the peak of predatory perfection. A massive bulk and its maw was encrusted with dried blood – soaked in fact. It must have had a rippin' bite like no other.
{@i Carcharodontosaurus} was a Cretaceous (99-94 million years ago) theropod dinosaur and one of the largest theropods in the fossil record.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Carcharodontosaurus} was an extremely large animal, comparable in size to {@i Tyrannosaurus rex} ({@b page 195}){@i.} It had an enlarged skull which was over 5 ft. long with jaws full of serrated knife-like teeth. Its eyes were positioned laterally, giving it an excellent range of vision, but compromising its binocular eyesight slightly.

While it shared its environment with another large carnivore, {@i Spinosaurus} ({@b page 75}), it is likely that these animals were niche partitioned. This means that they relied on different resources for survival and probably did not directly compete with each other for food. This was partially because {@i Carcharodontosaurus} was not a permanent resident of the Bahariya environment, and may have spent more time hunting in the dryer scrubland surrounding the mangroves.

{@i Carcharodontosaurus} was likely a generalist hunter, meaning that it fed on anything it could bring down or scavenge. Evidence suggests it was capable of lifting animals or chunks of meat weighing up to 1750 lb. Potential prey from the Bahariya Formation included immature sauropods, hadrosaurs, other theropods, reptiles, and washed-up fish.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: As a large carnivore, {@i Carcharodontosaurus} would have spent most of the day resting, and less time searching for food. Given its size, it would not have been able to hide from prey, and likely relied on chasing down slower-moving animals. We recommend that it be run as a pursuit hunter, which will chase prey over a long distance. When not hunting or resting it should be curious of, but not automatically hostile to, players if given a wide berth.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Carcharodontosaurus} was a member of the Carcharodontosauridae. This was a sub-group of the Allosauroidea, the group that includes {@i Allosaurus} ({@b page 197}). Carcharodontosaurids were medium-to-large sized theropods which included many giant species such as {@i Carcharodontosaurus, Concavenator} ({@b page 119}), {@i Giganotosaurus}, {@i Acrocanthosaurus} and {@i Meraxes}. They have been found globally in the Early-Middle Cretaceous, frequently occupying the role of arch-predators, and are considered a highly-successful group.

trait.name: Immutable Stature
entries: Paralititan is immune to being {@condition frightened} or knocked {@condition prone}. It has advantage on Strength saving throws, and any saving throw to resist being {@condition paralyzed} or {@condition poisoned}. However, it automatically fails any Dexterity saving throw.
Non-magical bludgeoning, piercing, and slashing attacks have no effect on it as its hide is far too thick. Attacks from Huge, Gargantuan, and Colossal creatures bypass this immunity.

trait.name: Bellowing Call
entries: As a bonus action, Paralititan may let out a bellowing call. This is a deep guttural rumble that shakes the very core of other creatures. Each other non-Paralititan creature within 60 ft. must succeed a {@dc 16} Wisdom saving throw or be {@condition frightened} of Paralititan for 1 minute. They may repeat this save at the end of their turn and on a successful save are immune to the effect for 24 hours.

action.name: Rear Up
entries: As an action, Paralititan can rear up onto its hind limbs. If it does, its speed is reduced to 0 ft. and it is able to use its Almighty Stomp attack until it is no longer rearing up.
If Paralititan takes the attack action, or makes an attack of opportunity as a reaction, it lands on all fours and it ceases rearing up.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Paralititan chooses the attack action, it may make two Huge Stomp attacks. Alternatively, it may make a single Almighty Stomp attack if it is rearing up.

action.name: Huge Stomp
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 11} to hit, reach 10 ft., one target. {@h}28 ({@damage 4d8 + 10}) bludgeoning damage.
A creature hit by this attack must succeed a {@dc 16} Strength saving throw or be knocked {@condition prone}.

action.name: Almighty Stomp
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 15} to hit, reach 10 ft., up to two targets. {@h}75 ({@damage 10d10 + 20}) bludgeoning damage. Paralititan must be rearing up to use this attack.

Any creature hit by this attack is knocked {@condition prone}. All other non-sauropod creatures within 30 ft. of Paralititan must succeed a {@dc 16} Strength saving throw or also be knocked {@condition prone}. Any non-magical metal, stone, or wooden object not being carried or worn hit by this attack is shattered and destroyed.
{@i "PAH-RA-LEE-TIE-TAN"} {@b (TIDAL GIANT)}

The whole time we were wadin' through the river delta, we could see towerin' sauropods in the distance. They were flankin' the edges of the delta mostly, feedin' on the lush vegetation without venturin' too close to the muddy waters. I reckoned they could easily stride through the water and walk on the sand, but gettin' caught in the wrong patch of mud could be lethal. Still, their long necks gave 'em ample reach to feed – archin' over the waterways. Funny really, they seemed unbothered by most of the big predators. I guessed they could pack a punch if somethin' got too close.
{@i Paralititan stromeri} (Stromer's Tidal Giant) was a large member of the Titanosauria, a group of sauropods which included the largest known land animals to ever live.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Paralititan} is a relatively poorly known sauropod despite its discovery dating back to 1912. Recorded by German palaentologist Ernst Stromer, the original material was among the large fossil collection destroyed in World War II. It was not until 2000 when a team of palaeontologists discovered new material. Initially, it was estimated to weigh approximately 65 tonnes with a projected length of 85 ft. although it has been estimated to have been as light as 33 tonnes. While neither estimate would make it a match for the very largest titanosaurs, it was considerably bigger than any other animal known from the Bahariya Formation.

Like all sauropods, {@i Paralititan} was a herbivore. Due to its enormous size, it must have been a non-selective feeder. This means it was not choosy about what it ate, ingesting whatever plant matter (including early grasses) it could without any sort of preference.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Paralititan}'s sheer size gave it enormous strength and healthy adults would have been safe from most predators. However, like for modern elephants, some predators (such as {@i Carcharodontosaurus} ({@b page 69})) would have been a potential threat if attacking in numbers, and especially to younger animals. Sauropods are frequently portrayed as being gentle giants. However, for many of them this is likely far from the truth, as modern large herbivores can be extremely aggressive and territorial (e.g., rhinos and buffalo). While sauropods may not have hunted for food, it is very possible that they would have met anything large enough to be a potential threat with a violent response.

Like most sauropods, {@i Paralititan} was not an involved parent. Juveniles grew rapidly and were capable of feeding without care (precocial). However, there is strong evidence that hatchlings of various ages grouped together for safety.

We recommend {@i Paralititan} be played as a gregarious animal, moving in herds while constantly feeding. Unfamiliar party members may spook them, resulting in unpredictable and aggressive behaviour, such as mock charges, displays of strength, or all-out attacks. When unthreatened they should be relatively calm animals.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: Titanosaurs were an unusual group of animals which arose in the Early Cretaceous to become the dominant sauropod across the world and survived up the end Cretaceous extinction. They were members of the Macronaria, a group of long limbed large and skulled sauropods including {@i Brachiosaurus} and {@i Giraffatitan} ({@b page 133}). Like brachiosaurs, their forelimbs were elongated, giving them a tall-chested giraffe-like profile. Titanosaurs possessed short, blocky reduced toes; with most of the foot being made up of the metacarpals (knuckle bones). In some species the toes were completely absent.

All other non-sauropod creatures within 30 ft. of Paralititan must succeed a {@dc 16} Strength saving throw or also be knocked {@condition prone}. Any non-magical metal, stone, or wooden object not being carried or worn hit by this attack is shattered and destroyed.
{@i "PAH-RA-LEE-TIE-TAN"} {@b (TIDAL GIANT)}

The whole time we were wadin' through the river delta, we could see towerin' sauropods in the distance. They were flankin' the edges of the delta mostly, feedin' on the lush vegetation without venturin' too close to the muddy waters. I reckoned they could easily stride through the water and walk on the sand, but gettin' caught in the wrong patch of mud could be lethal. Still, their long necks gave 'em ample reach to feed – archin' over the waterways. Funny really, they seemed unbothered by most of the big predators. I guessed they could pack a punch if somethin' got too close.
{@i Paralititan stromeri} (Stromer's Tidal Giant) was a large member of the Titanosauria, a group of sauropods which included the largest known land animals to ever live.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Paralititan} is a relatively poorly known sauropod despite its discovery dating back to 1912. Recorded by German palaentologist Ernst Stromer, the original material was among the large fossil collection destroyed in World War II. It was not until 2000 when a team of palaeontologists discovered new material. Initially, it was estimated to weigh approximately 65 tonnes with a projected length of 85 ft. although it has been estimated to have been as light as 33 tonnes. While neither estimate would make it a match for the very largest titanosaurs, it was considerably bigger than any other animal known from the Bahariya Formation.

Like all sauropods, {@i Paralititan} was a herbivore. Due to its enormous size, it must have been a non-selective feeder. This means it was not choosy about what it ate, ingesting whatever plant matter (including early grasses) it could without any sort of preference.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Paralititan}'s sheer size gave it enormous strength and healthy adults would have been safe from most predators. However, like for modern elephants, some predators (such as {@i Carcharodontosaurus} ({@b page 69})) would have been a potential threat if attacking in numbers, and especially to younger animals. Sauropods are frequently portrayed as being gentle giants. However, for many of them this is likely far from the truth, as modern large herbivores can be extremely aggressive and territorial (e.g., rhinos and buffalo). While sauropods may not have hunted for food, it is very possible that they would have met anything large enough to be a potential threat with a violent response.

Like most sauropods, {@i Paralititan} was not an involved parent. Juveniles grew rapidly and were capable of feeding without care (precocial). However, there is strong evidence that hatchlings of various ages grouped together for safety.

We recommend {@i Paralititan} be played as a gregarious animal, moving in herds while constantly feeding. Unfamiliar party members may spook them, resulting in unpredictable and aggressive behaviour, such as mock charges, displays of strength, or all-out attacks. When unthreatened they should be relatively calm animals.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: Titanosaurs were an unusual group of animals which arose in the Early Cretaceous to become the dominant sauropod across the world and survived up the end Cretaceous extinction. They were members of the Macronaria, a group of long limbed large and skulled sauropods including {@i Brachiosaurus} and {@i Giraffatitan} ({@b page 133}). Like brachiosaurs, their forelimbs were elongated, giving them a tall-chested giraffe-like profile. Titanosaurs possessed short, blocky reduced toes; with most of the foot being made up of the metacarpals (knuckle bones). In some species the toes were completely absent.

trait.name: Crocodile Mimic

trait.name: Rostral Dermal Pressure Sensors

action.name: Multiattack

action.name: Snapping Jaw
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 9} to hit, reach 10 ft., one target. {@h}27 ({@damage 5d6 + 10}) piercing damage.

A creature hit by this attack is {@condition grappled} (escape {@dc 16}) and pulled 5 ft. closer to Spinosaurus. While a creature is grappled by this attack, Spinosaurus cannot attack another target with its Snapping Jaw.

action.name: Hooked Claw
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 9} to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}21 ({@damage 3d8 + 8}) slashing damage.
A creature hit by this attack can be moved up to 5 ft. in any direction by Spinosaurus (no save allowed).
{@i "SPY-NO-SORE-US"} {@b (SPINE REPTILE)}

We had gotten complacent seein' so many of these giant spinos lazin' by the rivers. Despite their massive size and vicious teeth'n'claws, they seemed uninterested in us. Preferrin' to stand motionless in the water with their snouts submerged in the flow, occasionally snappin' their colossal jaws. When they did, they hurled their heads upwards and dragged huge fish out of the water to feast on. It was a sight to behold every time. All was fine passing them, so long as we didn't get too close while they was feedin'. At least that's what we thought... until we came across a territorial male.

{@i Spinosaurus} was the largest member of the Spinosauridae and is known from the Cretaceous Bahayria, Chenni, Kem Kem, and Echkar formations of North Africa. {@i Spinosaurus} is undoubtedly the most hotly debated dinosaur of the 21st century.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Spinosaurus} was a very large carnivore at about 45 ft. in length. It had an elongated snout filled with sharp peg-like teeth, a long muscular neck, and muscular forearms sporting large curving claws. The vertebrae on its back had extremely elongated spines, extending over 3 ft. above the backbone, forming a long sail along its back. Its tail was modified into a tall oar-like shape. Its hind legs were shorter than in most theropods, making it appear much squatter, with unusually long toes and less curved toe claws, similar to many waterbirds, suggesting that it had webbed toes.

{@i Spinosaurus} is one of the few dinosaurs known to be well adapted for hunting fish. Its long snout and rounded pointed teeth are perfect for spearing passing fish. Its large claws functioned well as fishhooks and its short, long toed feet made it a capable wader in shallow water. Its diet would have included a wide variety of fish including giant sawfish and sharks. Like many otherwise specialised carnivores, it would have been opportunistic and fed upon smaller land-dwelling prey or scavenged from carcasses where possible.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Spinosaurus} is now believed to have been a large, shoreline wader, hunting fish from the edge of rivers and beaches. It may have been a more capable swimmer than other theropods and able to easily move throughout estuaries in search of prey. It would have likely avoided other large carnivores where possible.

When running {@i Spinosaurus}, we recommend it be treated as a hunter that stuck to the shoreline of rivers or coasts. It should have a great deal of patience, being willing to stand still for long periods waiting for prey to approach. It may be relatively safe for a party to pass by, so long as it is given a wide enough berth. However, this seemingly peaceful animal may be waiting for a player to stray too close to the shoreline, giving it the opportunity to strike.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Spinosaurus} is the largest known spinosaurid, a group of highly successful Cretaceous predators found across the world from Brazil to China. This group included well-known animals such as the South American {@i Irritator} and the British {@i Baryonyx}. Spinosaurids are distinguished by their unusually elongated snouts filled with rounded teeth, enlarged claws on their forelimbs, and elongated spines on the vertebrae in many species.

entries.name: An Ever-changing Picture
entries: While {@i Spinosaurus} has been known since the early 1900s, the original specimen was destroyed in World War II. This has led to a great deal of debate and speculation over its morphology, biology, and ecology. New fossil discoveries in the 2010s provided a wealth of information regarding the animal and revealed it to be highly unusual in its proportions, which resulted in many years of debate over how it looked and lived. It has been reconstructed as a four-legged ambush predator, a wader, an entirely aquatic animal, a nearly 22 ton giant, and a more manageable 8 tons. What we present here is the most up-to-date summary of its morphology, but it serves as an excellent reminder that palaeontology is an ever-evolving science where new discoveries frequently upend our understanding of an animal.

trait.name: Aquatic
entries: Stomatosuchus has advantage on Stealth checks while submerged in water. It can hold its breath for up to 30 minutes.

trait.name: Size Matters
entries: Stomatosuchus will not attack a creature of Medium size or larger, unless to defend itself or its feeding grounds.

trait.name: Throat Pouch
entries: A creature within Stomatosuchus' throat pouch is {@condition restrained} and takes {@damage 2d4} bludgeoning damage at the start of each of their turns. At the end of its turn, the restrained creature may attempt to escape by succeeding on a {@dc 14} Strength check.
If Stomatosuchus falls below half hit points, it will regurgitate any creature in its throat pouch. If a creature dies while in the throat pouch, Stomatosuchus swallows it.

trait.name: Crocodilian Immune System
entries: Stomatosuchus is resistant to poison damage and immune to the {@condition poisoned} condition.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Stomatosuchus chooses the attack action, it may make one Needle Maw attack and one Tail Swipe attack.

action.name: Needle Maw
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 8} to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}13 ({@damage 2d8 + 4}) bludgeoning damage.

If Stomatosuchus' throat pouch is empty, it may attempt to swallow a Small or Tiny creature hit by this attack. The target must succeed a {@dc 14} Strength saving throw or be swallowed into Stomatosuchus' throat pouch.

action.name: Tail Swipe
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 7} to hit, reach 10 ft., one target. {@h}15 ({@damage 2d8 + 6}) bludgeoning damage.
{@i "STOH-MAH-TOE-SOO-CUS"} {@b (MOUTH CROCODILE)}

The riverways weren't just filled with monstrous threats and titanic predators. Believe it or not, there were a few docile beasties too. One of the most surprisin' was a giant croc that gently swam the riverways. It snapped at the water and raised its mouth high, gullet swollen. We could see lil' fish tails flickin' out the sides of its mouth and water poured through the gaps in its needle-like teeth as it squeezed its throat.
{@i Stomatosuchus} is a poorly understood crocodile-like animal with an unusual appearance, known only from a single specimen discovered in the 1920s.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: Little is known about {@i Stomatosuchus'} morphology beyond it possessing an unusual U-shaped head, 30 times longer than it was deep. Its upper jaw was full of closely packed thin pointed teeth, whereas its lower jaw is thought to have been toothless. It has been suggested by some that it possessed a deep throat pouch, but this remains speculative. The skull was extremely large, suggesting an animal 32 ft. in length.

The diet of {@i Stomatosuchus} is debatable. It lacks the large conical teeth seen in most other large crocodylomorphs and some have suggested it was a planktonic feeder, using a throat pouch to push water through its thin teeth. However, an alternative suggestion is that it was a predator of small fish and used its thin teeth in unison with the broad jaw to trap them, similar to the closely-related {@i Laganosuchus} and the more distantly-related {@i Aegisuchus}, both of which have more complete fossils{@i.} As planktonic filter-feeding requires highly-specific feeding structures, we think that a small vertebrate based diet is more plausible.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Laganosuchus} and {@i Aegisuchus} are thought to have been ambush predators, snapping passing fish or small animals and {@i Stomatosuchus} probably was too. Its jaws were remarkably slender, and therefore it would not have been able to easily hold large struggling prey, preferring smaller morsels or scavenging where possible.

We suggest {@i Stomatosuchus} be played as a patient predator, willing to wait several hours for prey to come within striking distance. Many playable races should be too large to be considered prey, but smaller races could be susceptible to attack. As long as these smaller party members do not approach the water, {@i Stomatosuchus} should be relatively benign.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: Stomatosuchids are thought to be part of the Neosuchia, the group of crocodylomorphs more closely related to modern crocodiles than other groups such as the notosuchians. The group remains poorly understood and it has been suggested they belong to the Eusuchia, the "true crocodiles", but without more material there remains a great deal of mystery surrounding {@i Stomatosuchus'} phylogenetic placement.

Like so many of the Bahariya fossils, {@i Stomatosuchs}' type specimen was described in the 1920s by Ernst Stromer, and was later destroyed in World War II by allied bombers. No new material has been found since, and the only information we have is from Stromer's published figures.

entries: Stomatosuchus gulps huge volumes of water daily as it filters out tiny fish to devour. In doing so, it occasionally swallows small gemstones or trinkets that wash into the water. Roll a {@dice d6} and consult the list below, Stomatosuchus gains the corresponding effect.

3 - Holy Symbol. Stomatosuchus gains immunity to radiant damage.
4 - Gold Coins. Stomatosuchus' throat pouch deals an additional {@damage 1d6} bludgeoning damage and it regurgitates 100 gp when slain.

5 - Wand Shard. Stomatosuchus knows the {@spell Firebolt}, {@spell Ray of Frost}, or {@spell Thunderclap} cantrip. It can cast them as though it were level 5, its spell attack modifier is +4 and any saving throw from its cantrips has a DC of 14.
6 - Ticking Clock. Stomatosuchus loses its Size Matters ability and becomes exceptionally aggressive. It also constantly makes a faint ticking sound.

trait.name: Ambush Predator
entries: Balaur has advantage on Stealth checks.

trait.name: Flutter-Leap
entries: Balaur can jump up to 30 ft. and is immune to falling damage.

action.name: Pair Bonding
entries: As an action, Balaur may give another allied Balaur within 60 ft. advantage on that Balaur's attacks and saving throws until the start of this Balaur's next turn.

action.name: Twin Claw Grapple
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 3} to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}7 ({@damage 2d4 + 2}) piercing damage.
A creature hit by this attack must succeed a {@dc 10} Strength saving throw or be {@condition grappled} by Balaur.
{@i "BAL-OR"} {@b (BALAUR, A DRAGON IN ROMANIAN MYTHOLOGY)}

As we pushed through the thick undergrowth, we entered a small clearin'. Light beamed down through the canopy revealin' a handful of nests sat on by some lil' theropods. We were immediately greeted by goose-like hissin'. Very angry lil' thin's. When they pounced, we learnt just how sharp their sickle claws are – and that they had two on each foot for twice the pain!
{@i Balaur} is a small and unusual theropod that is an excellent example of the difficulty in clarifying the relationships of fossil animals.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Balaur} is only known from a partial skeleton that lacks several major parts, including its skull. This makes reconstructing {@i Balaur} difficult, but researchers estimate that it was up to 8 ft. long and weighed about 33 lb. It was clearly an unusual animal as it had remarkably stocky feet with a pair of large dromaeosaur-like sickle claws on each foot. Dromaeosaurs like {@i Velociraptor} ({@b page 183}) and {@i Utahraptor} ({@b page 181}) hold these claws vertically, but {@i Balaur}'s could only be held flat, making it flat footed. Despite having wing-like forelimbs, it is also thought to be fully flightless, with a non-functional reduced third finger on each hand.

Without its skull, determining {@i Balaur}'s diet is difficult. Due to its dromaeosaur-like claws, it was originally classified as part of that group and therefore assumed to be carnivorous. However, later investigations noted that its relative bulkiness, large swept back pubic bone (suggestive of a big gut, but present in all paravian theropods), and robust limbs could indicate that it was herbivorous. A more recent study in 2015 focused on {@i Balaur}'s phylogeny, but also addressed its ecology and suggested that it was part of an evolutionary grade containing both herbivores and omnivores. Based on the more predatory elements of its morphology, they argued it was likely omnivorous.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: With so much debate around {@i Balaur}, it is hard to pin down much of its behaviour. Still, we can make some suggestions based on similar animals. We know it was probably ground-dwelling and may have lived in pairs or small groups. It would likely have foraged for fruits and berries, while also taking down suitably sized prey using its stocky build to overpower them. With this in mind, we recommend that {@i Balaur} be played as an alert and curious animal. It may approach a party or player out of interest or in search of food and, as an island dweller, it may not view humanoids as a threat at all. However, a lone player could find themselves approached by several {@i Balaur} that are much more willing to attack.

trait.name: Twin Spirited
entries: The first time Balaur is reduced to 0 hit points, so long as it used Pair Bonding at least once, or was the target of another Balaur's Pair Bonding, it is revived with full hit points although it has an ethereal ghost-like appearance. Its Twin Claw Grapple attack now deals necrotic damage instead of piercing.

trait.name: Crop
entries: Hatzegopteryx has a large throat pouch called a crop that is able to hold a Medium or smaller sized creature. Creatures inside this crop are {@condition restrained} and suffer {@damage 4d4} bludgeoning damage at the start of their turn. There is only enough air within the crop to breathe for 1 minute.
While a creature is inside its crop, Hatzegopteryx's fly speed is reduced by half, it cannot dash, and it will generally attempt to flee a fight to keep its meal.
A swallowed creature may attempt to escape by making a {@dc 17} Strength check. On a success, they are regurgitated. Alternatively, if Hatzegopteryx falls below 100 hit points, they are regurgitated.

trait.name: Evasive Flying
entries: If Hatzegopteryx makes a Dexterity saving throw while flying to take only half damage from an attack, spell, or effect, it instead takes no damage if the saving throw is succeeded.
Hatzegopteryx cannot make Dexterity saving throws against attacks, spells, or effects that originated from within its crop.

trait.name: Legendary Resistance (1/day)
entries: If Hatzegopteryx fails a saving throw, it may instead choose to succeed.

trait.name: Swallow
entries: So long as Hatzegopteryx has at least 100 hit points, as a bonus action it may attempt to swallow a creature that is lying {@condition prone}. The creature must succeed a {@dc 16} Strength or Dexterity saving throw (their choice) or be swallowed into Hatzegopteryx's crop.

trait.name: Heavy Flier
entries: Hatzegopteryx can only begin flying by using its Quad Launch Legendary Action, or if it is falling. Hatzegopteryx is also immune to thunder damage.

action.name: Grounded Multiattack
entries: If Hatzegopteryx chooses the attack action while standing on the ground, it may make one Beak Spear attack and two Beak Flurry attacks.

action.name: Beak Spear
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 8} to hit, reach 10 ft., one target. {@h}30 ({@damage 5d8 + 8}) piercing damage.
A creature hit by this attack must succeed a {@dc 12} Constitution saving throw or be knocked {@condition prone} and {@condition stunned} until the end of their next turn.

action.name: Beak Flurry
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 12} to hit, reach 10 ft., one target. {@h}12 ({@damage 2d6 + 5}) piercing damage.
A target hit by this attack must succeed a {@dc 12} Strength saving throw or be knocked {@condition prone}.

legendary.name: Quad Launch
entries: Hatzegopteryx launches itself into the air. Every other creature within 10 ft. of Hatzegopteryx must succeed a {@dc 18} Strength saving throw or be knocked {@condition prone}. Hatzegopteryx then begins to fly and must fly 20 ft. in a straight line (either horizontally, or vertically up).
Hatzegopteryx cannot use this Legendary Action next battle round.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Balaur}'s phylogeny has been the subject of debate since its discovery. Initially it was described as a dromaeosaurid based on similarities in shoulder girdle, forearm shape, and its sickle-like claws, but was considered highly unusual within the group for its reduced third finger, fused wrists, and fused ankles. These peculiarities were assumed to be a result of its island isolation.

Several subsequent studies challenged this identification, noting features that are unheard-of in dromaeosaurs, but common in avialans (the non-bird dinosaurs that are most closely related to birds). After discussions about other occurrences of dromaeosaur-like sickle claws in modern birds, it was determined to most likely be an avialan, with secondary flightlessness. This is a trait known to evolve in other island-dwelling birds, such as the dodo and kākāpō.
{@i "HATS-EGG-OP-TEAR-IX"} {@b (HAȚEG BASIN WING)}

We were told that it wasn't safe to explore these islands, but we didn't care for the stories. We should'a listened... We figured that the biggest critters would be towards the centre of the islands, and it'd be safe to skirt the edges. But after only a few hours walkin' along the coastline that hypothesis was flattened. The beast descended from the sky faster than any dragon I've ever seen and with more lethal ferocity than the nastiest rex. It downed two members of our crew on impact, snatched up one of our guides and took straight back off. I saw it swallow the poor sod whole. The entire attack took seconds and in just as much time we were all scrabblin' for the treeline as it circled above. We should'a listened.

{@i Hatzegopteryx} is a member of the Azhdarchidae, the giant, long-necked pterosaurs. It is one of the largest and heaviest flying animals known and is a close relative of the famous giant pterosaur {@i Quetzalcoatlus} ({@b page 165}).

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Hatzegopteryx} was an enormous pterosaur, with a wingspan estimated to be between 33 and 39 ft. It was also extremely heavy for a flying animal, weighing somewhere in the range of 440-550 lb., at least 10 times heavier than the heaviest flying birds alive today. Like other azhdarchid pterosaurs, it had long limbs and was very tall when standing, with forelimbs longer than its hindlimbs, giving it a sloping back. Its neck was elongated in comparison to most pterosaurs, but it was shorter and stockier than other azhdarchids. Its skull was massive, perhaps 5 ft. long, but again more robustly built than animals like {@i Quetzalcoatlus}.

{@i Hatzegopteryx} stood at about the height of a giraffe and towered above the (often) dwarfed fauna of the Hațeg Island. As it could fly, it was not affected by the resource limitations of the island and did not undergo insular dwarfism, making it the largest carnivore present by far. Azhdarchids were once assumed to be fish specialists that skim or dip fed, however the consensus now is that they were largely terrestrial animals that spent most of their time walking on the ground, hunting like giant storks. {@i Hatzegopteryx} would stalk the undergrowth, catching prey and killing it with its powerful beak. Its prey would have included any animal small enough for it to grab and swallow whole, but it may also have been able to skewer and pull apart slightly larger prey and carrion.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: As the dominant predator on the island, {@i Hatzegopteryx} would have had little to fear from other animals once fully grown. It was likely a relatively solitary animal that nested on the ground and may have had at least some level of parental care, although to what degree is still speculative.
Combat between {@i Hatzegopteryx} may have involved striking each other with their jaws or side-on blows using their powerful necks.

We recommend that {@i Hatzegopteryx} be played as an animal with little fear that would be highly curious of new creatures or objects in its territory. It would not hesitate to strike potential prey, including most humanoids. When faced with a party, it may choose to snatch and swallow a single target, before simply flying away. This makes it a particularly lethal threat to players. It can be portrayed moving in a bobbing, ungainly fashion (perhaps similar to a marabou stork).

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: Azhdarchid pterosaurs are a diverse group, with members ranging from relatively small animals (10 ft. wingspans) to giants like {@i Quetzalcoatlus} and {@i Hatzegopteryx} (>33 ft. wingspans). The group first arose around the middle of the Cretaceous and survived right up until the end-Cretaceous extinction. In this time, they spread globally and azhdarchids (or possible azhdarchids) are known from every continent except Antarctica.

trait.name: Sweeping Defence
entries: When hit by a melee attack, Magyarosaurus may use its reaction to make a Neck Bludgeon attack against the creature that attacked it.

trait.name: Pint-Sized Powerhouse
entries: Magyarosaurus has advantage on Strength saving throws.

action.name: Rear Up
entries: As an action, Magyarosaurus can rear up onto its hind limbs. If it does, its speed is reduced to 10 ft. and it is able to use its Mighty Stomp attack until it is no longer rearing up.
If Magyarosaurus takes the attack action, or makes an attack of opportunity as a reaction, it lands on all fours and it ceases rearing up.

action.name: Neck Bludgeon
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 8} to hit, reach 10 ft., one target. {@h}15 ({@damage 2d6 + 8}) bludgeoning damage.

action.name: Mighty Stomp
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 8} to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}33 ({@damage 6d6 + 12}) bludgeoning damage. Magyarosaurus must be rearing up to use this attack.
A creature hit by this attack must succeed a {@dc 14} Strength saving throw or be knocked {@condition prone}.
{@i "MAG-YAHR-OH-SORE-US"} {@b (}MAGYAR REPTILE{@b )}

As we pushed through the undergrowth, keepin' outa sight of the sky, we encountered dozens of strange island species, includin' many that were miniature versions of their mainland cousins. One of the most strikin' examples we came across were some titanosaurs. Hidden between the trees were lumberin' longnecks, usually towerin' over the treeline – but these ones were about the size of a horse, albeit much longer. Pretty calm thin's really. I guess they didn't have many land-based predators botherin' 'em in the forest.

{@i Magyarosaurus} was an exceptionally small titanosaur, a group famous for including the largest land animals ever to live. It is a dramatic example of the effect of living in a restricted environment, as it is one of the smallest sauropods discovered.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Magyarosaurus} was not only a modestly-sized dinosaur in general, but one of the smallest sauropods. It was tiny in comparison to its giant relatives like {@i Paralititan} ({@b see page 71}), at a measly 20 ft. long and about 1 tonne in weight. It was so small that initially all remains were assumed to have been from juveniles, however research in 2010 provided strong evidence that the animals were indeed simply tiny adults (at least by sauropod standards). This makes {@i Magyarosaurus} one of the most compelling examples of insular dwarfism among the Hațeg Island fauna.

entries: Although tiny, it is likely that {@i Magyarosaurus} behaved much like other titanosaurs. It would have lived in a herd, constantly moving to find new food. trait.name: Sweeping Defence
entries: When hit by a melee attack, Magyarosaurus may use its reaction to make a Neck Bludgeon attack against the creature that attacked it.

trait.name: Pint-Sized Powerhouse
entries: Magyarosaurus has advantage on Strength saving throws.

trait.name: Dynamic Camouflage (2/day)
entries: As an action, Magyarosaurus can cast {@spell Invisibility} at 2nd level on itself without requiring components or a spell slot.

action.name: Rear Up
entries: As an action, Magyarosaurus can rear up onto its hind limbs. If it does, its speed is reduced to 10 ft. and it is able to use its Mighty Stomp attack until it is no longer rearing up.
If Magyarosaurus takes the attack action, or makes an attack of opportunity as a reaction, it lands on all fours and it ceases rearing up.

action.name: Neck Bludgeon
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 8} to hit, reach 10 ft., one target. {@h}15 ({@damage 2d6 + 8}) bludgeoning damage.

action.name: Mighty Stomp
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 8} to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}33 ({@damage 6d6 + 12}) bludgeoning damage. Magyarosaurus must be rearing up to use this attack.
A creature hit by this attack must succeed a {@dc 14} Strength saving throw or be knocked {@condition prone}.
{@i "MAG-YAHR-OH-SORE-US"} {@b (}MAGYAR REPTILE{@b )}

As we pushed through the undergrowth, keepin' outa sight of the sky, we encountered dozens of strange island species, includin' many that were miniature versions of their mainland cousins. One of the most strikin' examples we came across were some titanosaurs. Hidden between the trees were lumberin' longnecks, usually towerin' over the treeline – but these ones were about the size of a horse, albeit much longer. Pretty calm thin's really. I guess they didn't have many land-based predators botherin' 'em in the forest.

trait.name: Bladed Osteoderms
entries: Any creature that hits Struthiosaurus with a melee attack suffers {@damage 1d4} slashing damage.

action.name: Defensive Stance
entries: As an action, Struthiosaurus may take up a defensive stance, lowering its head and limbs, only allowing its armoured back to be attacked. This stance lasts until it attacks. Struthiosaurus gains resistance to non-magical bludgeoning, piercing, and slashing damage while in a defensive stance.

action.name: Armoured Tackle
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 3} to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}2 ({@damage 1d4}) slashing damage plus 2 ({@damage 1d4}) bludgeoning damage.
{@i "STROO-TH-EE-OH-SORE-US"} {@b (OSTRICH LIZARD)}

After the first night, we stumbled across another species of dinosaur – quite literally. Our unaware wizard stepped over a shrub 'n' tripped on somethin'. Turns out it was a miniature nodosaur, one of the armoured dinosaurs. Adorable lil' thin' about the size of a large dog. Short, stout, and covered in spikey osteoderms – a creature after me own heart. It shuffled away into the brush and, thankfully, our wizard escaped with all but his pride bruised.

{@i Struthiosaurus} is a small member of the nodosaurids, a somewhat contested group of heavily armoured dinosaurs that with the ankylosaurids make up the Ankylosauria. Its name comes from the bird-like morphology of its braincase.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Struthiosaurus} was small for a nodosaur, being only 10 ft. long and weighing around 600 lb. As a nodosaurid, it was less heavily armoured than the more well known ankylosaurids and lacked a tail club, but was nonetheless still formidably defended. Its armour was made up of multiple individual sharp blade-like and domed osteoderms (bony structures in the skin) that dotted its flanks.

{@i Struthiosaurus} was a herbivorous dinosaur with coarse leaf-shaped teeth. Wear patterns on these teeth suggest that it fed mostly on tough plants. Ankylosaurs appear to have had long, flexible tongues which they would have used to strip low lying fresh plant growth. This specialisation towards ground level feeding allowed them to avoid competition with taller sauropods and hadrosaurs.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: While famous for their armour, nodosaurs are now thought to have been relatively inert animals (unless attacked). Micro-CT analysis of {@i Struthiosaurus}' skull reveal that it had less sophisticated senses than other dinosaurs, which could indicate that it was a solitary animal relying entirely on its armour for defense. This sensory loss also suggests that there were few direct predators of an adult {@i Struthiosaurus}, allowing it to reduce resource investment in its senses. It was probably oblivious to non-native threats in the same manner that dodos were reported to have been.

We suggest {@i Struthiosaurus} be played as a relaxed, almost lackadaisical animal, living a peaceful solitary life. If approached by a party it should react with mild curiosity or disinterest, but if attacked should default to a defensive stance, striking with its tail or tackling opponents.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Struthiosaurus} is usually identified as a nodosaurid, one of the main two groups of Ankylosauria. This group are identified as more lightly-built animals, with flexible, bladed tails rather than the giant, clubbed tails in animals such as {@i Zuul} ({@b page 188}). They appeared in the Middle Jurassic and survived until the end-Cretaceous extinction. Nodosaurs were a widespread group and a major part of the herbivore population across Laurasia (North America, Europe, and Asia) and South America. However, a 2023 study suggested that Nodosauridae was not a natural group and instead put {@i Struthiosaurus} within its own clade, the Struthosauridae.

trait.name: Stout Body
entries: Zalmoxes' unusually stout body makes it remarkably tough for its size. It has resistance to non-magical bludgeoning damage.

trait.name: Docile and Cowardly
entries: Zalmoxes will not attack unless provoked. It will flee from creatures it perceives as predators.

action.name: Beaked Bite
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 3} to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}4 ({@damage 1d6 + 1}) piercing damage.
{@i "ZAL-MOCKS-EES"} {@b (ZALMOXIS, A DACIAN GOD)}

By far the most common dinosaurs we encountered on that bizarre island were the miniature ornithopods. They were awfully calm considerin' we was so much bigger than 'em. I only saw 'em spook when they were out of cover – obviously knowin' what circled above, or when someone made lots 'o noise and commotion. Otherwise, they seemed to just eat and make lil' chirpin' sounds at each other.
{@i Zalmoxes} is a small bipedal ornithopod and has been used as the textbook example of insular dwarfism in the fossil record.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Zalmoxes} is thought to have reached about 8-10 ft. in length and weighed 100-110 lb. It was a stout animal with relatively long forelimbs and a robust skull. Its teeth were simple and leaf shaped, set in a mouth tipped with a sharp beak.

{@i Zalmoxes} is quite small for its group, the Rhabdodontidae. This group of herbivorous ornithopod dinosaurs includes many large animals such as {@i Rhabdodon} and {@i Iguanodon} ({@b page 135}), which could reach up to 20 ft. in length. This size difference, and the occurrence of {@i Zalmoxes} on Hațeg island, has led to it being the textbook example of insular dwarfism. However, a study in 2012 challenged this, arguing that the primitive {@i Zalmoxes} represents the ancestral size range for this group and that the other members instead evolved to be larger.

As a herbivore, {@i Zalmoxes}' strong jaws and powerful muscles allowed it to slice plants in a cutting action. Like many ornithopods, it was a capable chewer, allowing it to process a variety of tough plants effectively. However, its narrow head suggests that it may have instead been a selective feeder, picking out softer nutritious plant material. Either way, this allowed it to occupy a separate ecological niche on Hațeg Island from the larger herbivores, avoiding competition.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: While {@i Zalmoxes} had a strong bite, it was ultimately a small animal that would likely have run from threats, rather than fight. There is some evidence that rhabdodontids lived in herds and {@i Zalmoxes} may have moved in groups as a means of protection. We recommend that {@i Zalmoxes} be played as a very skittish animal. Herds should include sentries who frequently scan for threats and will sound an alarm if any are spotted. The sight of a party may cause them to flee, and they should only attack if cornered or trapped. Their stout body and timid nature would make them excellent options for taming as livestock.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: The Rhabdodontidae were a group of very successful relatively primitive ornithopods that included animals like {@i Iguanodon} and {@i Hypsilophodon}. Rhabdodonts are currently exclusively European, as species previously considered rhabdodonts from Australia ({@i Muttaburasaurus}) and America ({@i Tenontosaurus}) have recently been reclassified as a sibling taxon (closely related but not part of the true group).

The creature can repeat this saving throw at the end of each of its turns to end the {@condition frightened} condition (until it re-enters combat).
This curse can be removed by a {@spell Lesser Restoration} spell or similar effect, or ends after 24 hours.
