trait.name: Charming Display (2/day)
entries: Cratoavis can cast the spell {@spell Charm Person} with a spell save DC of 15. A charmed humanoid must attempt to provide food to Cratoavis.

trait.name: Swooping Flight
entries: So long as Cratoavis is flying and it moved last turn, its AC is increased by 3 and it does not provoke attacks of opportunity when it moves out of reach from an enemy.

action.name: Toothed Peck
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 2} to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}2 ({@damage 1d2 + 1}) piercing damage.
{@i "KRAH-TOE-A-VIS"} {@b (CRATO BIRD)}

Among the sun-scorched branches and chirpin' of crickets, we saw a small flash of vivid colour accompanied by a wonderful chorus of squarkin'. We stopped for a moment to see whether we could identify what it was. Once we spotted it, we glimpsed the most beautiful bird I've ever seen. It was performin' some sorta strange dancin' display in the treetops, hoppin' from branch to branch. It was absolutely hypnotic to watch.
{@i Cratoavis} is an enantiornithian, a group of birds (avialans) from the Early Cretaceous that shared many similarities with modern birds, but were their own distinctive group.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Cratoavis} looks quite similar to a modern bird. It stands out from its living cousins by having small peg-like teeth and short claws on its wings, giving it a characteristic 'prehistoric' appearance. Enantiornithians occupied a variety of ecological niches, but {@i Cratoavis} was likely an insectivore feeding on small insects it caught in trees or on the ground. It may have also opportunistically fed on fruits, berries, or even carrion, but peg/needle-like teeth are usually associated with eating insects.
{@i Cratoavis} had modified tail feathers that formed a twinned set of elongate feather vanes. These were undoubtedly a signalling device and were probably used in elaborate mating displays.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Cratoavis} bears such a strong similarity to modern birds that it is reasonable to expect it to behave in a similar fashion. Given its small size, it was likely a relatively vulnerable animal and would have been extremely wary of being approached by potential predators. We recommend that {@i Cratoavis} retreat when approached but possess curiosity about anything novel in its environment. Parties are highly unlikely to be attacked by {@i Cratoavis} unless they knowingly or unknowingly damage their nests.

entries.name: Exceptional Preservation
entries: When people think of fossils, they frequently think of large complete skeletons, isolated bones or partial fragments. Soft tissue like muscles, skin, feathers etc. are assumed to have degraded long before fossilisation can occur, yet there are numerous cases of exceptionally well-preserved fossils showing soft tissues. {@i Cratoavis}' fossil is one such example. Not only is the specimen fully articulated (joints still connected) and almost entirely complete, it also preserves exquisite impressions of its feathers and other soft tissues.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Cratoavis} belongs to the group Enantiornithes. This is a group of feathered theropods that looked very similar to modern birds, but retained primitive features like teeth and wing claws. They were an extremely successful group originating in the Early Cretaceous, with 80 species spread across every continent, bar Antartica, before dying out at the end-Cretaceous extinction. Despite their success, we are still a bit uncertain as to their relationships. While they are universally placed in Avialae (the group including modern birds and their closest relatives such as {@i Archaeopteryx} or {@i Balaur} ({@b page 84})), others go further and identify them as primitive members of the "true birds" Aves.

entries: Cratoavis can cast the spell {@spell Charm Person} with a spell save DC of 15. A charmed humanoid must attempt to provide food to Cratoavis.

entries: So long as Cratoavis is flying and it moved last turn, its AC is increased by 3 and it does not provoke attacks of opportunity when it moves out of reach from an enemy.

trait.name: Global Adventurer
entries: If Cratoavis successfully charms a member of the party, it will then begin to follow the party if able, keeping a reasonable distance from them (>50 ft.) for most of the time.
Unless it is regularly fed, once per day it will attempt to perform a Charming Display to either a party member or another humanoid it encounters.

entries: If Cratoavis is slain, its body does not decay or deteriorate in any way, and it instead enters a state of preservational stasis. While in this state, it is unconscious and can be revived by receiving any healing from a magical source.

trait.name: Death by Yucca
entries: Any creatures composed of or based on plants have advantage on attacks against Ludodactylus.

trait.name: Piscivorous Snatch Feeder
entries: Ludodactylus has advantage on attacks against creatures fully or partially submerged in water. If Ludodactylus is flying, it does not provoke attacks of opportunity when it moves out of an enemy's reach.

trait.name: Quad Launch (Ludodactylus)
entries: If not already flying, as a bonus action, Ludodactylus can launch itself into the air. Every other creature within 5 ft. of Ludodactylus must succeed a {@dc 13} Strength saving throw or be knocked {@condition prone}. Ludodactylus then begins to fly and must fly 15 ft. in a straight line (either horizontally, or vertically up).
Ludodactylus can only begin flying by using this ability, or if it is falling.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: When Ludodactylus selects the attack action, it may make two attacks with its Toothed-Beak Bite and one Projectile Vomit attack.

action.name: Toothed-Beak Bite
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 7} to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}10 ({@damage 4d4}) piercing damage.

action.name: Projectile Vomit
entries: {@atk rw} {@hit 6} to hit, range 15 ft., one target. {@h}6 ({@damage 1d6 + 3}) acid damage.

action.name: Snatch
entries: As an action, so long as it is flying, Ludodactylus may attempt to snatch an item being held by a creature or it may attempt to snatch a small item attached to a player's belt (i.e. a potion or small bag). The target creature must succeed a {@dc 11} Strength saving throw or Ludodactylus plucks the item from them and holds it in its beak.
{@i "LOO-DOH-DACK-TAL-US"} {@b (PLAY FINGER)}

We finally had a chance to take a decent rest near the lakeside. It was a beautiful day, so I took me pencil'n'pad out to sketch the view and some of the dartin' pterosaurs. They were soaring just above the water, dippin' their heads in as they go to snatch up fish. Those long pointed teeth look like the perfect fit for it. I was half-way through me sketch when a few of 'em took interest. One of the blighters snatched the pencil right out of my hands! Flew off and dropped it in the lake when it realised it couldn't eat it, the bastard. Good thing I always keep spares.
{@i Ludodactylus} is a relatively large anhanguerid pterosaur, slightly bigger than {@i Tupandactylus} ({@b page 109}){@i.}

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Ludodactylus} was a large pterosaur with a wingspan of approximately 13 ft. Like other anhanguerids, it possessed low convex crests on its upper and lower jaws, but uniquely, it also had a tall {@i Pteranodon}-like crest jutting out of the back of its skull, making its head highly ornamented.

Anhanguerids are well known to be piscivorous (fish-eating), and {@i Ludodactylus} had elongate teeth that formed a "fish trap" cage at the end of its snout, an adaptation to trap fleeing slippery prey. It would likely have hunted by flying low over the water's surface, plucking fish on the wing, or perhaps wading through shallows with its snout dipped in the water, waiting for fish to come too close.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Ludodactylus} would have primarily been associated with water and are unlikely to have travelled far inland, unless following a large river system or migrating to new coastal regions. Large oceanic pterosaurs have been known to form sizable colonies and it is possible that {@i Ludodactylus} also formed nesting colonies.

An individual {@i Ludodactylus} should be hesitant to approach players unless drawn by food, in which case it is likely to become more aggressive. Groups of {@i Ludodactylus} may mob players in a similar manner to modern herring gulls (albeit much, {@i much} bigger). They lacked the tools to hunt and devour anything other than Tiny prey, so would not try to hunt Small or larger party members. Nevertheless, they were certainly capable of delivering an extremely nasty bite. If a party encounters a colony, particularly one that is nesting, the animals should be much more aggressive. They would threaten intruders with raucous calls and displays before attacking, with individuals dive-bombing enemies from above with teeth or, worse, vomit and faeces.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: As mentioned above, {@i Ludodactylus} is an anhanguerid pterosaur, which are a group that are typically characterised by crests on their snouts and had a global distribution in the Early-Late Cretaceous. They are part of the larger pterosaur family Ornithocheiroidia, which includes the toothless Pteranodonia (like {@i Pteranodon}). Ornithocheiroidia (like {@i Ornithocheirus}) are distant relatives of the giant azhdarchids (such as {@i Quetzalcoatlus,} {@b page 165}).

entries.name: Moments in Time
entries: We usually develop our interpretations of the lives of extinct animals by examining and interpreting their fossils. These interpretations can vary depending on current evidence or researchers' differing opinions. However, sometimes we find "smoking gun" evidence, where exceptional fossils preserve an interaction irrefutably. {@i Ludodactylus} shows one such "smoking gun", with the original specimen fossilised with a frayed yucca tree leaf protruding through its jaws. This animal clearly died from this injury, as the leaf pierced through its mouth, preventing it from feeding and likely causing an infection. The frayed edge indicates that the animal tried to dislodge the leaf by scraping it against the ground. It probably snatched the leaf out of the water thinking it was a fish, a misjudgement that modern seabirds still make today.

trait.name: Tiny Squiggly Wriggly
entries: So long as Tetrapodophis is in water, attacks against it are made at disadvantage, it has advantage on Dexterity saving throws, and if it would take half damage after succeeding a Dexterity saving throw it instead takes none.

trait.name: Re-interpretation
entries: You may opt for Tetrapodophis to have a burrowing speed of 10 ft. instead of a swim speed.

action.name: Vicious Tiny Nip
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 1} to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}1 (1) piercing damage.
{@i "TEH-TRA-POD-OH-FIS"} {@b (FOUR-FOOTED SNAKE)}

We were wadin' through some shallow water, searchin' for edible aquatic shoots to supplement our rations. Seemed like a good idea at the time, since we were gunna be headin' into the desert soon. Turns out stickin' ya hands where you can't see ain't always a great idea. One of our party got bit by some squiggle lil' thin'. I only caught a glimpse of it, but it seemed to be more like a long lizard than a snake. We had our hearts in our throats for a few minutes after that, waitin' to see whether it had been venomous.
{@i Tetrapodophis} (literally four-footed snake) is a snake-like Early Cretaceous squamate (the group containing lizards, snakes, and mosasaurs), but is not a true snake.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Tetrapodophis} was a small reptile measuring about 8 inches in length. It had an extremely elongated snake-like body but retained four small, although fully functional, legs. Originally, {@i Tetrapodophis} was suggested to be a burrowing animal as the short tail and squat head were thought to match burrowing lizards and snakes. It was also argued that it was unlikely to be an aquatic animal as it lacks a paddle-like tail or dense bones. However, within a year of the original description of {@i Tetrapodophis}, a second research team examined the fossils and found that the morphology of its legs were comparable to some aquatic lizards and this, among other things, identified the animal as being well-adapted for an aquatic lifestyle. This makes it much more probable that {@i Tetrapodophis} was at least semi-aquatic and would have lived or hunted along the shores of the Crato Formation waters.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Tetrapodophis} was a carnivore and fed on fish, insects, and small reptiles (and possibly unguarded eggs), as demonstrated by the small bones found in its stomach. When playing {@i Tetrapodophis}, it should be a largely skittish animal, fleeing into water if disturbed. If a party member catches one and attempts to manhandle it, it should be quick to bite to make its captor drop it, then flee.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: When it was initially described, scientists argued that {@i Tetrapodophis} was the oldest member of the snake family and that its small legs showed it to be a transitional animal in the evolution of snake leg loss. However, later researchers re-examined the fossil and argued it belonged in the group Dolichosauridae. This is the sibling group (closest relatives) to snakes, largely consisting of small aquatic lizards that may have had similar lifestyles to modern sea snakes. While this identification is currently the most widely accepted, it's important to remember that science is constantly being tested and revised. This means that further research into {@i Tetrapodophis} may reveal new unsuspected details about its phylogeny.

entries.name: The Legality of Fossil Research
entries: The original {@i Tetrapodophis} material is suspected to have been illegally exported from Brazil. Unlike "Ubirajara" ({@b page 110}), however, there has been no commitment to return {@i Tetrapodophis} and the original work has not been redacted. Scientists are required to conduct ethical research, but they, in turn, also expect museums to ethically source and legally house specimens in the first place. Nevertheless, all research teams that examined this specimen after the first have included Brazilian palaeontologists, which is a requirement to study Brazilian vertebrate fossils under Brazilian law.

If a party member catches one and attempts to manhandle it, it should be quick to bite to make its captor drop it, then flee.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: When it was initially described, scientists argued that {@i Tetrapodophis} was the oldest member of the snake family and that its small legs showed it to be a transitional animal in the evolution of snake leg loss. However, later researchers re-examined the fossil and argued it belonged in the group Dolichosauridae. This is the sibling group (closest relatives) to snakes, largely consisting of small aquatic lizards that may have had similar lifestyles to modern sea snakes. While this identification is currently the most widely accepted, it's important to remember that science is constantly being tested and revised. This means that further research into {@i Tetrapodophis} may reveal new unsuspected details about its phylogeny.

entries.name: The Legality of Fossil Research
entries: The original {@i Tetrapodophis} material is suspected to have been illegally exported from Brazil. Unlike "Ubirajara" ({@b page 110}), however, there has been no commitment to return {@i Tetrapodophis} and the original work has not been redacted. Scientists are required to conduct ethical research, but they, in turn, also expect museums to ethically source and legally house specimens in the first place. Nevertheless, all research teams that examined this specimen after the first have included Brazilian palaeontologists, which is a requirement to study Brazilian vertebrate fossils under Brazilian law.

trait.name: Storm Flyer
entries: Tupandactylus has resistance to lightning and thunder damage.

trait.name: Focused on Flirting
entries: If Tupandactylus performed a Dazzling Display or Thundering Display, it has disadvantage on Perception checks for the next 1 minute.

trait.name: Quad Launch (Tupandactylus)
entries: If not already flying, as a bonus action, Tupandactylus can launch itself into the air. Every other creature within 5 ft. of it must succeed a {@dc 12} Strength saving throw or be knocked {@condition prone}. Tupandactylus then begins to fly and must fly 20 ft. in a straight line (either horizontally, or vertically up).
Tupandactylus can only begin flying by using this ability, or if it is falling.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Tupandactylus chooses the attack action, it may make two attacks with its Beak-Slash attack.

action.name: Beak-Slash
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 6} to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}8 ({@damage 1d10 + 3}) slashing damage.

action.name: Dazzling Display
entries: As an action, Tupandactylus can perform a Dazzling Display. Performing the display gives Tupandactylus advantage on all Charisma saving throws and checks for the next 1 minute.

Additionally, any creature within 20 ft. and line of sight of Tupandactylus must try and avert their gaze. They must succeed a {@dc 12} Dexterity saving throw or have disadvantage on all Charisma saving throws and checks for the next 1 minute.
{@i "TOO-PAN-DACK-TAL-US"} {@b (TUPAN FINGER)}

Some of the bigger pterosaurs were nestin' just up from the water's edge. Seemed to be mostly out of harms way, but still pretty exposed. That didn't seem to phase 'em though, since they had numbers on their side. They also had these huge intimidatin'
crests, nearly as big as me, and were prancin' about, swayin' their heads from side to side. They were so engrossed in their display, that they didn't even notice us pass by.
{@i Tupandactylus} was a medium-to-large sized tapejarid pterosaur with a wingspan of between 10 to 13 ft.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Tupandactylus'} most distinctive trait was its large vertical sail-like crest. This was exceptionally large on some individuals, raising the question of the function of such an elaborate structure. While it has been suggested to be some sort of steering aid, a crest that size would have likely made flight more difficult. Instead, it is much more likely that the crest developed as a means of sexual selection, with only the healthiest individuals able to grow a large cumbersome crest while maintaining the ability to fly well. It would have also been a means for both males and females to communicate through visual displays.

Like most Cretaceous pterosaurs, {@i Tupandactylus} was toothless, however it also had a relatively short jaw. This has led to a great deal of debate as to the most likely diet of this animal. It now appears that {@i Tupandactylus} was herbivorous, specifically frugivorous (fruit eating) much like modern toucans. The Crato Formation was laid down in a lagoonal/lake environment with freshwater influence and {@i Tupandactylus} would likely have been a transitional member of the fauna, primarily living and feeding in woodland areas where it foraged for food, perhaps coming to the water to drink and socialise.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Tupandactylus} was likely a primarily ground forager, moving through the undergrowth in search of food, as its huge crest would have hindered it feeding in trees. Flight would likely have been a means of moving between foraging spots or escaping predators. We recommend that {@i Tupandactylus} be played as a somewhat skittish animal foraging alone or in small flocks of a handful of individuals. They should be on the watch for potential threats and likely to take flight when threatened. They could be played more aggressive if they are nesting or defending a particularly fruitful feeding patch.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Tupandactylus} is one of the largest members of the Tapejarine. This is a group of Cretaceous pterosaurs found across the world and is most well-known for including members with large sail-like crests like {@i Tapejara} and, of course, {@i Tupandactylus}. Tapejarines were also close relatives of the giant azdarchid pterosaurs.

entries.name: Pycnofibres
entries: Since the 1950s, evidence of a fuzzy coat has been found on some pterosaurs, called pycnofibres. Several pterosaur fossils have a full-body covering of these hair-like filaments. The relationship between pycnofibres and feathers has been a topic of much debate, but a recently discovered {@i Tupandactylus} specimen preserves pycnofibre pigment that is extremely similar to those found in feathers, strongly suggesting that pycnofibres are a structure derived from feathers. This has profound implications for when feathers arose and just how many animals in our past may have been feathered.

trait.name: Filamentous Integument Mane
entries: Ubirajara has advantage on Stealth checks while in foliage and, when hit by an attack, can use its reaction to reduce any bludgeoning or piercing damage it would take from that attack by half. Ubirajara also gains a +5 bonus to Intimidation checks.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Ubirajara chooses the attack action, it may make three Gnashing Nip attacks.

action.name: Gnashing Nip
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 3} to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}3 ({@damage 1d4 + 1}) piercing damage.
{@i "OOH-BI-RAH-JAR-AH"} {@b (LORD OF THE SPEAR)}

Skirtin' around the edge of the woods to bypass the thickest undergrowth, we spotted somethin' particularly bizarre. There was this lil' fuzzy theropod dinosaur, screechin' at the top of its lungs and bouncin' around a fallen log. It had a few massive quills projectin' from its shoulders that look like you wouldn't want 'em stuck in your arm. I think it was performin' some kind of matin' dance, but whatever it was doin', we gave it a wide berth.

This compsognathid dinosaur from Brazil was described in 2020, with the name "Ubirajara", however as discussed below, controversy regarding the exporting of the fossil to Germany led to the manuscript being pulled. This means that the name "Ubirajara" is invalid, but following the recommendation of a study published in 2023, we will refer to the animal as "Ubirajara" informally with the name in inverted commas without italics until a formal name is assigned.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: "Ubirajara" was a relatively medium sized compsognathid, at about 3 ft. long. This group of small theropods are usually conservative in their morphology, that is they have three fingered arms, walk on hind legs, gracile bodies, long tails, and a 'generic theropod' appearance. This conservative morphology is indicative of a generalist predator/scavenger lifestyle (feeding on insects, small reptiles, mammals, fish, etc.), as it shows no feeding specialisations beyond predation.

"Ubirajara" is exceptional in that it had a dense mane of feathers, which likely would have given the animal quite a fluffy appearance. This was accompanied by a pair of long filaments on each shoulder, jutting out like rods. The function of these structures is not known but it has been suggested they may have had some role in sexual display.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Small carnivores tend to be curious, but skittish, creatures (e.g., foxes and mongooses). We suggest playing "Ubirajara" as a quick and alert animal, curious about parties but maintaining its distance. Medium and larger sized creatures/humanoids should be considered too big to hunt under normal circumstances, but weak/sickly Small sized creatures/humanoids could be seen as a potential prey. "Ubirajara" did not have the tools to pin down and wrestle prey, so we suggest that it nips and claws at prey, wearing it down before moving in for the kill.

Alternatively, given "Ubirajara"'s elaborate filamentous coat, it could also be played like a bird of paradise – leaping and dancing around while fluttering its display feathers. Territorial control could then be its primary concern.

entries.name: The Legality of Fossil Exportation
entries: Many countries have strict laws about fossil exportation. Brazil prohibits most fossil exportation, but fossils from Brazil are nevertheless available in numerous fossil shops and even museums. This shows an industrial-scale illegal exportation operation and a thriving black market for Brazilian fossils. "Ubirajara" became the cornerstone for the discussion of this issue after the fossil was held in Karlsruhe, Germany after evidence arose that it was illegally exported. Within days of the research being published, it became the focal point of social media backlash, eventually leading to the paper being withdrawn and (2 years later) the agreement to repatriate the fossil to Brazil.

This is an {@i extremely} complex political subject and there are competing views as to the validity of national laws on the international stage, the de-colonisation of science, the impact on scientific publication and funding, the impact on local tourism, the classification of fossils as georesources, the infrastructure required to safely store type specimens, and, of course, the morality of the issue. We fully support the repatriation of "Ubirajara" and other culturally significant fossils to their country of origin.
[Redacted]

entries: As an action, Ubirajara can attempt to return back to its home. It opens an interplanar portal 10 ft. in front of itself. The portal leads to a destination that it considers to be home anywhere in the multiverse and remains open for 1 minute or until Ubirajara falls unconscious. The portal is big enough to allow creatures up to a size of Large through it.

trait.name: Dorsal Sail
entries: As a bonus action, Arizonasaurus can flush its sail with blood, giving it advantage on Intimidation checks for 1 minute.

trait.name: Sail Reliant Reptilian Metabolism
entries: During the day, Arizonasaurus is resistant to cold damage. During the night, Arizonasaurus is resistant to fire damage.

action.name: Bite and Shake
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 5} to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}8 ({@damage 1d8 + 4}) piercing damage. A creature hit by this attack must succeed a {@dc 14} Strength saving throw or take an additional {@damage 1d6} slashing damage and, if they are Medium or smaller, are {@condition grappled} until the start of Arizonasaurus's next turn.
{@i "AR-RAH-ZONE-AH-SORE-US"} {@b (ARIZONA REPTILE)}

Occasionally, the doldrum of the scrub'n'dry rock was broken by large, fanned sails dottin' the horizon. We learnt pretty quickly to give these a wide berth, as the beasties that they was attached to were vicious predators. Although sluggish at first, these thin's could dash right up and deliver some really nasty bites. If you gotta pass em, do it in the early mornin' when they're baskin' to warm 'emselves.

{@i Arizonasaurus} is a Middle Triassic (243 million years ago) reptile from the Moenkopi Formation in Arizona, which was once an ancient floodplain. As a member of the Archosauria, it is a distant relative of modern crocodiles and the large Triassic predator {@i Postosuchus}. One of its distinguishing features was a large sail running down its back.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Arizonasaurus} was a quadrupedal (walking on all four legs) archosaur with hyper-elongated vertebral spines, extending up to 2 ft. above the animal's back, forming a sail-like structure similar to that seen in animals like {@i Dimetrodon} or {@i Spinosaurus} ({@b page 75}). It was a robust, powerful animal, with an estimated length of 10 ft. and height of 1.5 ft. (excluding the sail). Unlike many early reptiles, the limbs of {@i Arizonasaurus} were held beneath its body, giving it an erect posture.

{@i Arizonasaurus} was carnivorous, with a mouth full of blade-like teeth, and was one of the larger predators of the Middle Triassic (although smaller than several other members of its group). It would probably have predated upon pretty much anything smaller than itself that it could catch.

The function of {@i Arizonasaurus}' sail has been debated for many years and suggested uses include sexual display, threat display, and thermal regulation. The latter is plausible, given the hot climate of the Middle Triassic, and {@i Arizonasaurus} could have flushed blood into its sail to cool itself or orientated it perpendicular to the sun to warm itself in the early mornings.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: As a large predator for its day, {@i Arizonasaurus} likely spent much of its time conserving energy and resting. When hunting, it probably ambushed prey with a burst of speed, but likely also consumed carrion when available. {@i Arizonasaurus} shared its environment with other larger carnivores and would have been cautious about lingering near a carcass for too long.

We suggest playing {@i Arizonasaurus} as a patient predator, willing to rest for extended periods. This can give the impression that it is a sedate animal, but an attack could come at any moment. Smaller party members should be more at risk, as they are seen as easier prey.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Arizonasaurus} is a member of Poposauroidea, the cosmopolitan group that includes the huge {@i Postosuchus}. These animals were the dominant terrestrial predators in the Triassic, before the rise of the dinosaurs. Sails were a common feature of a subgroup of poposaurs called ctenosauriscids, of which {@i Arizonasaurus} is a member.
As the earliest member of Poposauroidea, its occurrence in the Middle Triassic pushes the divergence of crocodiles and dinosaurs from Archosauria back by millions of years.
This confirms an Early Triassic split of these groups and makes {@i Arizonasaurus} an important species for understanding the evolution of both crocodiles and dinosaurs.

trait.name: Dorsal Sail
entries: As a bonus action, Arizonasaurus can flush its sail with blood, giving it advantage on Intimidation checks for 1 minute.

trait.name: Sail Reliant Reptilian Metabolism
entries: During the day, Arizonasaurus is resistant to cold damage. During the night, Arizonasaurus is resistant to fire damage.

trait.name: Arizona Heat
entries: Arizonasaurus radiates incredible heat. Any creature that starts its turn within or comes within 20 ft. of Arizonasaurus immediately suffers {@damage 1d6} fire damage. This is increased to {@damage 2d6} if they are within 5 ft. of Arizonasaurus. Additionally, Arizonasaurus is immune to fire damage.
If there are multiple Arizonasaurus persisting in a region with this ability, that region will experience a prolonged drought.

action.name: Bite and Shake
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 5} to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}8 ({@damage 1d8 + 4}) piercing damage. A creature hit by this attack must succeed a {@dc 14} Strength saving throw or take an additional {@damage 1d6} slashing damage and, if they are Medium or smaller, are {@condition grappled} until the start of Arizonasaurus's next turn.
{@i "AR-RAH-ZONE-AH-SORE-US"} {@b (ARIZONA REPTILE)}

Occasionally, the doldrum of the scrub'n'dry rock was broken by large, fanned sails dottin' the horizon. We learnt pretty quickly to give these a wide berth, as the beasties that they was attached to were vicious predators. Although sluggish at first, these thin's could dash right up and deliver some really nasty bites. If you gotta pass em, do it in the early mornin' when they're baskin' to warm 'emselves.

{@i Arizonasaurus} is a Middle Triassic (243 million years ago) reptile from the Moenkopi Formation in Arizona, which was once an ancient floodplain. As a member of the Archosauria, it is a distant relative of modern crocodiles and the large Triassic predator {@i Postosuchus}. One of its distinguishing features was a large sail running down its back.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Arizonasaurus} was a quadrupedal (walking on all four legs) archosaur with hyper-elongated vertebral spines, extending up to 2 ft. above the animal's back, forming a sail-like structure similar to that seen in animals like {@i Dimetrodon} or {@i Spinosaurus} ({@b page 75}). It was a robust, powerful animal, with an estimated length of 10 ft. and height of 1.5 ft. (excluding the sail). Unlike many early reptiles, the limbs of {@i Arizonasaurus} were held beneath its body, giving it an erect posture.

{@i Arizonasaurus} was carnivorous, with a mouth full of blade-like teeth, and was one of the larger predators of the Middle Triassic (although smaller than several other members of its group). It would probably have predated upon pretty much anything smaller than itself that it could catch.

The function of {@i Arizonasaurus}' sail has been debated for many years and suggested uses include sexual display, threat display, and thermal regulation. The latter is plausible, given the hot climate of the Middle Triassic, and {@i Arizonasaurus} could have flushed blood into its sail to cool itself or orientated it perpendicular to the sun to warm itself in the early mornings.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: As a large predator for its day, {@i Arizonasaurus} likely spent much of its time conserving energy and resting. When hunting, it probably ambushed prey with a burst of speed, but likely also consumed carrion when available. {@i Arizonasaurus} shared its environment with other larger carnivores and would have been cautious about lingering near a carcass for too long.

We suggest playing {@i Arizonasaurus} as a patient predator, willing to rest for extended periods. This can give the impression that it is a sedate animal, but an attack could come at any moment. Smaller party members should be more at risk, as they are seen as easier prey.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Arizonasaurus} is a member of Poposauroidea, the cosmopolitan group that includes the huge {@i Postosuchus}. These animals were the dominant terrestrial predators in the Triassic, before the rise of the dinosaurs. Sails were a common feature of a subgroup of poposaurs called ctenosauriscids, of which {@i Arizonasaurus} is a member.
As the earliest member of Poposauroidea, its occurrence in the Middle Triassic pushes the divergence of crocodiles and dinosaurs from Archosauria back by millions of years.
This confirms an Early Triassic split of these groups and makes {@i Arizonasaurus} an important species for understanding the evolution of both crocodiles and dinosaurs.

entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 5} to hit, reach 5 ft., up to two targets. {@h}8 ({@damage 1d6 + 5}) slashing damage.

action.name: Horn Charge
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 8} to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}18 ({@damage 3d6 + 8}) piercing damage. Centrosaurus may only use this attack if it moved at least 20 ft. in a straight line before reaching the target on this turn.
{@i "SENT-TROW-SORE-US"} {@b (POINTED REPTILE)}

Some herbivores are much more aggressive than others. We had setup a small, fixed camp on the edges of a large forest, hoping to eventually establish a permanent settlement later. The area was perfect – clear flat shrubland with a small stream for fresh water. After a week of work, one afternoon we were alerted to an approachin' herd of ceratops. They were bearin' down on us at speed, hootin' and honkin'. Within moments, a bull had charged through our camp, trampling four tents and injurin'
two labourers. Evidently, this was their clearin' and they weren't happy to share.

{@i Centrosaurus} is a member of the horned dinosaurs (Ceratopsidae) from the Late Cretaceous (75 million years ago) of Canada and a smaller relative of the famous {@i Triceratops}. Its fossils have been discovered in colossal numbers within the Dinosaur Park Formation.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Centrosaurus} was a medium sized ceratopsid, measuring approximately 18 ft. long and weighing up to 2.5 tonnes. Its most distinctive feature was its skull, which bore the typical ceratopsian parrot-like beak and broad neck frill. This frill was ringed by small bones along its edge (epioccipitals) and the highest four were curved into crescent moon shapes. It had three horns, with two being small brow horns, and the third an enormous nasal horn. These horns were covered in a keratinous sheath that may have ended in a sharp point.

{@i Centrosaurus}, like all horned dinosaurs, had a fundamentally herbivorous diet. With a powerful beak and a shearing bite, it was well suited for snipping off tough plant material, browsing on ferns or stripping branches of their leaves. {@i Centrosaurus} lived in the temperate forests surrounding the swampland of the Dinosaur Park Formation of Cretaceous North America, browsing the shrubbery alongside a wide variety of other dinosaurs including ankylosaurs, other ceratopsians, many small theropods, and large tyrannosaurs.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Centrosaurus} lived in sizable herds and may have taken part in large seasonal migrations. Living in herds would have provided protection and increased the availability of reproductive partners. Like many other ceratopsians, while the horns would have been excellent defensive weapons they were also used for display and intraspecific (same species) squabbles. Like many ceratopsids (excluding {@i Triceratops}), {@i Centrosaurus}' frill was relatively thin and would not have provided defence against the powerful bite of a tyrannosaur and was primarily for display.

We suggest that {@i Centrosaurus} be played as a social animal, moving in groups. They should be hostile to an approaching party, but should not immediately attack. Instead, threat displays and false charges should be made to attempt to drive intruders away before a fight begins.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Centrosaurus} is a member of the Ceratopsidae, one of the most successful groups of Cretaceous dinosaurs and well-known for their impressive horns and large frills. Originating in Asia, this group spread throughout Asia and North America with a couple of fragments reported from Europe. Broadly speaking, the group has been divided along the lines of their frill and horn morphology (although there are exceptions). Animals with short frills, short brow horns and long nose horns belong to the Centrosaurinae (e.g., {@i Centrosaurus}) and those with long frills, long brow horns and short nose horns were in Chasmosaurinae (e.g., {@i Triceratops}).

Ceratopsids horns and frills can have a lot of variation within a single genus, sometimes leading scientists to misinterpret a variant as a different genus or species. {@i Centrosaurus} was part of a famous taxonomic (naming) debate, whereby some scientists proposed that its fossils were actually from a genus erected in the 1800s called {@i Monoclonius}, and did not warrant their own genus name (called a junior synonym). Eventually a consensus emerged, that the two were indeed the same genus, however the original material used to describe {@i Monoclonius} was insufficient, rendering the name invalid. We now exclusively use {@i Centrosaurus} to describe this animal.

trait.name: Mysterious Hump: Micro-thermoregulation
entries: When hit by an attack or when failing a saving throw, Concavenator can use its reaction to gain resistance to fire or cold damage until the end of the turn.

trait.name: Mysterious Hump: Display
entries: Concavenator has advantage on Charisma checks.

trait.name: Mysterious Hump: Fatty Storage
entries: Concavenator only needs to drink once per month.

trait.name: Muscular Forearms
entries: Concavenator has advantage on any Strength checks to avoid being grappled.

action.name: Combined Claw and Bite
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 7} to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}9 ({@damage 2d6 + 2}) slashing damage plus 9 ({@damage 2d6 + 2}) piercing damage.
{@i "CON-CAH-VEN-AH-TOR"} {@b (CONCAVE HUNTER)}

It took us forty minutes to realise that we were bein' hunted. By that point, an encounter was inevitable. We setup a defensive position to stand our ground and braced ourselves for battle. Before long, we were bein' circled by three meat-eatin' dinosaurs. Although your typical theropods with wicked claws and sharp teeth, these ones also had a strange lil' hump over their hips. Didn't have the time to ponder what those might be for though, as moments after I spotted 'em, they charged to attack all at once.

{@i Concavenator} is a small carcharodontosaurid from the Early Cretaceous (130 million years old) Las Hoyas fossil site in Spain and is a relative of the African giant {@i Carcharodontosaurus} ({@b page 69}).

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Concavenator} was relatively small for a carcharodontosaurid, at most 20 ft. long and weighing about 700 lb. It had elongate three clawed forelimbs, a robust but elongate skull, and a distinctive "hump" situated above its pelvis. This hump is created by elongated vertebral spines, creating a tall concave structure. While similar structures are seen in {@i Spinosaurus} ({@b page 75}) and some other carcharodontosaurids, they form large sails made of numerous vertebrae. {@i Concavenator} is unique in that it utilises only two vertebrae to create a small hump and its function remains uncertain. It has been suggested to be a form of display, a method of heat regulation, and even analogous to a camel hump. Of these, a display structure seems the most plausible.

When the fossil was first discovered, the authors noticed a series of strange knobs on its forearm. They suggested that these were anchoring points for quills, similar to the tail of {@i Psittaccosaurus} ({@b page 53}). However, further analysis revealed that the bone was deformed by taphonomy (the processes of fossilisation) and these were actually normal muscle attachment points.

{@i Concavenator} was a carnivorous dinosaur and while less massive than its relatives, is still the largest theropod known from the Las Hoyas site. This site formed around a lake which would have been a water source for many species including iguanodontians, other smaller theropods, mammals and reptiles, and {@i Concavenator} was the arch-predator of this locality.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Concavenator} would have been a light, agile predator capable of running down prey. Like other carcharodontosaurids, it may have lived in small groups and used the hump on its back as a means of signaling to other {@i Concavenator}. This might be sexual signaling, warnings of danger, or even intimidation displays.

We recommend that {@i Concavenator} be played as a large social carnivore – similar to a lion, resting long hours, highly communicative, and very agile when hunting. It should see all humanoids up to Large in size as prey and might be drawn to settlements to hunt livestock or pick off unwary travelers.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: While carchodontosaurids are best known for being giants, many of the earlier animals were much smaller. These smaller animals are known from Europe and South America and likely evolved reduced sizes to survive on much smaller prey. This would allow them to occupy a different niche to larger predators, avoiding direct competition.

action.name: Burrowing Dive
entries: As an action, Concavenator may burrow downwards to go deeper underground, preparing to strike its next target. While burrowing deeper underground, it is entirely obscured and cannot attack or be attacked, except when attacking/attacked by another burrowing creature.

On its next turn, Concavenator can burst upwards, unearthing itself and ending its burrowing. If it does so, it has advantage on attack rolls until the end of its turn, but cannot use the Burrowing Dive ability again until the start of its next turn.

entries: Deinocheirus can move through water up to 6 ft. deep without being slowed or having to swim.

trait.name: Pennaceous Display Feathers
entries: Deinocheirus has advantage on Intimidation and Persuasion checks.

trait.name: Mud Raker
entries: If a single creature is hit by both of Deinocheirus' Terrible Claw attacks in a single turn, they suffer an additional {@damage 1d6} poison damage, as the dregged mud from its claws coats their wounds.

trait.name: Grasping Tongue
entries: As a bonus action, Deinocheirus may pick up and wield an item (up to 20 lb.) with its tongue. If that item is a weapon and does not require ammunition, it may make an attack with it as a bonus action on its subsequent turns, although it is not proficient with it.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: When selecting the attack action, Deinocheirus may make two Terrible Claw attacks.

action.name: Terrible Claw
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 7} to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}22 ({@damage 3d12 + 3}) slashing damage. A creature hit by this attack must succeed a {@dc 16} Strength saving throw or drop an item they are wielding.
{@i "DYE-NO-KEIR-RUS"} {@b (HORRIBLE HAND)}

In the fetid swamp, we had the misfortune of havin' to wade through some pretty foul water. This was made all the more unpleasant by a huge oily, fuzzy, hump-backed theropod dinosaur that waded through the water. Thankfully, it was a herbivore, so there didn't appear to be any immediate danger of becomin' lunch. That said, it had some very mighty lookin'
claws and could no doubt rend a person in two fairly easily. For that reason, and the smell, we kept our distance.

{@i Deinocheirus} is a giant ornithomimosaur from the Late Cretaceous (70 million years old) Nemegt Formation of Mongolia. A relative of {@i Gallimimus}, {@i Ornithomimus,} and {@i Struthiomimus}, it is both the largest and most bizarre member of its family.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Deinocheirus} was an enormous ornithomimosaur, a group of otherwise ostrich-like theropods. It was at least 36 ft. long and weighed up to 5 tonnes when fully grown, putting it in the same size category as giant carnivorous theropods like {@i Carcharodontosaurus} ({@b page 69}) or {@i Tyrannosaurus} ({@b page 195}). Its arms were long with extremely large, but blunt, hooked claws. The vertebrae in the centre of its back had fused spines that stuck up, giving the animal a highly distinctive hump or sail (though much smaller than animals like {@i Spinosaurus} ({@b page 75})). Its face was long and narrow with a toothless snout that flared sideways at the tip, giving its jaws a shovel like appearance. Like other ornithomimosaurs, it likely had a full body covering of feathers, and possibly a broad fan of feathers on the end of its tail.

While a theropod, {@i Deinocheirus} was not the stereotypical carnivore. Its blunt hooked claws were well adapted for digging or grasping, allowing it to pull at plants or excavate soil while looking for invertebrates. Its stomach contained gastroliths (stones used to crush plants), as well as fish scales. Its jaw possessed anchor points for a powerful tongue that may have been long and possibly quite mobile. The Nemegt Formation of Mongolia is constituted of mudstone and sandstone sediments from a mixture of fluvial (river), alluvial (floodplain), paludal (marsh), and lacustrine (lake) settings. This unusual morphology, diet, and habitat leads us to think that {@i Deinocheirus} was a specialist wader, moving through wet or swampy environments, browsing on soft water plants and snapping up unwary fish.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Deinocheirus'} brain was relatively small and less complex than other ornithomimosaurs, suggesting a more sedate and less involved lifestyle. It may have been a solitary giant, feeding in wetland environments. An adult {@i Deinocheirus} would have been slow and would have had to stand its ground if attacked. Large predators like {@i Tarbosaurus} stalked the same regions and, while very large itself, these comparably sized animals may have predated upon {@i Deinocheirus}. While its claws were blunt, they were also powerful and a potent defensive weapon. We suggest that {@i Deinocheirus} be played as a slow-moving oblivious herbivore, wading through wetlands or lumbering through forests. It should be placid if ignored but extremely hostile if threatened, butchering threats within reach, although rarely pursuing fleeing targets. Yet, if treated with caution, {@i Deinocheirus} might be an easily appeased animal and excellent wetland mount.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Deinocheirus} was first described in 1970 by Osmólska and Roniewicz, after a giant pair of forelimbs and shoulder girdle were discovered in Cretaceous sediments from Mongolia. These huge forelimbs were suspected to be from a massive predatory theropod dinosaur, given their vicious claws. However, the rest of the animal remained a mystery for 44 years and in that time various hypotheses were presented, including the suggestion that it was a giant tree-climbing animal. It wasn't until 2014, when most of the rest of the holotype and several other specimens were discovered, that the truly bizarre nature of this dinosaur was revealed.

Ornithomimosauria was a diverse group of medium to huge sized ostrich-like theropods. They were very distinct from other theropods, as they were toothless, had long arms, long necks, long legs, and feet with short claws. They are an exclusively Cretaceous group, but were quite successful, occurring throughout Lauraisa (North America, Europe, and Asia) and survived until the end-Cretaceous extinction.

trait.name: Wader
entries: Deinocheirus can move through water up to 6 ft. deep without being slowed or having to swim.

trait.name: Pennaceous Display Feathers
entries: Deinocheirus has advantage on Intimidation and Persuasion checks.

trait.name: Mud Raker
entries: If a single creature is hit by both of Deinocheirus' Terrible Claw attacks in a single turn, they suffer an additional {@damage 1d6} poison damage, as the dregged mud from its claws coats their wounds.

trait.name: Grasping Tongue
entries: As a bonus action, Deinocheirus may pick up and wield an item (up to 20 lb.) with its tongue. If that item is a weapon and does not require ammunition, it may make an attack with it as a bonus action on its subsequent turns, although it is not proficient with it.

trait.name: Swamp Lord
entries: Deinocheirus gains resistance to cold and poison damage.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: When selecting the attack action, Deinocheirus may make two Terrible Claw attacks.

action.name: Terrible Claw
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 7} to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}22 ({@damage 3d12 + 3}) slashing damage. A creature hit by this attack must succeed a {@dc 16} Strength saving throw or drop an item they are wielding.

action.name: Swampy Vomit {@recharge 5}
entries: As an action, Deinocheirus vomits swampy water in a 40 ft. line that is 5 ft. wide. Each creature in that line must succeed a {@dc 15} Dexterity saving throw or take {@damage 4d8} poison damage and {@damage 4d8} bludgeoning damage. On a success they take half as much damage.
{@i "DYE-NO-KEIR-RUS"} {@b (HORRIBLE HAND)}

In the fetid swamp, we had the misfortune of havin' to wade through some pretty foul water. This was made all the more unpleasant by a huge oily, fuzzy, hump-backed theropod dinosaur that waded through the water. Thankfully, it was a herbivore, so there didn't appear to be any immediate danger of becomin' lunch. That said, it had some very mighty lookin'
claws and could no doubt rend a person in two fairly easily. For that reason, and the smell, we kept our distance.

trait.name: Hyper Resilience
entries: Deinosuchus' remarkable immune system and colossal bulk render it resistant to all damage and it is immune to the {@condition poisoned} condition (included above).

trait.name: Devourer of Giants
entries: Any creature with a size of Large or larger makes saving throws at disadvantage against Deinosuchus' Bone-Crushing Bite.

trait.name: Aquatic Ambush Predator
entries: Deinosuchus can hold its breath for up to 1 hour and has advantage on Stealth checks while submerged in water.

action.name: Bone-Crushing Bite
entries: Deinosuchus may attempt a Bone-Crushing Bite against one creature within 10 ft. of it. This bite is so powerful that armour is essentially useless. The target creature must succeed a {@dc 14} Dexterity saving throw or take 56 ({@damage 8d10 + 12}) piercing damage, be {@condition grappled}, and {@condition restrained} (escape DC 20). Deinosuchus then cannot select a different target for Bone-Crushing Bite until the grapple ends.

legendary.name: Thrash
entries: Deinosuchus may thrash around wildly. All creatures within 10 ft. of it must succeed a {@dc 12} Dexterity saving throw or take 21 ({@damage 2d20}) bludgeoning damage. A creature {@condition grappled} by Deinosuchus may not attempt to save against this damage.

legendary.name: Deathroll
entries: If Deinosuchus is grappling another creature that is Large or larger, it may perform a Deathroll. The grappled creature must succeed a {@dc 21} Strength saving throw or take 39 ({@damage 6d12}) force damage. On a success, they take half as much damage. Deinosuchus cannot use Deathroll next round.
{@i "DIE-NO-SOO-CUS"} {@b (TERRIBLE CROCODILE)}

Most of us who adventure are familiar with crocs, big'uns too. But this... this one was somethin' else. A gargantuan croc, far bigger than any other I've ever seen. Thankfully, we came upon it while it was baskin', rather than huntin'. It was so big that it was barely interested in us. I reckon it could take down even the biggest of dinosaurs with ease. Certainly wouldn't want to be on the receiving end of a bite from it. The heaviest plate armour wouldn't even make a difference.

{@i Deinosuchus} is from the Late Cretaceous (82 million years ago) of North America and is a giant relative of modern alligators. It was a highly successful animal that occurred on both sides of the Western Interior Sea.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Deinosuchus} is thought to have reached a maximum size of approximately 33 ft. and weighed around 2.5 tonnes, although some may have been larger. Aside from its size, it was very similar to a modern alligator, albeit with a slightly more bulbous snout. Like its modern relatives, {@i Deinosuchus} had extremely powerful jaws which are estimated to have had a bite similar in strength to {@i Tyrannosaurus} ({@b see page 195}). The estimated strength of this bite varies hugely between different studies, from as low as 2 tonnes and as high as 20 tonnes in force but, even at the low end this would be devastating against most animals.

{@i Deinosuchus} is known from multiple fossil localities along both sides of the Western Interior Sea. This was a huge inland sea that formed in the Cretaceous and divided what would become North America in two. Like modern alligators, {@i Deinosuchus} was a semi-aquatic ambush predator, slowly moving in muddy water before striking suddenly at unsuspecting prey. Based on bite marks in numerous fossils, we know that it fed on a range of prey from turtles to large dinosaurs.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: The similarities {@i Deinosuchus} shares with modern alligators suggests that it behaved similarly. Alligators are powerful, patient predators who can live alone or in large groups. When in groups, they regularly fight with each other. Given its size, {@i Deinosuchus} probably only formed groups of a dozen or so individuals at maximum. Many likely suffered horrific injuries from their fights that would have been debilitating for other animals, but {@i Deinosuchus'} remarkable resilience and exceptional immune system would have allowed them to continue largely unphased.
We suggest that {@i Deinosuchus} be played as an animal that rarely moves and prefers to either bask in the sun or lie motionless in water, with just its nostrils and eyes peeking out.

They should also have no fear of attacking anything that comes within striking range (excluding monsters like the Tarrasque or Ancient Dragons). We suggest that this power and resilience could cause {@i Deinosuchus} to be worshiped as a deity by pre-industrial cultures.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Deinosuchus} was one of the early members of Crocodilia, the only surviving group of crocodylomorphs today. Crocodiles, gharials and alligators are frequently called "living fossils" as they have changed little over many millions of years. However, they represent just a fraction of the various crocodylomorph species that existed. Appearing in the Late Triassic, the group included a huge variety of animals from dinosaur-like small predators, to oceanic animals that had lost the ability to come on land, and even armoured herbivores.

entries: Baker, C.J., Frère, C.H., Franklin, C.E., Campbell, H.A., Irwin, T.R., and Dwyer, R.G. 2023. Long-term tracking reveals a dynamic crocodylian social system. {@i Animal Behaviour}, {@b 199}, 59-78.

Cossette, A.P., and Brochu, C.A. 2020. A systematic review of the giant alligatoroid Deinosuchus from the Campanian of North America and its implications for the relationships at the root of Crocodylia. {@i Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology}, {@b 40}, e1767638.

trait.name: Regional Demigod
entries: Deinosuchus is worshiped by local humanoids as the embodiment of primal power and is accompanied by an entourage of humanoids that adorn it with giant flower rings, vividly coloured paints, and fine silks, and ritualistically clean its teeth as it basks in the sun.

Deinosuchus will not attack humanoids unless in self-defence and it is considered an extreme offence to these people to disrespect or attack Deinosuchus. Typically, these humanoids will demand an offering of food for Deinosuchus to safely pass through its territory.

trait.name: Top Triassic Predator
entries: Erythrosuchus was the top predator of its time, but only predated upon animals a similar size or smaller than itself. Erythrosuchus has advantage on attacks against Medium and Large creatures, but disadvantage on attacks against creatures of any other size category.

trait.name: Semi-arid Inhabitant
entries: Erythrosuchus only needs to drink water once every few weeks.

trait.name: Unknown Predatory Style
entries: If Erythrosuchus chooses the dash action, it may still make a single attack with its Monstrous Jaw as a bonus action.

trait.name: Legendary Resistance (1/day)
entries: If Erythrosuchus fails a saving throw, it can choose to succeed instead.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Erythrosuchus chooses the attack action, it may make two Monstrous Jaw attacks.

action.name: Monstrous Jaw
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 6} to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}15 ({@damage 2d10 + 4}) piercing damage. A creature hit by this attack is {@condition grappled} (escape {@dc 16}). While Erythrosuchus is grappling a creature, it can only target that creature with its attacks.

legendary.name: Ripping Thrash
entries: Erythrosuchus thrashes from side to side. If it is currently grappling a creature in its jaws, that creature must succeed a {@dc 16} Strength saving throw or take {@damage 4d6} slashing damage. On a success, they take half as much damage.

legendary.name: Drag Away
entries: Erythrosuchus may move up to 20 ft., dragging a grappled creature along with it. Any creature grappled by Erythrosuchus is moved with it.
{@i "ERR-EAT-THROW-SOO-CUS"} {@b (RED CROCODILE)}

Travelin' through the desert, we had had three nights of restless campin'. The sounds of huge bellowin' creatures filled every night, making sleep difficult and worrisome. On the dawn of the fourth day, we had the misfortune to bein' awoken by one of the beasts tryin' to drag away our paladin. She, weirdly, sleeps in her armour and we had mocked her for it before. That night it likely saved her though. The thin' was huge and bizarre lookin'. It had a gigantic head with a fearsome bite, but smaller body – almost comical. As we struck at it, it thrashed from side to side, and opened its maw to bare its teeth – thankfully droppin' our friend.

{@i Erythrosuchus} was a giant erythrosuchid from the Middle Triassic (245 million years ago) of South Africa (Beaufort Group). A close relative of {@i Garjainia} ({@b see page 129}), it was the largest and most powerful predator in its ecosystem.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Erythrosuchus} was, unsurprisingly, an erythrosuchid, a group of four-legged land predators, and was the largest of the group at about 16 ft. long. Its skull was enormous relative to its body, with extremely robust jaws and teeth. Its neck was short and powerful, meaning it could both bite very hard and forcibly thrash prey. Its body was typical of reptiles for the time, with robust limbs and a short tail. Like later archosaurs (the ancestors of dinosaurs), its pelvis allowed for an erect stance, so it stood upright rather than sprawling like many other reptiles.

{@i Erythrosuchus} was the largest carnivore in the Beaufort group, which was laid down in a semi-arid environment with seasonal rains. It is thought to have been the arch-predator of this area, feeding on a wide variety of prey such as early synapsids (mammal-like reptiles), amphibians, and reptiles. It likely specialised in tackling medium-large sized dicynodonts, the squat herbivorous synapsids that were extremely abundant at the time.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Very little information is known about the behaviour of erythrosuchids, with little to no research into their likely interactions or hunting strategies. As they were almost certainly arch predators, we suggest they would have behaved similarly to modern carnivores. This meant that much of the day was spent resting to avoid wasting energy. {@i Erythrosuchus} was too bulky to run down prey and likely ambushed it instead, wrestling anything it caught with its powerful jaws.

We recommend {@i Erythrosuchus} be played as a slow but persistent predator that is highly dangerous if close, but otherwise lazy if resting or given a safe margin by a party. Like many animals in an arid environment, it should be most active in the evening, night, and dawn to avoid the blistering midday heat. This makes it the ideal creature to ambush a resting party.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: Erythrosuchids were members of the Archosauriformes, the group which gave rise to the true archosaurs like pterosaurs, crocodiles, and dinosaurs. Like many archosaurs, they had an erect gait and rapid growth, suggesting that they were warm-blooded (endothermic). If this is true, this, along with other evidence from early archosaurs, suggests that being warm-blooded was a basal (primitive) condition for archosauriformes.

entries: Benton, M.J., 2021. The origin of endothermy in synapsids and archosaurs and arms races in the Triassic. Gondwana Research, 100, pp.261-289.
Broom, R. 1905. Notice of some new reptiles from the Karoo Beds of South Africa. {@i Records of the Albany Museum}, {@b 1}, 331-337.
Ezcurra, M.D., Butler, R.J., and Gower, D.J. 2013. 'Proterosuchia': the origin and early history of Archosauriformes. {@i Geological Society, London, Special Publications}, {@b 379(1)}, 9-33.

Hancox, P.J., Neveling, J., and Rubidge, B.S. 2020. Biostratigraphy of the Cynognathus Assemblage Zone (Beaufort Group, Karoo Supergroup), South Africa. {@i South African Journal of Geology}, {@b 123(2)}, 217-238.
Parrish, J.M. 1992. Phylogeny of the Erythrosuchidae (Reptilia: Archosauriformes). {@i Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology}, {@b 12(1)}, 93-102.

entries: If Erythrosuchus chooses the dash action, it may still make a single attack with its Monstrous Jaw as a bonus action.

trait.name: Legendary Resistance (1/day)
entries: If Erythrosuchus fails a saving throw, it can choose to succeed instead.

trait.name: Maw of Madness
entries: Any creature hit by Erythrosuchus' Monstrous Jaw attack must succeed a {@dc 12} Wisdom saving throw or have their Intelligence score temporarily reduced to 3 for 1 minute. During this time, they may only act on instincts, their proficiency bonus is 0, and they cannot speak, read, write, or understand language.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Erythrosuchus chooses the attack action, it may make two Monstrous Jaw attacks.

action.name: Monstrous Jaw
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 6} to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}15 ({@damage 2d10 + 4}) piercing damage. A creature hit by this attack is {@condition grappled} (escape {@dc 16}). While Erythrosuchus is grappling a creature, it can only target that creature with its attacks.

legendary.name: Ripping Thrash
entries: Erythrosuchus thrashes from side to side. If it is currently grappling a creature in its jaws, that creature must succeed a {@dc 16} Strength saving throw or take {@damage 4d6} slashing damage. On a success, they take half as much damage.

legendary.name: Drag Away
entries: Erythrosuchus may move up to 20 ft., dragging a grappled creature along with it. Any creature grappled by Erythrosuchus is moved with it.
{@i "ERR-EAT-THROW-SOO-CUS"} {@b (RED CROCODILE)}

Travelin' through the desert, we had had three nights of restless campin'. The sounds of huge bellowin' creatures filled every night, making sleep difficult and worrisome. On the dawn of the fourth day, we had the misfortune to bein' awoken by one of the beasts tryin' to drag away our paladin. She, weirdly, sleeps in her armour and we had mocked her for it before. That night it likely saved her though. The thin' was huge and bizarre lookin'. It had a gigantic head with a fearsome bite, but smaller body – almost comical. As we struck at it, it thrashed from side to side, and opened its maw to bare its teeth – thankfully droppin' our friend.

{@i Erythrosuchus} was a giant erythrosuchid from the Middle Triassic (245 million years ago) of South Africa (Beaufort Group). A close relative of {@i Garjainia} ({@b see page 129}), it was the largest and most powerful predator in its ecosystem.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Erythrosuchus} was, unsurprisingly, an erythrosuchid, a group of four-legged land predators, and was the largest of the group at about 16 ft. long. Its skull was enormous relative to its body, with extremely robust jaws and teeth. Its neck was short and powerful, meaning it could both bite very hard and forcibly thrash prey. Its body was typical of reptiles for the time, with robust limbs and a short tail. Like later archosaurs (the ancestors of dinosaurs), its pelvis allowed for an erect stance, so it stood upright rather than sprawling like many other reptiles.

{@i Erythrosuchus} was the largest carnivore in the Beaufort group, which was laid down in a semi-arid environment with seasonal rains. It is thought to have been the arch-predator of this area, feeding on a wide variety of prey such as early synapsids (mammal-like reptiles), amphibians, and reptiles. It likely specialised in tackling medium-large sized dicynodonts, the squat herbivorous synapsids that were extremely abundant at the time.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Very little information is known about the behaviour of erythrosuchids, with little to no research into their likely interactions or hunting strategies. As they were almost certainly arch predators, we suggest they would have behaved similarly to modern carnivores. This meant that much of the day was spent resting to avoid wasting energy. {@i Erythrosuchus} was too bulky to run down prey and likely ambushed it instead, wrestling anything it caught with its powerful jaws.

We recommend {@i Erythrosuchus} be played as a slow but persistent predator that is highly dangerous if close, but otherwise lazy if resting or given a safe margin by a party. Like many animals in an arid environment, it should be most active in the evening, night, and dawn to avoid the blistering midday heat. This makes it the ideal creature to ambush a resting party.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: Erythrosuchids were members of the Archosauriformes, the group which gave rise to the true archosaurs like pterosaurs, crocodiles, and dinosaurs. Like many archosaurs, they had an erect gait and rapid growth, suggesting that they were warm-blooded (endothermic). If this is true, this, along with other evidence from early archosaurs, suggests that being warm-blooded was a basal (primitive) condition for archosauriformes.

trait.name: Fruitbringer
entries: When Falcatakely is first encountered, it will always carry a berry or fruit in its mouth. If players approach it, it will fly to a nearby tree or bush, revealing an abundance of delicious fruits/berries that can provide rations for four people for up to two days.

trait.name: Morning Chorus
entries: As dawn breaks, Falcatakely makes loud chirping noises that can be heard for up to 300 ft.

trait.name: Island Isolation
entries: Falcatakely found on an island will be different colours from, and produce a different chorus to, those found on the mainland.

action.name: Recurved Peck
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 2} to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}1 ({@damage 1d2}) piercing damage.
{@i "FAL-KAH-TAKE-LEE"} {@b (SMALL SCYTHE)}

The mornin' chorus in this region was much more vibrant than most areas. It didn't take long for us to find out why, since the culprit was such a beautiful beastie. A stunnin', vividly-patterned bird with a long curved beak. Friendly thin' – seemed to have a fondness of fruits if I recall.

{@i Falcatakely} was a bird-like theropod from the Cretaceous (65-70 million years ago) of Madagascar. It was a relative of {@i Cratoavis} ({@b see page 102}) and was about the size of a raven. It possessed an unusual beak and appears to be another example of a specialised animal evolving on an isolated island.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Falcatakely} was a small animal with a wingspan of about 3 ft. that was outwardly very similar to a modern bird, albeit with clawed fingers and a toothed beak. It had a large beak-like snout, similar to a toucan, with small teeth in the front of its mouth (premaxilla). This toucan-like appearance has led scientists to hypothesise that {@i Falcatakely} shared a similar fruit-eating (frugivorous) lifestyle, while perhaps also eating insects and small vertebrate prey.

{@i Falcatakely} is from the Maevarano Formation, which was laid down in a seasonally wet/arid environment with shallow rivers and abundant flood plains in northern Madagascar. By this point in time Madagascar was already isolated from the mainland and {@i Falcatakely} may be an example of specialised adaptations in this island isolation.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Little is known about {@i Falcatakely}'s behaviour, but it is reasonable to presume that it shared similarities to toucans. It may have been social, forming breeding pairs that roosted within hollows in trees. We recommend that {@i Falcatakely} be played in much the same manner as you would a normal bird, meaning it will be skittish of players who disturb it, but loyal if tamed or hand-reared.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: Enantiornitheans have a complicated phylogeny and there is still debate over whether they are true birds. This is a common problem in the wider Avialae, the theropod group leading to birds, as much of them share the presence of complex feathers, wings, and beaks. Currently, there isn't a consensus on which features can be considered truly "bird"-like, and so {@i Falcatakely's} position in the tree of life is unlikely to be resolved until further analyses are complete.

trait.name: Bountiful Harvest
entries: Falcatakely radiate druidic energies and their presence increases the yield of all surrounding plants. If Falcatakely is present in an environment for more than a week, all plants in the local region double the amount of fruit, berries, and flowers they produce. This effect diminishes and productivity returns to normal over the course of a week if Falcatakely leaves the area.
Islands inhabited by colonies of many Falcatakely are usually tropical paradises.

trait.name: Familiar
entries: Falcatakely may be used as a familiar via the {@spell Find Familiar} spell or any similar effect. If you do so, we recommend that its Fruitbringer ability only activates each time it is summoned in a new area.

trait.name: Lock Jaw
entries: If Garjainia hits a creature with its Over-Sized Bite attack, it can opt to grasp onto it. While grasping, if either Garjainia or the hit creature attempts to move, they must make contested Strength checks. Whichever creature loses the contested Strength check has its speed reduced to 0 until its next turn. If Garjainia or the grasped creature moves, the other moves with it (without using any of its own movement) and is considered to be occupying the same space as it.

As an action, the hit creature may make a {@dc 14} Strength saving throw to remove Garjainia, ending this effect and pushing Garjainia 5 ft. directly away from it on a success. Alternatively, Garjainia may choose to end this effect at any time.

trait.name: High-Gait Scramble {@recharge 4}
entries: Garjainia can dash as a bonus action.

action.name: Over-Sized Bite
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 5} to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}7 ({@damage 1d8 + 3}) piercing damage.
When a creature is hit by this attack, roll a {@dice 1d3} and consult the list below, applying the effect to the hit creature so long as Garjainia is grasping it (see Lock Jaw):
1. Bitten body. The creature suffers an additional 4 ({@damage 1d4 + 2}) piercing damage at the start of its turn.
2. Bitten arm. Melee, ranged, and spell attacks made by the creature are at disadvantage.
3. Bitten leg. Halve the current speed of the creature.
Garjainia can only cause one of these effects at a time.
{@i "GAR-JAR-NEE-AH"} {@b (SWIFT ROAR?)}

When we first saw these lil' blighters, we thought they'd be unbothersome. But don't let their size fool ya. They've got a mean bite. Our Ranger approached one of 'em and before we knew it, it was latched onto his arm. Can't much fire a bow with one hand now. Funny at first, then we saw three more scurrying out of the brush to join the frenzy. Wouldn't be long before they'd disarm all of us!

{@i Garjainia} is an early erythrosuchid, a group of quadrupedal carnivores from the Early Triassic (249-237 million years ago) of Russia and Africa. It walked with a raised gait and had an enormous head, making it an unusual looking animal.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Garjainia} was a medium sized predator for the Triassic, measuring approximately 8 ft. long. It had a reptilian body structure that was typical for the era, except for two key features. Its legs were beneath its body giving it an erect gait, rather than a sprawling one, and its head was enormous, making up about a quarter of its total body length. Its skull was huge with a long and robust jaws, and a characteristic notch towards the front of the upper jaw, similar to {@i Spinosaurus} ({@b page 75}). Its teeth were long, fang-like, and partially fused to the jaw. Usually vertebrate teeth are either fused (ankylothedocont) or unfused (thecodont), and so {@i Garjainia} represents an unusual middle-ground.

Originally thought to have been semi-aquatic due to their dense bones, recent studies indicate that {@i Garjainia} was a capable terrestrial animal and its bone density was a result of its short robust stature. Its strong jaws and robust teeth indicate that it was capable of overpowering large struggling prey. It shared its environment with a wide variety of other animals including amphibians, a variety of synapsids (mammal-like reptiles), and other erythrosuchids, many of which were larger than itself. Although able to tackle large animals, it may have been hunted by bigger erythrosuchids like {@i Erythrosuchus} ({@b page 126}).

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Erythrosuchid behaviour is poorly understood, but we know that they grew relatively fast and may have been endothermic (warm-blooded). {@i Garjainia} was clearly built for strength, rather than speed and was probably an ambush predator, lying in wait until prey was close enough for a rapid strike. Some species possessed bony bumps on the side of their heads, which may have been used for display or fights for dominance rights.

We suggest that {@i Garjainia} be played similar to a Komodo Dragon; a powerful animal that slowly stalks the undergrowth and occasionally charges large prey. It may aggregate in groups, simultaneously attacking to bring down huge prey, essentially forming a swarm. While a single {@i Garjainia} may be a reasonable threat, a swarm is a significant one, able to mob and disable party members.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: As an erythrosuchid, {@i Garjainia} is part of the Archosauriformes, placing it in the sibling group to crocodiles, dinosaurs, and pterosaurs. The Erythrosuchidae were unusual high-gait lizard-like animals that ranged from dog- to cow-sized. They are known from Europe, Africa, India, and China, where they were major predators in their ecosystems.

entries: Ezcurra, M., Gower, D., Sennikov, A., and Butler, R. 2019. The osteology of the holotype of the early erythrosuchid {@i Garjainia prima} Ochev, 1958 (Diapsida: Archosauromorpha) from the upper Lower Triassic of European Russia. {@i Zoological Journal of the Linnean Society}, {@b 185(3)}, 717-783.

Gower, D.J., Hancox, J.P., Botha-Brink, J., Sennikov, A.G., and Butler, R.J. 2014. A New Species of {@i Garjainia} Ochev, 1958 (Diapsida: Archosauriformes: Erythrosuchidae) from the Early Triassic of South Africa. {@i PLOS ONE}, {@b 9(11)}, e111154.

trait.name: Swarm
entries: The swarm can occupy another creature's space and vice versa, and the swarm can move through any opening large enough for a Small beast. The swarm can't regain hit points or gain temporary hit points.

The swarm is immune to being {@condition charmed}, {@condition frightened}, {@condition grappled}, {@condition paralyzed}, {@condition petrified}, {@condition prone}, {@condition restrained}, and {@condition stunned} (included above).

entries: Garjainia (Swarm) can dash as a bonus action.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Garjainia (Swarm) chooses the attack action, it may make four Over-Sized Bite attacks.

They are known from Europe, Africa, India, and China, where they were major predators in their ecosystems.

trait.name: Swarm
entries: The swarm can occupy another creature's space and vice versa, and the swarm can move through any opening large enough for a Small beast. The swarm can't regain hit points or gain temporary hit points.

The swarm is immune to being {@condition charmed}, {@condition frightened}, {@condition grappled}, {@condition paralyzed}, {@condition petrified}, {@condition prone}, {@condition restrained}, and {@condition stunned} (included above).
