{@i "GAR-JAR-NEE-AH"} {@b (SWIFT ROAR?)}

When we first saw these lil' blighters, we thought they'd be unbothersome. But don't let their size fool ya. They've got a mean bite. Our Ranger approached one of 'em and before we knew it, it was latched onto his arm. Can't much fire a bow with one hand now. Funny at first, then we saw three more scurrying out of the brush to join the frenzy. Wouldn't be long before they'd disarm all of us!

{@i Garjainia} is an early erythrosuchid, a group of quadrupedal carnivores from the Early Triassic (249-237 million years ago) of Russia and Africa. It walked with a raised gait and had an enormous head, making it an unusual looking animal.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Garjainia} was a medium sized predator for the Triassic, measuring approximately 8 ft. long. It had a reptilian body structure that was typical for the era, except for two key features. Its legs were beneath its body giving it an erect gait, rather than a sprawling one, and its head was enormous, making up about a quarter of its total body length. Its skull was huge with a long and robust jaws, and a characteristic notch towards the front of the upper jaw, similar to {@i Spinosaurus} ({@b page 75}). Its teeth were long, fang-like, and partially fused to the jaw. Usually vertebrate teeth are either fused (ankylothedocont) or unfused (thecodont), and so {@i Garjainia} represents an unusual middle-ground.

Originally thought to have been semi-aquatic due to their dense bones, recent studies indicate that {@i Garjainia} was a capable terrestrial animal and its bone density was a result of its short robust stature. Its strong jaws and robust teeth indicate that it was capable of overpowering large struggling prey. It shared its environment with a wide variety of other animals including amphibians, a variety of synapsids (mammal-like reptiles), and other erythrosuchids, many of which were larger than itself. Although able to tackle large animals, it may have been hunted by bigger erythrosuchids like {@i Erythrosuchus} ({@b page 126}).

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Erythrosuchid behaviour is poorly understood, but we know that they grew relatively fast and may have been endothermic (warm-blooded). {@i Garjainia} was clearly built for strength, rather than speed and was probably an ambush predator, lying in wait until prey was close enough for a rapid strike. Some species possessed bony bumps on the side of their heads, which may have been used for display or fights for dominance rights.

We suggest that {@i Garjainia} be played similar to a Komodo Dragon; a powerful animal that slowly stalks the undergrowth and occasionally charges large prey. It may aggregate in groups, simultaneously attacking to bring down huge prey, essentially forming a swarm. While a single {@i Garjainia} may be a reasonable threat, a swarm is a significant one, able to mob and disable party members.

They are known from Europe, Africa, India, and China, where they were major predators in their ecosystems.

{@i "GI-RAF-AH-TIE-TAN"} {@b (GIRAFFE GIANT)}

The heat had been gettin' to us pretty bad and we'd start'd to run low on water. Headin' down to the coast seemed like a good idea at the time. There, we could boil some of the salt water and condense out somethin' fresh to drink. At first, we couldn't make out the gigantic forms on the horizon. The blarin' sun hazin' our view. When we got a bit closer, we saw em—towerin' sauropods traipsin' through the waves to keep cool and scavengin' what few plants grew on the coast. Aproachin' was a bad decision. They was pretty defensive of their feedin' patch and boy, those things can't half give ya a whack when they wanna.

{@i Giraffatitan} is a giant brachiosaurid sauropod from the Late Jurassic (145 million years ago) Tendaguru Formation of Tanzania. A larger relative of the American {@i Brachiosaurus}, it was considered the biggest land animal until fossils of the giant titanosaurs, like {@i Paralititan} ({@b see page 71}), were discovered.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Giraffatitan} is known from incomplete remains, leading to several estimations of its size. The most recent analyses suggest it was around 85 ft. long and weighed 45 tonnes. This may seem exceptionally heavy, but is much less than another animal of the same size would be. This is because sauropods had weight reduction adaptations, such as hollow air sac-filled bones (pneumatisation). It had a very tall shoulders, elevating the front of its body and sloping its back. Its tail was relatively short for a sauropod, but its neck was very long, held erect and tipped by a blunt snouted skull that had a tall bony arch on its forehead.

{@i Giraffatitan} was a herbivorous animal with peg-like teeth that it used to strip tall conifer trees of leaves. It was not a permanent resident of the Tendaguru Formation, which was a tidal flat environment, as its upright posture meant it was a high browser. Instead, it must have lived in a forested area and may have visited the tidal flats in times of drought or while migrating elsewhere.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Due to its size, {@i Giraffatitan} would have been a slow-moving animal, travelling in groups from place to place, stripping the greenery from the tallest trees. An adult {@i Giraffatitan} would have been safe from all but the largest of predators, although young {@i Giraffatitan} may have been quite vulnerable. Currently, there is no evidence of any predators in the Tendaguru Formation large enough to threaten an adult {@i Giraffatitan}. However, its biggest threat was probably other {@i Giraffatitan} as it may have undertaken intraspecific (same species) fighting.

We recommend {@i Giraffatitan} be largely dismissive of most smaller animals, so long as they are not perceived as a threat to their young. Parties should be able to get relatively close to adults without disturbing them, as they slowly travel across the landscape looking for food. {@i Giraffatitan} are too slow to chase or charge opponents and will instead stand their ground, crushing enemies within reach.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: Brachiosaurids were among the largest dinosaurs ever to live. They arose in the Late Jurassic (160 million years ago) and survived into the Late Cretaceous (93 million years ago). Initially very successful, they spread to every continent bar Antarctica and Australia before becoming restricted to North America in the Early Cretaceous.

entries.name: Periscope Up
entries: Sauropods were such massive animals that early palaeontologists wondered how they could possibly support their massive weight on land. Most fossils were found in sites that represented wetlands, coasts, and riverbeds and some palaeontologists argued that they must have been semi-aquatic. They suggested that their long necks and tall forelimbs were adaptations to wading in deep water, keeping their heads at the surface like a giant snorkel. This hypothesis has now been extensively disproven, as pressure at that depth would have collapsed their lungs, and their hollow bones would have made them very buoyant, causing them to float and then topple over. We now know that they were terrestrial animals of the forests and plains, and their abundance in watery environments in the fossil record is a preservational bias.

{@i "IG-WAN-OH-DON"} {@b (IGUANA TOOTH)}

One of the more common dinosaurs we encountered was those large ornithopods, Iguanodon. Easily recognisable by their large thumb spikes and grumpy attitude, they were a staple prey for all of the big predators in this area but rarely moved alone. If you wanted to pick a fight with one, you'd usually end up outnumbered. Fine if you're a big predatory dinosaur, less fine if you're a lil' adventurer. Despite their moderate size compared to other dinosaurs, these thin's were still pretty dangerous when they heft their weight around.

{@i Iguanodon} is an iguanodontian ornithischian dinosaur from the Early Cretaceous (126-120 million years ago) of Europe. The second dinosaur to be described and named; it is the most famous example of how our understanding of dinosaurs has changed over time.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Iguanodon} was a large ornithopod, measuring up to 36 ft. long and weighing 4-5 tonnes. Like hadrosaurs, it had long robust hindlimbs and shorter forelimbs. It was capable of running on two legs but spent most of its time on all fours. One of its most distinctive features was a thumb-like spike modified from the first digit on each forelimb. When first discovered in 1830, this thumb spike was mistakenly assumed to be a nasal horn. That interpretation was ubiquitous and was even incorporated into the life-sized sculptures of {@i Iguanodon} at Crystal Palace, which still stand today. Since its identification as a thumb spike, the function of this structure has been debated. Most researchers now agree that it was used for combat, probably more often against other {@i Iguanodon} rather than predators.

{@i Iguanodon} takes its namesake from its teeth, which are superficially similar to modern iguanas. Its head was large, elongated, and tipped with a well-developed beak. Its slightly broad snout suggests that it may have been a generalist herbivore and, like {@i Bolong} ({@b page 48}), was capable of chewing. Its diet may have included conifers, ferns, cycads, and early flowering plants, and it could effectively process tough plant material by chewing it.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Iguanodon} has been found in mass mortality assemblages (bones of many individuals found in one spot). It's thought that these assemblages were formed either during a flash flood or while a group was crossing a river. In any case, these indicate that {@i Iguanodon} moved in large herds, similar to bison or zebra.

We suggest that {@i Iguanodon} be played as a highly social animal, moving in large herds constantly courting, squabbling, and vocalising. When disturbed or threatened, a herd should stampede away, running on two legs. Only individuals who end up isolated or those who can't keep up should turn to fight their attackers. The stampeding mass of {@i Iguanodon} should be a danger in and of itself, trampling smaller creatures. We also suggest that {@i Iguanodon} migrates in these herds, following a well-established route and even possibly grouping with other species. These mass migrations can be followed by predators that will pick off weaker animals.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Iguanodon} has a complex phylogenetic history. Traditionally, it was considered a member of the Iguanodontidae, a group of iguanodontians which were the sister group to the hadrosaurs. However, that became a 'wastebasket group', meaning that similar animals with poorly known phylogenetic relationships were 'dumped' in there without much evidence.

A series of reviews starting in the 2000s argued that many animals thought to belong to this family were part of the Hadrosauroidea (hadrosaurs and their relatives). Currently, Iguanodontidae is not a well-supported group and researchers are not in agreement if it exists or if {@i Iguanodon} should simply be seen as a basal iguanodontian, related to but outside of Hadrosauroidea.
Greensand Formation) near Maidstone, Kent. {@i Edinburgh New Philosophical Journal}, {@b 17}, 200-201.

trait.name: Crystal Palace Horned History
entries: You may choose for Iguanodon to have a much more lizard-like appearance and a large, pointed horn on its snout instead of clawed thumbs. If you do, replace all instances of "Thumb Gore" in its stat block with "Horn Gore".

trait.name: The Bone Wars
entries: One of two greedy palaeontologists (Marsh or Cope) refuse to allow anyone to study Iguanodon's remains and have hidden explosives on every member of this species. If Iguanodon is slain, do not end combat. A loud ticking sound can be heard emanating from its remains and, after 2 rounds, they detonate with a large explosion.

Each creature within a 15 ft. radius of Iguanodon's remains must succeed a {@dc 12} Dexterity saving throw or take {@damage 3d6} fire damage and {@damage 3d6} bludgeoning damage. On a success they take half as much damage. Iguanodon's remains are then completely destroyed and irrecoverable.

{@i "JUR-RAH-VEN-AH-TOR"} {@b (JURA MOUNTAINS HUNTER)}

The third night that we camped along the riverbank, I was on first watch. After a few hours, I could feel myself noddin' off, so wandered down to the river's edge to splash myself with some water. It were deathly quiet, bar the chirpin' of crickets. As I crouched down into the water, I saw the shine of a tiny pair of eyes off in the reeds a few feet ahead. It was some kind of small theropod pluckin' minnows out of the water. I took a step forward to try and get a closer look, but the slosh of me foot spooked it, and it darted off into the night.

{@i Juravenator} was a very small theropod dinosaur from the Late Jurassic Francoinian Jura (151 million years ago) of Germany. The holotype (diagnostic specimen) is based on a juvenile, meaning that we have a limited understanding of its adult form.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: The only fossil of {@i Juravenator} is an exceptionally well-preserved tiny immature individual at just 30 inches long. It was a bipedal theropod with unusually large eyes. These could suggest that it was nocturnal but might also simply be a result of its immaturity, as many young animals have relatively large eyes (neoteny). {@i Juravenator} had a mouth full of sharp teeth and almost certainly fed on small animals like insects, fish, and other smaller vertebrates. Alternatively, an adult may have fed it.

{@i Juravenator} was first interpreted as a scaly animal, as a patch of preserved skin on the tail appeared featherless with scales. However, further research including high-resolution CT scans showed that this skin actually had a thin covering of feathers, although it may have been sparser than in other feathered theropods. Newer research also reinterpreted these scales as a by-product of fat decay, suggesting that the animal had a fatty skin layer. Another recent study argued instead that these were indeed scales and were similar to the sensory scales of crocodiles, suggesting a semi-aquatic wading lifestyle (although this is not well supported by the rest of the anatomy). Ultimately, research is ongoing and many questions still remain unanswered about {@i Juravenator}.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: The limited information available for {@i Juravenator} and the myriad interpretations of its fossil leave a lot of room for speculation about how this animal behaved. Here we take a mixed approach, including several elements from the studies mentioned above.

We suggest playing a baby {@i Juravenator} as a highly skittish creature that is largely non-hostile and prefers to flee from danger. It may be attracted to the light of a campfire or the smell of food, and could be relatively easy to befriend if fed. The behaviour of an adult {@i Juravenator} is unknown, but perhaps it could be a more aggressive predator.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: As the only specimen of {@i Juravenator} is a juvenile, its phylogenetic placement is particularly difficult. Originally, {@i Juravenator} was considered a compsognathid, closely related to the small theropod {@i Compsognathus} from Germany. However, it has since then been re-placed multiple times, including in Maniraptora (see {@i Velociraptor} {@b page 183}) and even Megalosauroidea (see {@i Megalosaurus} {@b page 149}). The anatomy of animals usually changes as they mature, and we can only estimate what an adult {@i Juravenator} may have looked like, let alone firmly establish its place in the tree of life.

trait.name: Reactionary Strike
entries: When Kentrosaurus is hit by a melee attack, it can use its reaction to make a single Thagomise attack at the creature that attacked it.

trait.name: Sexually Dimorphic
entries: Male and female Kentrosaurus differ in appearance. In a herd of 3 or more Kentrosaurus, select 1-2 animals to be male. They are a different colour than the females.

trait.name: Vicious Defences
entries: A creature damaged by an attack made by Kentrosaurus using its Reactionary Strike must succeed a {@dc 14} Charisma saving throw or become {@condition frightened} of Kentrosaurus for 1 minute. At the end of that creature's turn, it may repeat the saving throw. On a successful save it is no longer {@condition frightened} of Kentrosaurus and is immune to Vicious Defences for 24 hours.

trait.name: Anterior-Facing Spikes
entries: A creature attacking Kentrosaurus does not gain advantage for any ability or effect that would grant them advantage on attacks for outnumbering or flanking Kentrosaurus.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: When Kentrosaurus chooses the attack action, it can make two Thagomise attacks, or a single Tailsweep attack.

action.name: Thagomise
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 6} to hit, reach 10 ft., one target. {@h}9 ({@damage 1d12 + 3}) piercing damage.

action.name: Tailsweep
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 6} to hit, reach 10 ft., up to three targets. {@h}8 ({@damage 1d10 + 3}) piercing damage. A creature hit by this attack must succeed a {@dc 14} Strength saving throw or be knocked {@condition prone}.
{@i "KENT-TROW-SORE-US"} {@b (PRICKLE REPTILE)}

Over the rollin' hills and rocky shrubland, we spied some medium-sized spikey-armoured dinosaurs. They was pretty calm 'n largely uninterested in us, but we kept our distance nonetheless. The front half of 'em was covered with broad plates standin' on end, but the back half and tail had massive bony spikes. Can't imagine a big predator would fancy chompin' on that – seems like a pretty good deterrent.

{@i Kentrosaurus} is a relatively small stegosaur from the Late Jurassic (165 million years ago) Tendaguru Formation of Tanzania. A close relative of {@i Gigantspinosaurus} and the famous {@i Stegosaurus}, it is well known for having a mix of defensive plates and spines along its back.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Kentrosaurus} was approximately 15 ft. long and weighed up to 1.5 tonnes, making it relatively small for a stegosaur. Its morphology was typical for the group with a robust body, long tail, low shoulders, tall hips, a small head with a sharp keratinous beak, and large osteoderms (bones embedded in its skin). It had a huge backwards pointing spike on each shoulder, and two parallel rows of osteoderms along its back that transition from plates to large spikes after the 7th pair, and a double pair of spikes on the end of its tail (thagomizers).

{@i Kentrosaurus'} narrow and pointed beak suggests that it was a selective herbivore, picking out lush plant growth at ground level. This would have allowed it to feed without competing with other much taller herbivores from the Tendaguru Formation, such as {@i Giraffatitan} ({@b page 133}). Some stegosaurs are known to have swallowed pebbles (gastroliths) that aided in breaking up plant material and {@i Kentrosaurus} probably did as well, allowing it to consume tougher stems.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Kentrosaurus'} armaments pose many questions; were they for social display or combat, and how could animals like this mate? The latter is hypothesised to have required extremely elongate male genitalia, however, the former can be investigated mechanically. There is strong evidence that {@i Kentrosaurus'} tail was a functional weapon as it was powerfully muscled, could be swung rapidly, and was capable of wide motions in a 180-degree arc. This, combined with its formidable defences, suggests that these weapons were used for intraspecific (same species) fighting, and there is evidence that {@i Kentrosaurus} lived in herds. Nevertheless, these tails were still used to defend it from attackers, as thagomizer wounds (from a different stegosaur) have been identified in some {@i Allosaurus}.

We suggest {@i Kentrosaurus} be portrayed as a gregarious (grouping) animal, moving in small herds between feeding spots. When encountered by a party, they should be alert but not necessarily aggressive, with the dominant animal making its presence clear and visible. Once a party gets too close, the herd will probably move away, relying on their defences to protect them, and only stand and fight if continually harassed.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Kentrosaurus} is a member of the Stegosauridae, a family which includes {@i Stegosaurus} and {@i Gigantspinosaurus}. Stegosauridae is part of the larger group Thyreophora, which alongside stegosaurs includes the ankylosaurs such as {@i Zuul} ({@b page 188}) and other related animals like {@i Scelidosaurus} ({@b page 172}). All members are herbivores and have bony weaponry or armour embedded in their skin. The Thyreophora arose in the Early Jurassic (200 million years ago) and were highly successful, colonising every continent until the end-Cretaceous extinction.

trait.name: Snatch Feeder
entries: If Klobiodon is flying, it does not provoke attacks of opportunity when it moves out of an enemy's reach.

trait.name: Tooth Cage
entries: If Klobiodon hits a creature with its Toothed Gnaw attack, Klobiodon can opt to grasp onto it. Whenever that creature moves, Klobiodon moves with it (without using any of its own movement) and is considered to be occupying the same space as it. While grasping onto a creature, Klobiodon's AC is 10.

As an action, the hit creature may make a {@dc 8} Strength saving throw to remove Klobiodon, ending this effect and pushing Klobiodon 5 ft. directly away from it on a success. Alternatively, Klobiodon may choose to end this effect at any time.

A creature with Klobiodon grasping onto it has its movement speed reduced by 5 ft. and takes {@damage 1d2} piercing damage at the start of its turn. These effects are cumulative if more than one Klobiodon is grasping a single creature.

action.name: Toothed Gnaw
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 2} to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}2 ({@damage 1d4}) piercing damage.
{@i "CLO-BI-OH-DON"} {@b (CAGE TOOTH)}

This whole area was filled with lil' fish-snatching pterosaurs. They kept their distance from us – I guess they're used to being plucked off of the ground by small predators. Still, beautiful creatures to see flyin' and fascinatin' to observe perchin'
on rocks. They fed by flyin' low over the water and quickly dippin' their heads in, nabbin' unaware fish. Nifty stuff.
{@i Klobiodon} is a Jurassic (166 million years old) European pterosaur found in the Taynton Limestone Formation.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Klobiodon} is only known from an isolated jaw, but we can make reasonable deductions about its morphology, as it is very similar to {@i Rhamphorynchus} ({@b page 168}), albeit larger with a wingspan of at least 6.5 ft. Its wings would have been long and thin with a broadly similar silhouette to a gull, and it likely had a long tail tipped by a triangular vane. {@i Klobiodon}'s most distinctive feature was a set of robust protruding spike-like teeth that were longer towards the tip of the jaw. These formed an interlocking cage that helped grab slippery wriggling prey (often called a "fish trap").

The Taynton Limestone Formation was laid down in a coastal environment with influence from both fresh and saltwater. This resulted in a diverse assemblage of wildlife including insects, ammonites, numerous fish, early mammals, crocodiles, dinosaurs, turtles, and, of course, pterosaurs.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Klobiodon} was a near-shore hunter, eating fish, squid, and other surface-dwelling aquatic prey. Groups would likely congregate around the edges of seas, lagoons, and estuaries to nest or socialise. They would have been skittish if surprised but may have been willing to mob threats that entered their territory.

We recommend {@i Klobiodon} be played in a similar manner to modern herring gulls, albeit much larger and with a much more vicious bite. Small numbers of {@i Klobiodon} can be easily dispersed, but large groups may mob intruding players to drive them away from nesting grounds or to steal food. When incorporating its magical rules, parties in near-shore environments run the risk of wandering into a camouflaged flock.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Klobiodon} was part of the Rhamphorhynchidae group, which were an extremely successful group of pterosaurs that arose in the Middle Jurassic (160 million years ago) and survived until the Late Jurassic (148 million years ago). They spread across Laurasia (the modern Northern Hemisphere), with some additional new material recently found in South America.

entries: {@i Klobiodon} is only known from an isolated jaw, but we can make reasonable deductions about its morphology, as it is very similar to {@i Rhamphorynchus} ({@b page 168}), albeit larger with a wingspan of at least 6.5 ft. Its wings would have been long and thin with a broadly similar silhouette to a gull, and it likely had a long tail tipped by a triangular vane. {@i Klobiodon}'s most distinctive feature was a set of robust protruding spike-like teeth that were longer towards the tip of the jaw. These formed an interlocking cage that helped grab slippery wriggling prey (often called a "fish trap").

The Taynton Limestone Formation was laid down in a coastal environment with influence from both fresh and saltwater. This resulted in a diverse assemblage of wildlife including insects, ammonites, numerous fish, early mammals, crocodiles, dinosaurs, turtles, and, of course, pterosaurs.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Klobiodon} was a near-shore hunter, eating fish, squid, and other surface-dwelling aquatic prey. Groups would likely congregate around the edges of seas, lagoons, and estuaries to nest or socialise. They would have been skittish if surprised but may have been willing to mob threats that entered their territory.

We recommend {@i Klobiodon} be played in a similar manner to modern herring gulls, albeit much larger and with a much more vicious bite. Small numbers of {@i Klobiodon} can be easily dispersed, but large groups may mob intruding players to drive them away from nesting grounds or to steal food. When incorporating its magical rules, parties in near-shore environments run the risk of wandering into a camouflaged flock.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Klobiodon} was part of the Rhamphorhynchidae group, which were an extremely successful group of pterosaurs that arose in the Middle Jurassic (160 million years ago) and survived until the Late Jurassic (148 million years ago). They spread across Laurasia (the modern Northern Hemisphere), with some additional new material recently found in South America.

trait.name: River Skulker
entries: Kulindadromeus has advantage on Stealth checks while in thick foliage and can attempt to hide in sparse foliage or shallow water that would normally be too exposed to hide in. It also has darkvision 40 ft. and a passive Perception of 16 (both included above).

trait.name: Protofeathered Wader

entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 2} to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}4 ({@damage 1d4 + 2}) piercing damage.
{@i "COO-LIN-DAH-DROME-E-US"} {@b (KULINDA RUNNER)}

One of the thin's I love most about our journeys is when we catch a glimpse of an animal and it doesn't know we're watchin' it. We get to see thin's that no one else has ever seen. We spotted one lil' group of ornithopod dinosaurs in a small forest clearin', preparin' to make nests. They were kickin' back the leaf litter and usin' their lil' beaks to pick up the remainin' leaves. Covered in soft downy fuzz, they were the cutest lil' critters you could imagine, peepin' away at each other as they squabbled for space.

{@i Kulindadromeus} is a small bipedal neornithiscian (a diverse clade of ornithiscian dinosaurs) from the Middle Jurassic (166-168 million years ago) Ukureyskaya Formation of Russia. {@i Kulindadromeus} is an important species as it shows the earliest evidence for filaments in a non-theropod dinosaur.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Kulindadromeus} was fairly typical for early neornithischians as it walked on two legs and had short forelimbs. It was relatively small at 3-5 ft. long and weighed about 4.5 lb. It had a toothless snout with a keratinous sheath, giving it a short beak, and a reduced number of teeth at the back of its mouth. It was herbivorous and likely fed on ferns, although may have supplemented its diet with insects. {@i Kulindadromeus} possessed a combination of scales on its arms, underbelly, legs and tail, and feather-like filaments across the rest of its body. These were the earliest possible feather-like structures identified in a non-theropod dinosaur.

{@i Kulindadromeus} was found in the Ukureyskaya Formation of Russia, which was deposited in a freshwater lake environment with a nearby volcano. The formation contains numerous fossils of plants and insects, but does not have a large vertebrate assemblage. Little is known about the other dinosaurs from this environment beyond sparse evidence of an unknown medium sized theropod and unidentified ornithischians.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Kulindadromeus} would have likely behaved similarly to many small herbivores. It would have been quite skittish, constantly checking for potential predators. Little is known about how social it was, but small and medium herbivores tend to live in groups for safety.

We recommend playing {@i Kulindadromeus} as an alert animal that will flee if startled. If a group flees, they should scatter in different directions rather than as a unit. It may also be rather curious and, if unthreatened, may approach the edges of camps in search of discarded food.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Kulindadromeus} was a primitive neornithischian. This was a varied group that appeared in the Early-Middle Jurassic (166-168 million years ago) and included a variety of dinosaurs from the bipedal, tusked heterodontosaurs, to giant "duck-billed" hadrosaurs, and horned ceratopsians. The group was so successful that by the Late Cretaceous they were the most common and diverse herbivorous dinosaurs.

entries: Leptonectes can hold its breath for 2 hours and has resistance to cold and thunder damage (included above).

trait.name: Large Fusiform

entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 4} to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}7 ({@damage 2d4 + 2}) piercing damage.
If Leptonectes swam at least 40 ft. in a straight line before using this attack this turn, it deals an additional {@damage 2d6} piercing damage.

action.name: Giant Paddle Slap

{@i "LEP-TOE-NECK-TEES"} {@b (SLENDER SWIMMER)}

After a couple days at sea, I'd become restless in the night and decided to sit up on deck for a few hours. The calm breeze blowin' and rockin' boat was pretty soothin'. I noticed the sound of rollin' splashes starboard and decided to take a peek. The waters were dully lit by bioluminescent jellies and in the murk, I could see several large dolphin-like shapes dartin' between the shadows and occasionally snappin' up a jelly or two. They were ichthyosaurs, feedin' in the moonlight and unbothered by our presence.

{@i Leptonectes} is an ichthyosaurid from the Late Triassic to Early Jurassic (205-185 million years ago) of Europe. It was a fairly typical ichthyosaur, but is one of a handful of taxa that have specimens preserved with unborn embryos still within the mothers.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Leptonectes} was a medium to large sized (10-20 ft. in length) ichthyosaur, which are a group of fully-aquatic marine reptiles. Its morphology was typical of ichthyosaurs, with a fusiform (spindle-like) body, triangular dorsal fin, four paddle-like limbs, a crescent-shaped tail, and extremely elongated slender jaws. {@i Leptonectes'} jaws were lined with uniform conical pointy teeth and its mouth curved downwards at the back, which gave the animal a frowning appearance. Its highly modified forelimbs were large and broad paddles, while the hind paddles were much smaller. Its tail bent sharply downwards at the tip, forming the bottom half of a crescent shape, with the upper half formed by a soft tissue fluke. Overall, {@i Leptonectes} would have had a similar profile to a large dolphin or shark.

Different ichthyosaur species exploited niche partitioning, whereby concurrent organisms utilise different resources (or the same resources in different ways) which prevented or reduced competition, increasing survivability. Some fed on fish, turtles, ammonites, and possibly even birds, whereas others like {@i Leptonectes} may have specialised in soft bodied organisms like jellyfish and squid. This is suggested by their stomach contents and the shape of their teeth. In all cases, the ichthyosaurs were marine animals and could not leave the water.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: If {@i Leptonectes} was a specialist in hunting squid, octopuses, and jellyfish, it may have been most active at night when these animals most frequently visit the upper water column to feed. Little is known about the social behaviour of ichthyosaurs, but we can make some inferences based on the number and size of their preserved unborn embryos. A specimen described in 2012 was found with two relatively large embryos, whereas other species of ichthyosaur have been found with up to ten smaller ones. Assuming that no embryos are missing, it's possible that {@i Leptonectes} followed a similar strategy as the Bahariyan Polycotylid ({@b page 66}), investing more time into fewer infants in order to increase their individual chances of survival.

We suggest that {@i Leptonectes} be played as a semi-solitary animal, with females living alongside their young and potentially forming small maternity pods. They should be quick to attack potential threats and may be curious if a party enters their territory on a boat. As they may be more active at night, this means players run a greater risk of unknowingly encountering them in low light. Males should be more solitary but also more sedate, only becoming dangerous if they feel their space has been invaded or their food source disturbed.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Leptonectes} is a member of the Ichthyosauridae. This is an exceptionally successful group of marine reptiles that arose in the Late Triassic and diversified rapidly. While the classic ichthyosaur is dolphin-like in appearance, they had a variety of forms and included the largest aquatic reptiles known. The group survived multiple extinction events and remained diverse up until the Cretaceous, where they are thought to have been pushed to extinction by rapid environmental change.

trait.name: Amphibious
entries: Mastodonsaurus can breathe in both air and water. When in water, it gains a +3 bonus to Dexterity saving throws.

trait.name: Dermal Pressure Sensors
entries: While in water, Mastodonsaurus has a blindsight of 30 ft. (included above).

trait.name: Perfect Ambusher
entries: While motionless at the bottom of a body of water, Mastodonsaurus is indistinguishable from the sediment. If it attacks from this position, it is always considered to be first in the initiative order (regardless of all other abilities, like the Alert feat), has advantage on its first attack, and that attack deals an additional {@damage 1d10} piercing damage.

action.name: Tusked Bite
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 8} to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}17 ({@damage 2d10 + 6}) piercing damage.
A creature hit by this attack is {@condition grappled} (escape {@dc 14}).
{@i "MASS-TOE-DON-SORE-US"} {@b (NIPPLE TOOTH REPTILE)}

The swamps are a particularly dangerous place to venture. Not only are they slow to wade through, but many nasty predators hide in the murky waters. One of the scarier ones is a giant amphibian that lies in wait, fully submerged and totally indistinguishable from the mud its squalorin' in. Those who have the misfortune to step too close are met with an explosion of tusked fury – water flyin' everywhere. Ambushes like this were painfully common and we lost a few good adventurers over the course of the weeks spent there.

{@i Mastodonsaurus} is an enormous amphibian from the Middle Triassic (245 million years ago) of Europe. It was one of the largest amphibians in the fossil record and superficially looked like a cross between a frog and a crocodile.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Mastodonsaurus} was huge for an amphibian, measuring up to 20 ft. long. It had an elongate body with a powerful tail and reduced, sprawling limbs. It had a very large triangular-shaped head, measuring 5 ft. long in the largest adults. Its eyes were on the top of its skull, rather than the side, and its jaws were lined with a double row of sharp conical teeth, as well as two tusks on the lower jaw that stuck out through holes in the upper jaw.

{@i Mastodonsaurus} was a powerful aquatic carnivore and, based on the position of its eyes, likely ambushed prey from below. Given its size, it probably ate a variety of other animals, presumably anything small enough for it to swallow. This idea is supported by tooth marks on other amphibian fossils that appear to be from {@i Mastodonsaurus}, although these could be the result of scavenging. Bite marks on {@i Mastodonsaurus} itself suggest that it was predated upon by large terrestrial carnivores, perhaps while trapped in a drying-up pool.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Mastodonsaurus} likely spent much of its time unmoving at the bottom of rivers, swamps, and pools of water, hiding in wait beneath mud. When prey came within range, it would rush forward with its mouth agape, sucking the prey towards it. {@i Mastodonsaurus} would then snap down, piercing the prey with its teeth and tusks. If a terrestrial animal was drinking on the waters edge, it may have slowly moved into position before rushing it and attempting to drag it back into the water. It's unlikely {@i Mastodonsaurus} was a social animal and they probably lived solitary lives, apart from coming together to mate. It would have spent as little time on land as possible, only leaving the water to move to new hunting grounds or find a mate.

We suggest {@i Mastodonsaurus} be played essentially as a crocodile-like animal, willing to lie in wait for prey for hours or even days. While able to attack creatures on land, it should be cautious of leaving the water and will quickly retreat after lunging out at prey. It should be solitary, although a party may encounter multiple {@i Mastodonsaurus} along a given river or waterway, evenly spaced in their own territories.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Mastodonsaurus} is a member of the Mastodonsauridae, a group of large seemingly piscivorous (fish-feeding) amphibians, many of which had prominent tusks. They were a successful group surviving from the Middle Triassic (250 million years ago) until the border of the Jurassic (199 million years ago). Mastodonsaurids were part of a wider order of amphibians called the Temnospondyli. entries: Mastodonsaurus can breathe in both air and water. When in water, it gains a +3 bonus to Dexterity saving throws.

trait.name: Perfect Ambusher
entries: While motionless at the bottom of a body of water, Mastodonsaurus is indistinguishable from the sediment. If it attacks from this position, it is always considered to be first in the initiative order (regardless of all other abilities, like the Alert feat), has advantage on its first attack, and that attack deals an additional {@damage 1d10} piercing damage.

Roll a {@dice 1d4} and consult the list below to determine the type of damage this ability deals. Additionally, Mastodonsaurus gains immunity to that damage type until its next turn.
{@dice 1d4} | Type
1 | Fire
2 | Cold
3 | Lightning
4 | Force

action.name: Tusked Bite
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 8} to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}17 ({@damage 2d10 + 6}) piercing damage.
A creature hit by this attack is {@condition grappled} (escape {@dc 14}).
{@i "MASS-TOE-DON-SORE-US"} {@b (NIPPLE TOOTH REPTILE)}

The swamps are a particularly dangerous place to venture. Not only are they slow to wade through, but many nasty predators hide in the murky waters. One of the scarier ones is a giant amphibian that lies in wait, fully submerged and totally indistinguishable from the mud its squalorin' in. Those who have the misfortune to step too close are met with an explosion of tusked fury – water flyin' everywhere. Ambushes like this were painfully common and we lost a few good adventurers over the course of the weeks spent there.

{@i Mastodonsaurus} is an enormous amphibian from the Middle Triassic (245 million years ago) of Europe. It was one of the largest amphibians in the fossil record and superficially looked like a cross between a frog and a crocodile.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Mastodonsaurus} was huge for an amphibian, measuring up to 20 ft. long. It had an elongate body with a powerful tail and reduced, sprawling limbs. It had a very large triangular-shaped head, measuring 5 ft. long in the largest adults. Its eyes were on the top of its skull, rather than the side, and its jaws were lined with a double row of sharp conical teeth, as well as two tusks on the lower jaw that stuck out through holes in the upper jaw.

{@i Mastodonsaurus} was a powerful aquatic carnivore and, based on the position of its eyes, likely ambushed prey from below. Given its size, it probably ate a variety of other animals, presumably anything small enough for it to swallow. This idea is supported by tooth marks on other amphibian fossils that appear to be from {@i Mastodonsaurus}, although these could be the result of scavenging. Bite marks on {@i Mastodonsaurus} itself suggest that it was predated upon by large terrestrial carnivores, perhaps while trapped in a drying-up pool.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Mastodonsaurus} likely spent much of its time unmoving at the bottom of rivers, swamps, and pools of water, hiding in wait beneath mud. When prey came within range, it would rush forward with its mouth agape, sucking the prey towards it. {@i Mastodonsaurus} would then snap down, piercing the prey with its teeth and tusks. If a terrestrial animal was drinking on the waters edge, it may have slowly moved into position before rushing it and attempting to drag it back into the water. It's unlikely {@i Mastodonsaurus} was a social animal and they probably lived solitary lives, apart from coming together to mate. It would have spent as little time on land as possible, only leaving the water to move to new hunting grounds or find a mate.

We suggest {@i Mastodonsaurus} be played essentially as a crocodile-like animal, willing to lie in wait for prey for hours or even days. While able to attack creatures on land, it should be cautious of leaving the water and will quickly retreat after lunging out at prey. It should be solitary, although a party may encounter multiple {@i Mastodonsaurus} along a given river or waterway, evenly spaced in their own territories.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Mastodonsaurus} is a member of the Mastodonsauridae, a group of large seemingly piscivorous (fish-feeding) amphibians, many of which had prominent tusks. They were a successful group surviving from the Middle Triassic (250 million years ago) until the border of the Jurassic (199 million years ago). Mastodonsaurids were part of a wider order of amphibians called the Temnospondyli. These were giant amphibious carnivores with a global range that appeared in the Middle Triassic (220 million years ago) and persisted for 100 million years, up until the Early Cretaceous (120 million years ago).

action.name: Predatory Strike

Megalosaurus lashes out with one of its myriad attacks - headbutting, clawing, biting, or lashing with its tail. When making a Predatory Strike, you can select either bludgeoning, piercing, or slashing as the damage type.

{@i "MEG-AH-LOW-SORE-US"} {@b (GREAT REPTILE)}

This is a beast that I'd read lots about in the ancient libraries of my university – the first dinosaur fossil ever described by scientists. When we first sighted it, I was all giddy with excitement. But, nothin' prepared me for how magnificent and deadly it was. It attacked without warnin' and unleashed a flurry of claws, teeth, kicks, and tail swipes. We were able to fend it off with some cold steel, but our cleric had a hearty job of healin' us up afterwards.

{@i Megalosaurus} was a medium sized theropod from the Middle Jurassic (166 million years ago) Taynton Limestone and Chipping Norton formations of England. {@i Megalosaurus} is one of the most famous dinosaurs as it was the first taxon to be formally described.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Megalosaurus'} fossils are incomplete, but it is thought to have been approximately 30 ft. long and weighed between 1.5 – 2 tonnes. While smaller than later giant theropods, it was still one of the largest carnivorous dinosaurs of the Jurassic. Overall, it was a robust animal, with thick legs and short powerful forelimbs. It had a robust skull that was relatively low and long, filled with curved blade-like teeth.

As the biggest and heaviest carnivore known from the Middle Jurassic of England, {@i Megalosaurus} may have been the arch-predator of its habitat. Its heavy build suggests that it was perhaps analogous to tyrannosaurs, overpowering prey rather than engaging in fast chases. The Taynton Limestone and Chipping Norton formations were both deposited in sub-tropical lagoons, conditions that attract a variety of animals, all of which would have been potential prey for {@i Megalosaurus}. However, it may also have fed on fish or aquatic reptiles pulled from the lagoon.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Based on the shape of its jugal (cheek bone), {@i Megalosaurus'} eyes were probably on the sides of its head, similar to {@i Allosaurus} ({@b page 197}). This suggests that it chased prey down over relatively long distances, rather than ambushing over short distances. Ambushing requires binocular vision for bursts of speed, but chasing allows a predator to determine distance by swinging its head. Like most large carnivores, it would have also been an opportunistic scavenger, using its size to bully other carnivores away from a carcass.

We suggest {@i Megalosaurus} be played as a patient animal that patrols a territory. It could patrol a watering hole and take advantage of desperate, dehydrated animals trying to drink, charging them. However, large modern land predators spend most of their time resting, and {@i Megalosaurus} almost certainly did the same. It is more likely that a party will encounter a dozing {@i Megalosaurus} than an actively hunting one, although it will take the opportunity to strike if someone wanders too close.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Megalosaurus} was one of the largest members of the Megalosauridae. This was a group of small-medium sized theropods with relatively low but elongated skulls that are primarily known from Europe, with some occurrences in the Americas and Africa. Interestingly, within the larger group Megalosauroidea, their closest relatives appear to be the highly derived and unusual spinosaurids like Spinosaurus ({@b page 75}). Most megalosaurs are from Jurassic formations, although some did survive into the Late Cretaceous (93 million years ago).

entries.name: The First of Many
entries: The first record of {@i Megalosaurus} was the end of an isolated fragmentary femur (sadly now lost) described in 1763 by Brookes. He gave it the comedic name of {@i Scrotum humanum} due to its unfortunate shape. Later in the 1700s, a partial jaw was discovered that was eventually named {@i Megalosaurus} by William Buckland in 1824. It was considered to be some kind of lizard or crocodile and in 1842 Richard Owen erected the group Dinosauria to house it, {@i Iguanodon} ({@b page 135}), and {@i Hylaeosaurus}. While {@i Megalosaurus} would ultimately be eclipsed by the more spectacular dinosaurs of the American fossil rush, it remains one of the most historically important taxa and sculptures of its original reconstruction still stand in The Crystal Palace, London.

entries: The first time a humanoid (including player characters) sees Megalosaurus while within 60 ft. of it, they are affected by a curse that causes them to momentarily lose all understanding of dinosaurs and other Mesozoic creatures (no save allowed). The curse persists for two rounds or until they take damage. For each creature afflicted, roll a {@dice 1d4} and consult the table below to determine how they behave:
1. Curious - The humanoid becomes unaware of any threat Megalosaurus poses. They cannot attack it or cast detrimental spells/cantrips against it and must move directly towards it if possible.

2. Threatened - On the humanoid's next turn, they must make a ranged or melee attack against Megalosaurus or cast a cantrip that targets it. If the humanoid has Multiattack, they instead only make a single attack.

3. Adoring - The humanoid must attempt to feed or heal Megalosaurus on their next turn. Megalosaurus can accept food as a reaction and will then prioritise killing other creatures over any that have fed it or healed it.
4. Terrified - The humanoid becomes {@condition frightened} of Megalosaurus.

trait.name: Speciose
entries: Early Titanosaurs diversified rapidly. Each time the party encounters a new Mnyamawamtuka (including this one), select or roll for an adaptation on the Minor Mutation Table (page 218). Apply that mutation to that Mnyamawamtuka. You do not need to increase Mnyamawamtuka's CR for the mutation gained.

trait.name: Columnar Limbs
entries: Mnyamawamtuka's strong legs make it exceedingly difficult to topple. It has an additional +5 modifier and advantage on saving throws to avoid being knocked {@condition prone}. However, Mnyamawamtuka has a further -3 modifier (total -5, included above) and disadvantage on Dexterity saving throws.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Mnyamawamtuka chooses the attack action, it may make one Shovelling Bite attack and two Whipping Tail attacks.

action.name: Shovelling Bite
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 5} to hit, reach 15 ft., one target. {@h}6 ({@damage 1d8 + 2}) piercing damage.
Mnyamawamtuka's semi-spatulate shaped teeth pull at any target they bite. A creature hit by this attack must succeed a {@dc 15} Strength saving throw or drop an item it is wielding.

action.name: Whipping Tail
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 5} to hit, reach 10 ft., one target. {@h}5 ({@damage 1d6 + 2}) slashing damage.
{@i "MM-NYA-MA-WAH-MM-TOO-KA"} {@b (BEAST OF THE MTUKA RIVER DRAINAGE)}

Among our travels we had seen myriad behaviours of various dinosaurs, includin' complex matin' rituals. None were so excitin' as these huge sauropods. They pranced around each other with uncharacteristic grace in a wonderful' ballet that had no doubt been practiced hundreds of times. When we encounter such a thin', we stay to watch but ensure never to interfere. That policy gifted us their complete matin' ritual and it was well worth our patience.

{@i Mnyamawamtuka} is an Early Cretaceous (110 million years ago) titanosaur from the Galula Formation in Tanzania. Known from a single immature specimen, it is an important fossil for understanding sauropod diversification.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: The {@i Mnyamawamtuka} fossil is from a relatively small sauropod, 25 ft. long and weighing about 1.5 tonnes. Like all sauropods, it had hollow bones filled with air sacs (pneumatisation) that greatly reduced its weight and gave it unidirectional breathing (air flowing through the lungs and air sacs in one direction). As the bones weren't completely fused when the animal died, it is likely it was immature. In many ways it was a typical titanosaur with large columnar limbs, shovel-like teeth, and a long neck and tail. The middle vertebrae in the tail had an unusual heart-shaped cross-section and it is speculated to have had bony osteoderms (bones embedded in the skin) dotting its hide.

Titanosaurs were all herbivores and, based on its teeth, {@i Mnyamawamtuka} likely had a similar diet to its relatives. This would have included ferns, conifers, cycads, and early grasses. It may have competed with other sauropods for food, as they are one of the few dinosaurs known from the Galula Formation, although their apparent abundance is likely a result of biases in this site's type of fossilisation.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Little is known of {@i Mnyamawamtuka} and its behaviour, but based on other studies we suggest it behaved in a similar fashion to its larger relatives like {@i Paralititan} ({@b page 71)}, with young animals growing up separately from adults before joining a herd when large enough to avoid being trampled. As the specimen we have is from an immature animal, we can't be certain of the maximum size that this animal reached.

We suggest taking a fairly conservative approach when playing {@i Mnyamawamtuka} by making it relatively peaceful when unchallenged, but aggressive if threatened. Adults should roam open spaces constantly feeding, whereas juveniles should congregate in larger numbers within the safety of dense forests. Given the high diversity of early titanosaurs, feel free to alter or add behaviour based on any adaptations given to {@i Mnyamawamtuka.}

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Mnyamawamtuka} is a titanosaur sauropod, one of the most successful groups of Cretaceous herbivores. The earliest member of this group ({@i Ninjatitan}) arose 140 million years ago in South America, and within 30 million years the group had a global population and were highly diverse. By the Late Cretaceous, they had become the last surviving sauropods and continued to thrive until the end-Cretaceous extinction event.

{@i "MOE-SAH-SORE-US"} {@b (MEUSE RIVER REPTILE)}

Sailin' on the ancient sea ain't without its dangers. All the usual monsters still haunt the deep oceans, but there's also some pretty mean reptiles that swim the surfaces too. Durin' one stormy night, we sighted a huge one breach – its slick body glistening in the moonlight. It seemed completely unphased by the bad weather and was probably scoutin' us out – figurin' out what our ship was and whether it could eat us. If someone had fallen in, I'm sure they wouldn't have stood a chance.

{@i Mosasaurus} is a large aquatic reptile from the Late Cretaceous (80 million years ago) and inhabited oceans across the world. A member of the squamates (snakes and lizards), it is one of the largest aquatic predators in the fossil record.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Mosasaurus} was undeniably huge but, due to a lack of complete specimens, our size estimates vary dramatically from 36 - 56 ft. in length, with a potential maximum weight of 11 tonnes. Its body was elongate, broader towards the front and tapered from the middle. Its tail ended in an asymmetrical fluke, with a longer lower boned fin and a smaller soft-tissue upper fin. Its skull was long and large, accounting for 1/7th of the total body length. It had large conical teeth and a second set of palatal teeth on the roof of its mouth. {@i Mosasaurus'} limbs were adapted into swimming paddles, although without the extreme skeletal modifications seen in plesiosaurs. Its nostrils were set on the top of the skull like a dolphin and, as with all marine reptiles, it breathed air.

{@i Mosasaurus} was carnivorous and likely had a wide diet. Based on stomach contents, we know that small mosasaurs ate fish, but bite marks and isotopic analyses demonstrate that {@i Mosasaurus} was an apex carnivore feeding on turtles, plesiosaurs, fish, nautiloids, and other smaller mosasaurs. It is known to have inhabited the North American Western Interior Sea, the European Tethys ocean, and waters around Antarctica.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Mosasaurus} probably hunted close to the surface, perhaps using countershading (dark on top, light on the bottom) as camouflage before rushing prey from underneath. They likely gave birth to live young and, based on low numbers of babies birthed (k-selected), may have had some form of parenting behaviour. However, infants would have been able to swim and feed shortly after birth. While it is highly unlikely these predators lived in social groups, there is strong evidence of intraspecific (same species) combat. Several specimens have been found with bite wounds from other {@i Mosasaurus}, some of which have healed and others that were likely fatal. These may have been caused by territorial fighting or cannibalism.

We suggest that {@i Mosasaurus} be played as a largely solitary predator with strong territorial instincts. It will not tolerate any intruders into its territory, with the exception of its own young offspring. It should live in relatively deep waters and be most dangerous to parties in small-medium sized boats that have the same silhouette as {@i Mosasaurus}' prey from underneath. When hunting, its countershading will camouflage it and its presence may only be revealed by the panicked disappearance of smaller marine life. If a boat is viewed as a territorial threat, players might be warned by the sight or sound of a {@i Mosasaurus} slapping the surface of the water with its paddle.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: Mosasaurids are the last of the Mosasauroidea, a group of specialised squamate reptiles that adapted for permanent life in the water. Mosasaurids were extremely successful, appearing 100 million years ago and becoming the dominant oceanic predators in the Late Cretaceous, outcompeting ichthyosaurs and plesiosaurs. They spread throughout the world's oceans and survived up until the end-Cretaceous extinction.

There is ongoing debate about where in Squamata the mosasaurids sit, with them usually being placed as either the sister group to snakes or monitor lizards. However, there now appears to be increasing consensus that they are more closely related to snakes.

{@i "NO-TOE-OH-SORE-US"} {@b (FALSE REPTILE)}

The beach was a raucous place. Along the rocks and shingle there were dozens of large four-flippered reptiles baskin'. They were makin' loud low grumbles that echoed off the cliffs. I reckon they were complain' to each other about the lack of space on the best rocks and some were pushin' and shovin'. They were cumbersome on land, but the ones out at sea were rollin'
with the waves with ease, usin' their protrudin' teeth to snatch fish.
{@i Nothosaurus} was a large semi-aquatic reptile from the Middle Triassic (240-210 million years ago). It was a sauropterygian, just like its distant relatives, the aquatic plesiosaurs.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Nothosaurus} was a highly successful carnivorous animal found in shallow ocean deposits in many countries, including in the Netherlands, Germany, and China. It had a low, rounded body with short limbs and an elongate neck. Its toes were elongated with webbing between them, turning its feet into pseudo-paddles. Its skull was wide and low, with long jaws full of sharp, needle-like teeth. {@i Nothosaurus} varied in length between 13-22 ft., meaning the largest individuals were bigger than modern great white sharks.

{@i Nothosaurus} lived in open water and so shared its environment with a wide variety of animals including fish, cephalopods, and other marine reptiles. Its teeth were sharp, circular in cross-section, and needle-like, making them excellent at grabbing slippery fish, or soft bodied animals like cephalopods and jellyfish. Given their large size, other smaller marine reptiles were also potential prey. Fossil trackways also indicate {@i Nothosaurus} may have swum low over sandy bottoms, stirring them up in search of hiding prey.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Nothosaurus} was likely a near-shore predator, hunting in shallow seas and coming onto the land to rest and possibly mate. While it possessed functional legs, they were not well adapted to life out of the water and it would have been clumsy on land. While in water, it would have been a swift and dangerous predator. Like ichthyosaurs and plesiosaurs, several species of {@i Nothosaurus} gave birth to live young (likely in water), although the number of offspring and subsequent level of parental care is unknown.

We suggest that {@i Nothosaurus} should act quite differently depending on whether it is on land or in water. On land it should be defensive, making threatening calls and displays at a party that gets too close. In water it should be a much more direct threat, willing to stalk or strike without fear. Players near the surface of the water should be especially vulnerable as attacking prey from underneath is a common strategy used by aquatic predators.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Nothosaurus} was the largest member of the Nothosauridae. This group arose in the Middle Triassic (247 million years ago) and spread globally before becoming extinct in the Late Triassic (210 million years ago). The group was quite conservative in their morphology, with most members sharing similar traits. They were the sibling group to the Pachypleurosaura, which were smaller, more primitive, and less well adapted for the ocean. Together, these two groups were close relatives of the Plesiosaura, an incredibly successful group of marine reptiles that would dominate the oceanic environment of the Mesozoic. Combined, these three families were part of a larger group, the Sauropterygia.

Nyctosaurus may only perform this attack if it flew at least 50 ft. this turn.

{@i "NICK-TOE-SORE-US"} {@b (NIGHT REPTILE)}

Sometimes you see somethin' that makes you double-take. While hikin' up a cliff, we spotted a small group of pterosaurs circling below. They were using the air currents to gain altitude. It took 'em a few minutes to rise, but as they passed us, we saw that they had the strangest huge Y-shaped crests protrudin' from the backs of their heads. How the hell they could fly with such unwieldly ornamentation is beyond me, but they were!

{@i Nyctosaurus} was a medium sized pterosaur from the Late Cretaceous Niobara Formation (86-83 million years ago). It was a relative of the much larger {@i Pteranodon}, and had a highly distinctive crest and wing morphology.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Nyctosaurus} was medium sized with a wingspan of approximately 6.5 ft. Its wings were extremely long relative to its body size, which would have given it a very upright posture when standing on the ground. Unlike the majority of pterosaurs, it had lost almost all of its fingers, only retaining the hyper-elongated wing finger, and that was also composed of only three bones rather than the usual four. Its jaws were long and toothless, and it had an unusual head crest composed of a short base with one long bar extending upwards, and another pointing backwards. These bars were up to 3 ft. in length on some individuals and were superficially antler-like.

{@i Nyctosaurus} is found exclusively in the Niobrara Formation, which is comprised of Late Cretaceous chalky rock formed along the edge of the Western Interior Sea, a stretch of shallow water that divided North America in two. This was a highly productive shallow seaway, brimming with life. In this setting, {@i Nyctosaurus} is seen as an analogue to the modern albatross, spending much of its time soaring over open ocean. This, combined with the strong similarity to the piscivorous (fish-eating) {@i Pteranodon}, suggests that it fed on the same food, catching fish on-the-wing as it flew low over water. Alternatively, it could have had the ability to plunge into the water like a modern Gannet. {@i Nyctosaurus} probably ate a wide diversity of fish, but may have consumed soft bodied invertebrates like squid or jellyfish as well.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Nyctosaurus}' extremely long wings and lack of fingers would have made it one of the more awkward and ungainly pterosaurs on land. It likely spent a short amount of its life on the ground, either when nesting or resting, and spent the majority of its time soaring. It may even have rested on-the-wing.

We recommend that {@i Nyctosaurus} be played in a manner befitting modern sea birds. It should prefer to remain in the air when possible and take any opportunity to snatch an easy meal, whether this is an unwary fish or the discarded remains of a party member's dinner. It should be cautious about being approached, retreating but never truly being driven off. If defending a nesting site, several {@i Nyctosaurus} should mob intruders. Its crest will largely be used for communication with other {@i Nyctosaurus}.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Nyctosaurus} was the most well-known member of the small family Nyctosauridae, with only two other taxa in the group. Members of this group have been found in Africa, North America, and South America, suggesting that they were fairly widespread. Nyctosauridae were exclusively from the Late Cretaceous and were related to the more well-known Pteranodontidae.

trait.name: Snatch Feeder
entries: If Nyctosaurus is flying, it does not provoke attacks of opportunity when it moves out of an enemy's reach.

trait.name: "Night Lizard" (2/day)
entries: Nyctosaurus can cast {@spell Darkness} at will without requiring components or a spell slot. However, it automatically loses concentration if it takes any damage.
Nyctosaurus has a blindsight of 60 ft.

trait.name: Aura of Blindsight
entries: Any other friendly Nyctosaurus that starts its turn within or moves within 100 ft. of this Nyctosaurus gains a blindsight of 10 ft. for 1 minute if it was not already using these optional magical rules.

action.name: Headcrest 'Antler' Crash
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 4} to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}3 ({@damage 1d6}) bludgeoning damage plus 3 ({@damage 1d6}) piercing damage.
Nyctosaurus may only perform this attack if it flew at least 50 ft. this turn.
When Nyctosaurus makes this attack, it lands on the ground.

action.name: Beaked Peck
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 3} to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}4 ({@damage 1d4 + 2}) piercing damage.
{@i "NICK-TOE-SORE-US"} {@b (NIGHT REPTILE)}

Sometimes you see somethin' that makes you double-take. While hikin' up a cliff, we spotted a small group of pterosaurs circling below. They were using the air currents to gain altitude. It took 'em a few minutes to rise, but as they passed us, we saw that they had the strangest huge Y-shaped crests protrudin' from the backs of their heads. How the hell they could fly with such unwieldly ornamentation is beyond me, but they were!

{@i Nyctosaurus} was a medium sized pterosaur from the Late Cretaceous Niobara Formation (86-83 million years ago). It was a relative of the much larger {@i Pteranodon}, and had a highly distinctive crest and wing morphology.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Nyctosaurus} was medium sized with a wingspan of approximately 6.5 ft. Its wings were extremely long relative to its body size, which would have given it a very upright posture when standing on the ground. Unlike the majority of pterosaurs, it had lost almost all of its fingers, only retaining the hyper-elongated wing finger, and that was also composed of only three bones rather than the usual four. Its jaws were long and toothless, and it had an unusual head crest composed of a short base with one long bar extending upwards, and another pointing backwards. These bars were up to 3 ft. in length on some individuals and were superficially antler-like.

{@i Nyctosaurus} is found exclusively in the Niobrara Formation, which is comprised of Late Cretaceous chalky rock formed along the edge of the Western Interior Sea, a stretch of shallow water that divided North America in two. This was a highly productive shallow seaway, brimming with life. In this setting, {@i Nyctosaurus} is seen as an analogue to the modern albatross, spending much of its time soaring over open ocean. This, combined with the strong similarity to the piscivorous (fish-eating) {@i Pteranodon}, suggests that it fed on the same food, catching fish on-the-wing as it flew low over water. Alternatively, it could have had the ability to plunge into the water like a modern Gannet. {@i Nyctosaurus} probably ate a wide diversity of fish, but may have consumed soft bodied invertebrates like squid or jellyfish as well.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Nyctosaurus}' extremely long wings and lack of fingers would have made it one of the more awkward and ungainly pterosaurs on land. It likely spent a short amount of its life on the ground, either when nesting or resting, and spent the majority of its time soaring. It may even have rested on-the-wing.

We recommend that {@i Nyctosaurus} be played in a manner befitting modern sea birds. It should prefer to remain in the air when possible and take any opportunity to snatch an easy meal, whether this is an unwary fish or the discarded remains of a party member's dinner. It should be cautious about being approached, retreating but never truly being driven off. If defending a nesting site, several {@i Nyctosaurus} should mob intruders. Its crest will largely be used for communication with other {@i Nyctosaurus}.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Nyctosaurus} was the most well-known member of the small family Nyctosauridae, with only two other taxa in the group. Members of this group have been found in Africa, North America, and South America, suggesting that they were fairly widespread. Nyctosauridae were exclusively from the Late Cretaceous and were related to the more well-known Pteranodontidae.

trait.name: Brooder
entries: Oviraptor are excellent parents and fiercely territorial of their nests. If Oviraptor is defending its nest, it attacks recklessly, giving it advantage on all attacks, but all attacks against it also have advantage.

entries: When hit by an attack, Oviraptor can use its reaction to reduce any incoming bludgeoning damage by {@dice 1d4}. When taking falling damage, Oviraptor can use its reaction to reduce the falling damage it takes by {@dice 2d10}.

action.name: Multiattack

entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 4} to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}5 ({@damage 1d6 + 2}) piercing damage.

{@i "OH-VIH-RAP-TOR"} {@b (EGG PLUNDERER)}

We had started to run low on rations while trekkin' through the badlands. We had made sure we had surplus water, but food was the problem. After a few more hours of walkin' with growlin' stomachs, we encountered a series of nests guarded by honkin' squawkin' beaked gangly theropods. There was a wealth of eggs, but I knew we'd be in for a fierce fight to get 'em.
Still, hunger pushes a man to do dangerous thin's.

{@i Oviraptor} is a small Late Cretaceous (75-71 million years ago) theropod from the Djadochta Formation of Mongolia and several other localities. Its egg-thieving name is the result of a misinterpretation of a remarkable fossil.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Oviraptor} was a small theropod at about 5 ft. long, with well-developed feathered plumage, a toothless beaked jaw, and a crest on the middle of its skull. Its legs and arms were quite long for its size with elongated fingers and large claws. By contrast, its tail was quite short for a theropod and ended in a pygostyle (the vertebrae were fused together), an adaptation that has been extended to the entire tail in modern birds.

{@i Oviraptor} is known from a number of formations in Mongolia which shared an arid/semi-arid environment with seasonal rains and rivers. While they do occur in wetlands, higher numbers are found in more desert-like environments. This seems to correspond with the size of other dinosaurs present, with {@i Oviraptor} being more common in arid formations with generally smaller dinosaurs. It is thought to have been an omnivore, hunting small prey while also feeding on low lying vegetation.

The original {@i Oviraptor} specimen (holotype) discovered in 1923 was a partial skeleton found lying on top of a nest of eggs. These eggs were initially misidentified as {@i Protoceratops} eggs and {@i Oviraptor}'s unusual mouth morphology led scientists to presume that it was a specialist egg feeder. This image of {@i Oviraptor} as an egg thief took hold in both scientific and non-scientific media as the defining aspect of the animal. Later CT scans revealed that the eggs in fact belonged to {@i Oviraptor}, and the fossil actually represented a protective parent shielding its nest from a colossal sandstorm.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Oviraptor} was probably an opportunistic feeder, foraging for anything that it could devour and snatching up small prey items, rather than actively hunting. It was a protective parent that guarded its nest with its life and almost certainly formed mated pairs. Multiple pairs then probably lived in small flocks, in a similar manner to many modern social birds.

We recommend {@i Oviraptor} be played as a highly social creature, with loud and expressive communication between its own species. It should readily flee from threats unless it is guarding a nest, where it should be exceptionally aggressive.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Oviraptor} is the most well-known member of the Oviraptoridae. These were generally small theropods with toothless jaws covered in keratin, often sporting a head crest that varied in shape from species to species. They were common in the arid environments of the Late Cretaceous, throughout what is now the Gobi Desert.

These creatures will now steal eggs and/or young of other species (including humanoids), but rather than devouring them, will instead care for them diligently and raise them as their own. Oviraptor gains proficiency in Stealth checks while stealing offspring.

entries: Pterodaustro cannot be {@condition poisoned} or damaged by contaminated or laced food or water.

Every other creature within 5 ft. of it must succeed a {@dc 8} Strength saving throw or be knocked {@condition prone}. Pterodaustro then begins to fly and must fly 10 ft. in a straight line (either horizontally, or vertically up).
Pterodaustro can only begin flying by using this ability, or if it is falling.

{@i "TEAR-OH-DOW-STROW"} {@b (WING FROM THE SOUTH)}

Not all of our adventures were bombastic fights of life'n'death. Some days we really were just able to enjoy the sights. One warm evenin', while the sun was settin', we were relaxin' on a lakeside. We watched a flock of a dozen pterosaurs wadin'

just off the shore. They had heads like upturned hairbrushes and were filterin' the water through their bristle-like teeth. With each slosh, they pulled small invertebrates out of the silt and gobbled 'em down. The sound of the water lappin' as they fed was so soothin', it almost put me to sleep right then and there.
{@i Pterodaustro} is a pterosaur from the Early Cretaceous (105 million years ago) Lagarcito Formation of Argentina. It has a distinctive and bizarre comb of tightly packed elongated teeth.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Pterodaustro} was a medium-sized pterosaur with a 10 ft. wingspan and weighed around 20 lbs. It had relatively robust limbs, large feet, and a long tail for its group, although much shorter than earlier long-tailed pterosaurs. {@i Pterodaustro}'s most distinctive feature was its head, which was very elongate, with most of that length being the curved jaws. Its lower jaw had over a thousand exceptionally thin, tall, blunt, and densely packed teeth that were 0.04 in. (1 mm) wide and 1.5 in. tall. These teeth formed a distinctive bristly comb superficially similar to the baleen of whales or the beak filaments of flamingos and are so unusual that they form the basis for interpreting {@i Pterodaustro}'s ecology.

{@i Pterodaustro} is considered to be a filter-feeding animal and it almost certainly gulped water, pushed it through its fine teeth, and swallowed whole any small invertebrates, fish, plankton, or plant fragments that remained. These would then be broken down in its stomach by small stones (gastroliths). Filter-feeding has been suggested for other closely related pterosaurs, but {@i Pterodaustro} possesses the most obvious and specialised adaptations for it.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Pterodaustro} is usually depicted as the pterosaur analogue for modern flamingos. Its strong legs and wide feet would have allowed it to wade through shallow water comfortably or perhaps even swim. Research on {@i Pterodaustro}'s eggs indicate that its hatchlings were precocial (able to be independent) and probably had little parental care. This adaptation allowed {@i Pterodaustro} to evolve its cumbersome feeding apparatus, which would have otherwise prevented parental care in other lineages.

We suggest that {@i Pterodaustro} live in large flocks that settle in lakes and marshlands to feed. Each flock should have sentries: individuals who periodically scan the horizon for potential threats. When startled, the flock should simultaneously launch into the air, fleeing and confusing predators. As they swallow stones, {@i Pterodaustro} might accidentally ingest small gems washed out into lakes by local rivers. This makes them a high-value target for hunters, and {@i Pterodaustro} will be very wary of humanoids.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Pterodaustro} is a member of the Ctenochasmatoidea. This is a group of pterosaurs that arose in the Late Jurassic (152 million years ago), survived until the Early Cretaceous (105 million years ago), and includes the famous {@i Pterodactylus}. The group was reasonably successful, with fossils found on most continents. Basal animals like {@i Pterodactylus} were more generalist carnivores but the group became more specialist wading or aquatic feeders in later forms. One of the most derived subgroups, the Ctenochasmatidae (which includes {@i Pterodaustro}) became the most heavily specialised filter feeders.

You may roll a {@dice 1d10} or select from the table below to determine the gemstone swallowed, colour hue, and damage type:
{@dice 1d10} | Gemstone, Colour, Type
1 | Ruby, Red, Fire
2 | Sapphire, Sky Blue, Cold
3 | Topaz, Yellow, Lightning
4 | Augite, Black, Poison
5 | Jade, Green, Acid
6 | Tanzanite, Cerulean, Thunder
7 | Citrine, Golden, Radiant
8 | Amethyst, Purple, Psychic
9 | Malachite, Viridian, Necrotic
10 | Labradorite, Iridescent Rainbow, Force
When Pterodaustro is slain, the gemstone it swallowed is regurgitated (worth 50 gp).
