entries: Each creature within a 15 ft. radius in front of Quetzalcoatlus (a semi-circle with the centre of the flat edge positioned on Quetzalcoatlus) must succeed a {@dc 16} Constitution saving throw or take 17 ({@damage 5d6}) bludgeoning and 17 ({@damage 5d6}) thunder damage. On a success they take half as much damage.
{@i "QUET-ZAL-COH-AH-TA-LUS"} {@b (AFTER THE AZTEC GOD QUETZACOATL)}

Few thin's compare to the monumental sight of a full-grown Quetz soarin' above. While sailin' along the coast we had the opportunity to witness their annual migration, with several spotted each day. Their huge blade-like wings let 'em glide effortlessly over the waters, as they made their way to their inland nestin' grounds. Biggest flyin' thin' I ever saw. We caught the sight of a couple more many hundreds of feet up too – tiny shapes that lost all sense of scale in the endless sky.

{@i Quetzalcoatlus} was a giant azhdarchid pterosaur from the Late Cretaceous (68-66 million years ago) of North America. Well known for being one of the largest flying animals, it stood tall enough to look a {@i Tyrannosaurus} in the eye.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Quetzalcoatlus} is among the tallest azdarchid pterosaurs, reaching a height of at least 10 ft. at the shoulder and 16 ft. at the head while standing. Its wings were much broader than other pterosaurs like {@i Nyctosaurus} ({@b page 158}) or {@i Rhamphorhynchus} ({@b page 168}) and, when fully outstretched, could span over 30 ft. across. Like other azdarchids, {@i Quetzalcoatlus} was well adapted for terrestrial movement, with sturdy legs and forearms. Its neck was very long and muscular, topped with an elongate toothless skull that had a hard keratinous beak and bony crest on the top. While not as heavily built as {@i Hatzegopteryx} ({@b page 89}), it was still one of the heaviest ever flying animals at over 400 lb. in weight.

{@i Quetzalcoatlus} is known from the Javelina Formation in Texas, North America. This Late Cretaceous Formation was deposited in a rich floodplain with nearby rivers and lakes. It is thought that these were situated far inland, with surrounding subtropical forests. {@i Quetzalcoatlus} was certainly capable of flying great distances and probably inhabited many environments, but would have favoured areas where there was room for it to take off and land. It did this via the 'quad-launch' method, propelling itself into the air using all four limbs, rather than taking a running start like some large birds.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Much of the behaviour of {@i Quetzalcoatlus} is still unknown, but some evidence suggests that the largest ones were solitary. It may have flown long distances to move between feeding sites, but otherwise spent most of its life walking along the ground, searching for prey. {@i Quetzalcoatlus} was previously thought to have been a specialised skim-feeder, but biomechanical analysis demonstrated that this was impossible. It is now thought to have hunted like a Indian hornbill, searching for smaller creatures while walking.

{@i Quetzalcoatlus}' size and proportions meant that it could not incubate its eggs by sitting on them, and instead likely buried them in warm rotting plant matter. Larger pterosaurs seem to have been less precocial than smaller ones, and hatchlings were probably fed and protected by a watchful adult.

We recommend that {@i Quetzalcoatlus} be played as a confident predator, stalking the landscape in search of prey. It may have been indiscriminate in its attempts to eat creatures smaller than itself, similar to a pelican, or curious of novel objects. While Medium-sized party members would likely be on the upper limit of prey, {@i Quetzalcoatlus} should still be a major predatory threat. As it was probably solitary, adult {@i Quetzalcoatlus} should view each other as direct competition and may prioritise fighting each other over hunting prey, so long as they aren't courting.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Quetzalcoatlus} is the tallest member of the Azdarchidae. This is a group of medium-to-giant sized pterosaurs that occurred globally during the Cretaceous. They are generally characterised by their strongly-elongated neckbones and their long limbs, believed to be well adapted for a walking lifestyle. They are all toothless, with some having spear-like beaks. Their closest relatives are the Chaoyangopterids, a group of smaller pterosaurs that are thought to have lived similar lifestyles.

trait.name: Quad Launch (Quetzalcoatlus)
entries: If not already flying, as a bonus action, Quetzalcoatlus can launch itself into the air. Every other creature within 10 ft. of it must succeed a {@dc 16} Strength saving throw or be knocked {@condition prone}. Quetzalcoatlus then begins to fly and must fly 20 ft. in a straight line (either horizontally, or vertically up).
Quetzalcoatlus can only begin flying by using this ability, or if it is falling.

trait.name: Stalking Stalk, Silent Glider
entries: If Quetzalcoatlus is walking within a forest or is flying, it has advantage on Stealth checks.

trait.name: Vicious Descent
entries: If Quetzalcoatlus began the turn flying and subsequently lands before making an attack, increase the damage of its first Colossal Peck attack by {@damage 1d10} this turn.

trait.name: Eye in the Sky
entries: While flying, Quetzalcoatlus has advantage on Perception checks that involve sight.

trait.name: Low-Gravity Aura
entries: Quetzalcoatlus drastically reduces the weight of objects and creatures in contact with it (including itself). A real Quetzalcoatlus would usually be able to carry a maximum weight of about 80-100 lb. This ability increases its carry weight limit to 500 lb. and any howdah or saddle attached to it are considered weightless for the purposes of its carry weight. For each 100 lb. Quetzalcoatlus is carrying, reduce its fly speed by 10 ft.

trait.name: Aircraft-Sized Animal
entries: Quetzalcoatlus can carry up to three Medium (or smaller) humanoids on its back, and two further Medium (or smaller) humanoids in its hind claws. For each creature carried in this way, Quetzalcoatlus' fly speed is reduced by 10 ft.
If Quetzalcoatlus is carrying two or more creatures using this rule, it cannot use its Lift Off action.

trait.name: Feathered God
entries: You may choose for Quetzalcoatlus to be covered in vivid feathers.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: When Quetzalcoatlus chooses the attack action, it may make three Colossal Peck attacks.

action.name: Colossal Peck
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 8} to hit, reach 10 ft., one target. {@h}19 ({@damage 2d10 + 8}) piercing damage.
If a creature hit by this attack is Medium or Small in size, it must succeed a {@dc 16} Strength saving throw or be knocked {@condition prone}.

action.name: Thunderous Flap {@recharge 5}
entries: Each creature within a 15 ft. radius in front of Quetzalcoatlus (a semi-circle with the centre of the flat edge positioned on Quetzalcoatlus) must succeed a {@dc 16} Constitution saving throw or take 17 ({@damage 5d6}) bludgeoning and 17 ({@damage 5d6}) thunder damage. On a success they take half as much damage.

action.name: Lift Off
entries: While flying, as an action, Quetzalcoatlus may pick up an object (usually) weighing up to 500 lb. and up to Large in size. While carrying this object, its fly speed is reduced by 10 ft. for each 100 lb. the object weighs.

Quetzalcoatlus may drop a carried object at any point during its turn. If this object is dropped on a creature, that creature must succeed a {@dc 16} Dexterity saving throw or take {@damage 2d10} bludgeoning damage for each 100 lb. the object weighs. If the object is dropped from 50 ft. or higher, the bludgeoning damage is doubled, but the Dexterity saving throw DC is reduced to 12.

trait.name: Morbid Regurgitation
entries: Rhamphorhynchus vomits up its stomach contents upon death. When Rhamphorhynchus dies, one creature within 5 ft. must succeed a {@dc 8} Dexterity saving throw or take {@damage 1d4} acid damage.

trait.name: Swooping Evasion
entries: If Rhamphorhynchus is flying, it can use its reaction to increase its AC by 3 when an enemy makes an attack of opportunity against it.
Rhamphorhynchus can use its reaction to give itself advantage on any Dexterity saving throw when forced to make one.

trait.name: Growth Spurt
entries: Rhamphorhynchus can be found as either a juvenile (Tiny) or adult (Small) creature.

action.name: Spike-Toothed Snap
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 3} to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}3 ({@damage 1d4 + 1}) piercing damage.
{@i "RAM-FOR-RING-CUS"} {@b (BEAK SNOUT)}

These tiny lil' pterosaurs are such a pain. They're highly inquisitive and have a nasty habit of snatchin' stuff right out of your hands. I guess they're used to grabbin' food, since they sometimes swallow the stuff without even thinkin'. Reminds me of herring gulls back in our time. Difference is, herring gulls ain't armed with dozens of protrudin' teeth! The hatchlin's of this species are gregarious – they find safety in numbers and bunch up into swarms. They get pretty hungry too and anyone carryin' food tends to get mobbed pretty quick. For somethin' so small, they can be quite fearsome in numbers. Almost like lil' angry flyin' piranhas.

{@i Rhamphorhynchus} was a medium sized rhamphorhynchid pterosaur from the Late Jurassic (150 million years ago) of Germany and Britain. It is one of the most famous Jurassic pterosaurs and has been found in huge numbers from famous sites like the Solnhofen Limestone Formation.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Rhamphorhynchus} was a medium-sized pterosaur, with the largest individuals reaching a wingspan of 6 ft. It had a jaw full of large, pointed, spaced teeth that interlocked when closed, forming a "fish trap", in the same manner as {@i Klobiodon} ({@b page 140}) and {@i Ludodactylus} ({@i page 105)}. It had a very small body for its wingspan, giving it a broad profile, while also having a long thin tail that ended in a triangular vane.

Like several other rhamphorhyncids, {@i Rhamphorhynchus} was an oceanic predator, flying over the sea and plucking prey from the water below. This is corroborated by its abundance in the Solnhofen Limestone Formation, which was deposited in a tropical coastal environment, with some freshwater influence. It probably hunted both near- and off-shore, plucking up fish and squid that were near the surface or being pursued by marine predators from below.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Based on the large number of specimens found, it's likely that {@i Rhamphorhynchus} was common along the Late Jurassic coasts and may have congregated in groups, forming shore-line colonies. Pterosaur hatchlings were precocial, meaning they could feed and climb from the moment they hatched. In fact, unlike modern birds, it seems that hatchlings may also have been able to fly very soon after hatching. This raises the question of what, if any, parental care existed for {@i Rhamphorhynchus}. Perhaps adults gathered to breed, but quickly moved on once the eggs were hatched, with little direct care for their young.

We suggest playing {@i Rhamphorhynchus} in a similar fashion to a gull. It should be an alert animal that is willing to snatch food wherever it can. It should also be an animal quick to adjust to player interaction and may become relatively friendly over time, especially if routinely fed. However, entering a creche or nesting area should result in a mobbing by angry adults or a swarm of juveniles.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Rhamphorhynchus} is the most well-known rhamphorhynchid, which are the stereotypical long-tailed pterosaurs with large fangs, elongate jaws, long wings, and a large tail tipped by a vane. While medium-sized for Pterosauria as a whole, until the Cretaceous these were the largest flying animals, with the biggest reaching a 10 ft. wingspan. The group is known from multiple sites throughout Europe, Asia, and the Americas. They arose in the Early Jurassic (180 million years ago) and persisted until the Late Jurassic (148 million years ago), where they seem to have disappeared as part of a major faunal turnover event between the Jurassic and Cretaceous, along with several other unrelated groups.

trait.name: Snatch & Swallow
entries: When hitting with its Spike-Toothed Snap attack, Rhamphorhynchus may opt to deal no damage and instead try to snatch and swallow a small item (trinket, potion, wand, dagger, etc.) that it can see on the hit creature. The hit creature must succeed a {@dc 14} Dexterity saving throw or have the item snatched and swallowed by Rhamphorhynchus.
If the item is magical, Spike-Toothed Snap becomes a magical attack and deals a damage type appropriate to the item (i.e., a swallowed Wand of Magic Missile changes it to force damage).
If the item provides healing (i.e., a healing potion), Rhamphorhynchus gains {@dice 1d4 + 2} temporary hit points.
Any swallowed non-food or non-potion item is regurgitated upon Rhamphorhynchus' death, and potions are regurgitated as empty vials.

trait.name: Morbid Regurgitation (Swarm)
entries: Each time Rhamphorhynchus (Swarm) drops below the hit point thresholds of 34, 24, 14, and 4, one of its members vomits up its stomach contents. One creature within 5 ft. of Rhamphorhynchus (Swarm) must succeed a {@dc 12} Dexterity saving throw or take {@damage 1d4} acid damage.

trait.name: Swarming Flurry
entries: Melee attacks against Rhamphorhynchus (Swarm) are made at disadvantage.

trait.name: Naive Juveniles
entries: This swarm is composed entirely of inexperienced juvenile animals. It has disadvantage on Wisdom saving throws.

trait.name: Swarm
entries: The swarm can occupy another creature's space and vice versa, and the swarm can move through any opening large enough for a Tiny beast. The swarm can't regain hit points or gain temporary hit points.

The swarm is immune to being {@condition charmed}, {@condition frightened}, {@condition grappled}, {@condition paralyzed}, {@condition petrified}, {@condition prone}, {@condition restrained}, and {@condition stunned} (included above).

action.name: Multiattack
entries: Whenever Rhamphorhynchus (Swarm) chooses the attack action, it can make up to five Spike-Toothed Snap attacks.

trait.name: Morbid Regurgitation (Swarm)
entries: Each time Rhamphorhynchus (Swarm) drops below the hit point thresholds of 34, 24, 14, and 4, one of its members vomits up its stomach contents. One creature within 5 ft. of Rhamphorhynchus (Swarm) must succeed a {@dc 12} Dexterity saving throw or take {@damage 1d4} acid damage.

trait.name: Swarming Flurry
entries: Melee attacks against Rhamphorhynchus (Swarm) are made at disadvantage.

trait.name: Naive Juveniles
entries: This swarm is composed entirely of inexperienced juvenile animals. It has disadvantage on Wisdom saving throws.

trait.name: Swarm
entries: The swarm can occupy another creature's space and vice versa, and the swarm can move through any opening large enough for a Tiny beast. The swarm can't regain hit points or gain temporary hit points.

The swarm is immune to being {@condition charmed}, {@condition frightened}, {@condition grappled}, {@condition paralyzed}, {@condition petrified}, {@condition prone}, {@condition restrained}, and {@condition stunned} (included above).

trait.name: Enchanted Swarm
entries: Rhamphorhynchus (Swarm) has already snatched dozens of magical items and incorporated them into their attacks. Each time Rhamphorhynchus swarm makes a Spike-Toothed Snap attack, you may roll a {@dice 1d10} and change the damage type of the attack according to the list below:
{@dice 1d10} | Damage Type
1 | Fire
2 | Cold
3 | Lightning
4 | Poison
5 | Force
6 | Psychic
7 | Thunder
8 | Necrotic
9 | Acid
10 | Radiant

action.name: Multiattack
entries: Whenever Rhamphorhynchus (Swarm) chooses the attack action, it can make up to five Spike-Toothed Snap attacks.

action.name: Spike-Toothed Snap
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 3} to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}3 ({@damage 1d4 + 1}) piercing damage.
{@i "RAM-FOR-RING-CUS"} {@b (BEAK SNOUT)}

These tiny lil' pterosaurs are such a pain. They're highly inquisitive and have a nasty habit of snatchin' stuff right out of your hands. I guess they're used to grabbin' food, since they sometimes swallow the stuff without even thinkin'. Reminds me of herring gulls back in our time. Difference is, herring gulls ain't armed with dozens of protrudin' teeth! The hatchlin's of this species are gregarious – they find safety in numbers and bunch up into swarms. They get pretty hungry too and anyone carryin' food tends to get mobbed pretty quick. For somethin' so small, they can be quite fearsome in numbers. Almost like lil' angry flyin' piranhas.

{@i Rhamphorhynchus} was a medium sized rhamphorhynchid pterosaur from the Late Jurassic (150 million years ago) of Germany and Britain. It is one of the most famous Jurassic pterosaurs and has been found in huge numbers from famous sites like the Solnhofen Limestone Formation.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Rhamphorhynchus} was a medium-sized pterosaur, with the largest individuals reaching a wingspan of 6 ft. It had a jaw full of large, pointed, spaced teeth that interlocked when closed, forming a "fish trap", in the same manner as {@i Klobiodon} ({@b page 140}) and {@i Ludodactylus} ({@i page 105)}. It had a very small body for its wingspan, giving it a broad profile, while also having a long thin tail that ended in a triangular vane.

Like several other rhamphorhyncids, {@i Rhamphorhynchus} was an oceanic predator, flying over the sea and plucking prey from the water below. This is corroborated by its abundance in the Solnhofen Limestone Formation, which was deposited in a tropical coastal environment, with some freshwater influence. It probably hunted both near- and off-shore, plucking up fish and squid that were near the surface or being pursued by marine predators from below.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Based on the large number of specimens found, it's likely that {@i Rhamphorhynchus} was common along the Late Jurassic coasts and may have congregated in groups, forming shore-line colonies. Pterosaur hatchlings were precocial, meaning they could feed and climb from the moment they hatched. In fact, unlike modern birds, it seems that hatchlings may also have been able to fly very soon after hatching. This raises the question of what, if any, parental care existed for {@i Rhamphorhynchus}. Perhaps adults gathered to breed, but quickly moved on once the eggs were hatched, with little direct care for their young.

We suggest playing {@i Rhamphorhynchus} in a similar fashion to a gull. It should be an alert animal that is willing to snatch food wherever it can. It should also be an animal quick to adjust to player interaction and may become relatively friendly over time, especially if routinely fed. However, entering a creche or nesting area should result in a mobbing by angry adults or a swarm of juveniles.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Rhamphorhynchus} is the most well-known rhamphorhynchid, which are the stereotypical long-tailed pterosaurs with large fangs, elongate jaws, long wings, and a large tail tipped by a vane. While medium-sized for Pterosauria as a whole, until the Cretaceous these were the largest flying animals, with the biggest reaching a 10 ft. wingspan. The group is known from multiple sites throughout Europe, Asia, and the Americas. They arose in the Early Jurassic (180 million years ago) and persisted until the Late Jurassic (148 million years ago), where they seem to have disappeared as part of a major faunal turnover event between the Jurassic and Cretaceous, along with several other unrelated groups.

trait.name: Razor Osteoderms
entries: Any creature that hits Scelidosaurus with a melee attack suffers {@damage 1d6} slashing damage. Scelidosaurus may use its reaction to increase this to {@damage 2d4} slashing damage.
Scelidosaurus is resistant to non-magical bludgeoning, piercing, and slashing damage (included above).

trait.name: Oblivious
entries: Scelidosaurus automatically fails any Intelligence saving throws.

action.name: Serrated Tail
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 4} to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}6 ({@damage 1d6 + 3}) slashing damage.
{@i "SKI-LIE-DOH-SORE-US"} {@b (LIMB REPTILE)}

We'd been travellin' through that accursed forest for days, barely able to see the sky through the thick canopy. When we reached the forest edge, the burstin' blindin' sky over the ocean was quite a sight to behold. I daren't let us rest though, as some mighty big beasties roam these shores. That's when I saw the first of 'em. A livin' mass-o-blades. But they was nothin'

like I thought they'd be. Gentle to the touch — so long as you ain't touchin' the wrong spot! One took a likin' to me and, after I gave her a bit of bread, followed me for three days! Heh, never thought I'd befriend a dinosaur so easily.

{@i Scelidosaurus} is a small basal thyreophoran, the group of armoured dinosaurs that includes stegosaurs and ankylosaurs. It is known from several Early Jurassic (195 million years ago) sites across the British Isles and is currently the only described dinosaur known from Ireland.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Scelidosaurus} was small for an armoured dinosaur, measuring about 12 ft. long and weighing around 600 lbs. Originally thought to walk on four legs (quadruped), it is now thought to have been a facultative biped (it could walk on two or four legs). It had a long and squat body, long tail, a relatively short neck, and a small skull with a pointed beak. Much of its skin was covered in thick osteoderms (bones embedded in the skin), forming either plated armour or raised pointed blades. Both types were covered in keratin, which may have given them a sharp point.

Like many thyreophorans, {@i Scelidosaurus'} narrow jaws and beak suggest that it was a selective browser, moving through ground foliage and feeding primarily on ferns and cycads. Its heavy armour would have made it relatively slow, but well defended.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Little is known about {@i Scelidosaurus'} behaviour, but research into other thyreophorans suggest that it may have lived in small groups. Its armour helped protect it from larger predators while its bladed tail could be used as a weapon, although most probably more often to hit other offending {@i Scelidosaurus}.

We recommend that {@i Scelidosaurus} live in small herds, moving through dense foliage in search of food. They should be wary but not particularly aggressive, rather like a herd of domestic sheep. While some may respond to being approached with warning swipes of their tail, others could be placid and tempted in with food. Once domesticated, they can function as livestock, mounts, or pack animals.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Scelidosaurus} is a member of Thyreophora, but its exact position within that group has been the subject of debate. Initially placed as an early ankylosaur (Ankylosauria), it was later moved to lower in the Thyreophora clade, as a separate early member belonging to neither Stegosauridae or Ankylosauria. More recent studies have rearranged Thyreophora and {@i Scelidosaurus} may have been accompanied by stegosaurs at the base of the group, with ankylosaurs being their more derived relatives.

trait.name: Domesticatable
entries: Scelidosaurus is particularly trustful of Small or Medium-sized creatures, largely due to its formidable defences. It is relatively easy to domesticate, and players can befriend a Scelidosaurus by feeding it consistently for a {@dice 1d4 + 1} days. However, their Razor Osteoderms prevent Scelidosaurus from being ridden without a bespoke saddle. Nevertheless, they make for friendly travelling companions.

trait.name: Pelvic Membrane
entries: Sharovipteryx is immune to falling damage and can move up to 2 ft. horizontally for every 1 ft. it descends in the air, at no movement cost.
While descending in the air in this manner (or while flying if you are using the optional magical rules), Sharovipteryx does not provoke attacks of opportunity when it moves out of an enemy's reach.

action.name: Gliding Snap
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 4} to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}1 (1) piercing damage.
Sharovipteryx may only use this attack while descending in the air (or while flying if you are using the optional magical rules).
{@i "SHAR-OF-IP-TER-RIX"} {@b (SHAROV'S WING)}

The jungle was bustlin' with life. Lizards, pterosaurs, and small dinosaurs filled the canopy above. As we walked below, I spied one particularly unusual critter soarin' between branches. It was a lil' lizard-like thing that was gliding usin' only its hind legs! Never seen anythin' like that before, how bizarre. We tried to get a closer look, but it was quite skittish and leapt from the tree whenever we went to climb up.

{@i Sharovipteryx} is a bizarre basal archosauromorph from the Middle Triassic (225 million years ago) Madygen Formation of Kyrgyzstan. It had extremely elongate hindlimbs that supported a gliding membrane.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Sharovipteryx} was a small animal at approximately 8in. long and is known from a single exceptional fossil. The front half of its body was rather unremarkable, with a simple reptilian head, sharp teeth, and short forelimbs, although some soft-tissue details may have been lost due to damage. Its hind quarters, however, were very unusual, with a stiff tail accounting for half of its total length and hyper-elongated hindlimbs with a gliding membrane. Specially adapted hips allowed the legs to be held out horizontally and the membrane stretched from the innermost toe on each foot to the tail, forming gliding wings.

Since {@i Sharovipteryx}'s discovery, most research has focused on its hindlimb membrane. It is unlike any other vertebrate known and there has been extensive discussion about how well it could glide. The current consensus is that it would have required a stabilising membrane on its forelimbs to help control its movement. Unfortunately, the specimen was over-prepared (too much of the rock was removed) when it was first collected, destroying soft tissue around the upper body. This means we don't know whether or not it had a second gliding membrane connected to its arms, but aerodynamic modelling suggests that it probably did.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Sharovipteryx} almost certainly lived in wooded areas, climbing up the sides of trees and along branches. While searching for food or fleeing predators, it would have leapt into the air, extended its hindlimbs, and glided to a neighbouring tree, in a similar manner to gliding squirrels or frogs. Its size and sharp teeth suggest that it probably ate insects, snatching them up along tree trunks and branches.

We suggest that {@i Sharovipteryx} be played as an alert animal that is most active during the daytime. Adults should be territorial of their trees, defending them from competitors who might threaten their food supply. A party is unlikely to get close to one in the day but at night as light draws clouds of insects to a campsite, {@i Sharivopteryx} may descend from the trees hoping for an easy meal. {@i Sharivopteryx} should be skittish, but quickly accustomed to humanoids if they feed it. Once tamed, it can be a useful and stealthy companion.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Sharovipteryx} was originally named {@i Podpteryx} (foot wing) in its initial description, but it was quickly highlighted that this name had already been assigned to a genus of damselfly. It was subsequently renamed in honour of Aleksandr Grigorevich Sharov, the author who originally described it. {@i Sharivopteryx}'s phylogenetic relationships are still poorly understood, although it can be placed in Archosauromorpha with confidence. Beyond that, there is much uncertainty. It has previously been considered a close relative of pterosaurs, but also has been placed within its own group Sharovipteryigidae as a distant relative of true archosaurs. Ultimately, {@i Sharovipteryx}'s position in the tree of life is likely to change as research continues.

trait.name: Dip Feeder
entries: Tanystropheus has advantage on attacks against creatures that are submerged in water, so long as Tanystropheus' body is not also submerged in water. Tanystropheus can hold its breath for 5 minutes.

trait.name: Farstrike
entries: Tanystropheus often attacks from a concealed position, hiding its body while reaching out with its long neck to strike prey.
If Tanystropheus attacks while hidden, its first attack deals an additional {@damage 1d6} piercing damage.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Tanystropheus chooses the attack action, it may make one Neck Strike attack and one Nip attack.

action.name: Neck Strike
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 4} to hit, reach 10 ft., one target. {@h}4 ({@damage 1d6 + 1}) bludgeoning damage.
A Medium or Small creature hit by this attack must succeed a {@dc 12} Strength or Dexterity saving throw (their choice) or be knocked {@condition prone}.

action.name: Nip
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 4} to hit, reach 10 ft., one target. {@h}3 ({@damage 1d4 + 1}) piercing damage.
{@i "TAN-IH-STROF-E-US"} {@b (LONG HINGED)}

We were followin' a small river upstream, searchin' for a good place to camp for the evenin'. Out of nowhere, a long neck and lil' head whipped out of the reeds and nipped one of our party members on the leg. At first, we thought it was a snake, but then it reared up several feet into the air and burst from the reeds, scurryin' into the water. As it dived, we saw the rest of its body. It was a weird lookin' beastie, with a neck twice as long as its body!
{@i Tanystropheus} is a reptile from the Middle Triassic (245 million years ago) of Europe and North America. It is well known for having one of the longest necks relative to body size of any animal.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Tanystropheus} was one of the longest basal archosauromorphs, reaching 16-20 ft. in length. Over half of that length is neck, which supported a small skull with elongate fangs. Like some pterosaurs (e.g., {@i Rhamphorhynchus} ({@b see page 168})), these fangs interlocked to form a "fish trap" that could grasp wriggling slippery prey. Its legs were unusual, with the hindlimbs being much larger and more robust than the forelimbs.

The lifestyle of {@i Tanystropheus} is debated, with some authors suggesting a near-water terrestrial ecology and others asserting that it was entirely aquatic. In either case, its primary food source was probably fish. The most recent study supports a semi-aquatic lifestyle, living in either marginal marine environments (near-shore) or freshwater, swimming in a frog-like manner by kicking its hind legs. In these habitats, it may have used its long neck to dip-feed whereby it hid its body onshore and plunged its head into shallow water to snatch fish and squid.

However, some small {@i Tanystropheus} had very different dentition with conical teeth changing to flatter teeth towards the back of the mouth, suggesting that it crushed harder foodstuffs, perhaps small shelly organisms.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Tanystropheus} almost certainly lived in and around water. It probably spent a significant proportion of its time swimming or wading through reedy shallows, hunting for fish, or it may also have remained stationary at the water's edge. In either case, it would have been able to flee from one medium to the other to escape predators.

We suggest that {@i Tanystropheus} be played with different behaviours depending on which environment it is in. On land it should be relatively static, dipping its head into the water to snap at fish. It will be passive until approached, when it will likely dive into the water to escape. However, it may be more aggressive if encountered in water, striking or snapping at those who disturb it while hiding its body among aquatic reeds. It will only leave the water if a large aquatic predator approaches it. A tamed {@i Tanystropheus} could be a popular companion for fishing cultures, assisting them by snatching up fish while on their boats, similar to real-world cormorant fishing.

{@i "TAN-IH-STROF-E-US"} {@b (LONG HINGED)}

We were followin' a small river upstream, searchin' for a good place to camp for the evenin'. Out of nowhere, a long neck and lil' head whipped out of the reeds and nipped one of our party members on the leg. At first, we thought it was a snake, but then it reared up several feet into the air and burst from the reeds, scurryin' into the water. As it dived, we saw the rest of its body. It was a weird lookin' beastie, with a neck twice as long as its body!
{@i Tanystropheus} is a reptile from the Middle Triassic (245 million years ago) of Europe and North America. It is well known for having one of the longest necks relative to body size of any animal.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Tanystropheus} was one of the longest basal archosauromorphs, reaching 16-20 ft. in length. Over half of that length is neck, which supported a small skull with elongate fangs. Like some pterosaurs (e.g., {@i Rhamphorhynchus} ({@b see page 168})), these fangs interlocked to form a "fish trap" that could grasp wriggling slippery prey. Its legs were unusual, with the hindlimbs being much larger and more robust than the forelimbs.

The lifestyle of {@i Tanystropheus} is debated, with some authors suggesting a near-water terrestrial ecology and others asserting that it was entirely aquatic. In either case, its primary food source was probably fish. The most recent study supports a semi-aquatic lifestyle, living in either marginal marine environments (near-shore) or freshwater, swimming in a frog-like manner by kicking its hind legs. In these habitats, it may have used its long neck to dip-feed whereby it hid its body onshore and plunged its head into shallow water to snatch fish and squid.

However, some small {@i Tanystropheus} had very different dentition with conical teeth changing to flatter teeth towards the back of the mouth, suggesting that it crushed harder foodstuffs, perhaps small shelly organisms.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Tanystropheus} almost certainly lived in and around water. It probably spent a significant proportion of its time swimming or wading through reedy shallows, hunting for fish, or it may also have remained stationary at the water's edge. In either case, it would have been able to flee from one medium to the other to escape predators.

We suggest that {@i Tanystropheus} be played with different behaviours depending on which environment it is in. On land it should be relatively static, dipping its head into the water to snap at fish. It will be passive until approached, when it will likely dive into the water to escape. However, it may be more aggressive if encountered in water, striking or snapping at those who disturb it while hiding its body among aquatic reeds. It will only leave the water if a large aquatic predator approaches it. A tamed {@i Tanystropheus} could be a popular companion for fishing cultures, assisting them by snatching up fish while on their boats, similar to real-world cormorant fishing.

{@i "YOU-TAH-RAP-TOR" "} {@b (UTAH PLUNDERER)}

Unlike their smaller cousins, these ones are truly somethin' to be feared. Boundin' out of the brush in a flurry of teeth, claws, and feathers, they'll rip all but the hardiest foes to shreds in a matter of moments. No qualms about takin' on something much bigger than themselves either. We spied five workin' their way through a clearin', takin' out a large hadrosaur in one go. Thankfully, we were way up a steep cliff, otherwise we might've been puddin'.

{@i Utahraptor} is a dromaeosaurid from the Early Cretaceous (135 million years ago) Cedar Mountain Formation of Utah, North America. It was the heaviest and possibly the largest member of the dromaeosaurid family.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: By dromaeosaur standards {@i Utahraptor} was enormous, measuring at over 16 ft. long and weighing more than 600 lb. It was very robust and powerfully built, with strong jaws and limbs. Like most dromaeosaurs, it had a large retractable sickle-shaped claw on each foot which would have been used to puncture and hold prey, rather than slash or cut. Its forelimb claws were also very large and robust. While there is no direct evidence of feathers in {@i Utahraptor}, we are confident that it was feathered, as all closely related animals are (determined through phylogenetic bracketing (see {@b page 13})). {@i Utahraptor}'s most distinctive feature, other than its size, is a slightly downturned tip of its lower jaw, splaying its lower teeth forward.

{@i Utahraptor}'s fossils are found in the Cedar Mountain Formation, a series of non-marine sediments that were deposited by rivers, lakes, and floodplains over a very long time period. During this prolonged time, the surrounding environment varied with climate, from hot arid scrubland to humid forest. {@i Utahraptor} was one of the larger predators in its environment and is clearly built for power. It would have predated upon almost every other large animal in the Cedar Mountain Formation.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Some fossils preserve remarkable behaviour and there is one particularly spectacular specimen for {@i Utahraptor} that preserves nine individuals in a single sandstone block. These animals include adults, subadults, juveniles, and hatchlings all clustered above one iguanodont herbivore. This is hypothesised to be a "predator trap" whereby one herbivore died in quicksand and subsequently so too did many predators while trying to reach it. The age range of {@i Utahraptor} present suggests that these were large family groups and that they may have been pack hunters. However, it is also possible that this association is by chance (actually representing a flash flood deposit), or that the {@i Utahraptor} were unrelated and drawn to the same trap one after the other.

We suggest that {@i Utahraptor} be played as a highly social predator, living in groups of mated adults with subadults, juveniles, and babies in close association, generally protected by the adults. Within these groups individuals should be communicative and playful with each other. While hunting, cooperation should vary with age, with the eldest {@i Utahraptor} leading subadults on hunts, and younger {@i Utahraptor} following at a distance. Young animals may hunt small prey themselves but will also scavenge from the adult's kills in a strict pecking-order.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: Dromaeosaurs were a highly successful group of mostly small-sized predatory theropods, but {@i Utahraptor} highlights that some became very large indeed. Currently only four giant dromaeosaur species are known, but these belong to different subgroups that may have had very different lifestyles, suggesting that giantism occurred independently multiple times within Dromaeosauridae.

trait.name: Grasping Predator
entries: If Velociraptor hits a creature the same size or larger than itself with its Clawed Kick, it can opt to grasp onto it. Whenever that creature moves, Velociraptor moves with it (without using any of its own movement) and is considered to be occupying the same space as it. If two or more Velociraptor are grasping the same Medium or Large creature with this ability, halve its movement speed.

These quick lil' things really lived up to their name. Vicious as anything – two of 'em jumped me while I was takin' a wizz.

{@i Velociraptor} is the most famous member of the Dromaeosauridae (popularly known as the 'raptors'). A small theropod from the Djadochta and Bayan Mandahu formations, it is one of the best-preserved dromaeosaurs with several complete specimens. Despite this, its fame has made it one of the most frequently misrepresented dinosaurs in media.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Velociraptor} was a small dromaeosaur at 2 ft. tall and 6 ft. long. It had an unusually narrow and elongate skull which gave it a distinct profile. Like most dromaeosaurs, it had long fingers ending in hooked claws and a single strongly-enlarged sickle shaped claw on each foot. While large, this claw was not suited to slashing or cutting. Instead, it was for pinning or grappling small prey. Like other dromaeosaurs, {@i Velociraptor} was covered in feathers with well-developed 'wings' (though it couldn't fly) and a broad tail. As with many modern birds, it is plausible that males and females had sexually dimorphic plumage (possessing different feather colours and patterns).

{@i Velociraptor} was an active predator, hunting prey by leaping onto it and pinning it with its large claws while stabilising itself with its wings. It likely killed prey by biting at their necks, causing death by blood loss. One exceptional fossil even preserves the moment a {@i Velociraptor} was fighting with a {@i Protoceratops}. Both died and were preserved by a collapsing sand dune. In addition to hunting, {@i Velociraptor} would have also scavenged, like most modern carnivores.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Velociraptor} would have been an active semi-nocturnal opportunistic hunter. Alert and curious, it could have hunted alone or in pairs. Hatchlings probably stayed with their parents until they were old enough to hunt small prey themselves. {@i Velociraptor}'s wings may have been used for communication, with swift flicks similar to modern crows, and perhaps also used to mantle kills (extending them over a carcass while feeding to hide it from other predators).

We suggest {@i Velociraptor} be played as an alert predator, actively monitoring its territory. It may stalk intruding parties for a while before determining whether to attack and should not necessarily be scared off by humanoids' presence alone. Large groups may be found scavenging corpses but {@i Velociraptor} should not hunt in a pack. Instead, each individual or pair should function as their own unit, similar to modern birds of prey.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Velociraptor} was a dromaeosaurid, a very well-known family of generally small to medium sized theropods that occurred on every continent and are commonly referred to as "raptors". Within Dromaeosauridae, {@i Velociraptor} is part of the Velociraptorinae sub-family, which are mostly small dromaeosaurs with elongate skulls.

entries.name: The Price of Fame
entries: {@i Velociraptor} rose to fame in the late 80s and early 90s through its prominent role in the {@i Jurassic Park} franchise, based on Michael Crichton's books. While dramatic and popular, it was inaccurately portrayed in the franchise. This was, in part, due to science at the time considering {@i Velociraptor} a potential synonym of the larger {@i Deinonychus}, which Crichton incorporated into his writing. This resulted in {@i Velociraptor} being misrepresented in media as a large hyper-intelligent pack hunting animal for decades. While recent studies have suggested some large predatory dinosaurs may well have been much more intelligent than previously assumed, {@i Velociraptor} is not believed to have been particularly smart or prone to pack hunting. Today, incorrect depictions of animals like {@i Velociraptor} in the media have led to an increasingly vocal movement to find a balance between scientific accuracy and engaging science fiction – exactly what we are attempting in this book!

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Velociraptor} was a small dromaeosaur at 2 ft. tall and 6 ft. long. It had an unusually narrow and elongate skull which gave it a distinct profile. Like most dromaeosaurs, it had long fingers ending in hooked claws and a single strongly-enlarged sickle shaped claw on each foot. While large, this claw was not suited to slashing or cutting. Instead, it was for pinning or grappling small prey. Like other dromaeosaurs, {@i Velociraptor} was covered in feathers with well-developed 'wings' (though it couldn't fly) and a broad tail. As with many modern birds, it is plausible that males and females had sexually dimorphic plumage (possessing different feather colours and patterns).

{@i Velociraptor} was an active predator, hunting prey by leaping onto it and pinning it with its large claws while stabilising itself with its wings. It likely killed prey by biting at their necks, causing death by blood loss. One exceptional fossil even preserves the moment a {@i Velociraptor} was fighting with a {@i Protoceratops}. Both died and were preserved by a collapsing sand dune. In addition to hunting, {@i Velociraptor} would have also scavenged, like most modern carnivores.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Velociraptor} would have been an active semi-nocturnal opportunistic hunter. Alert and curious, it could have hunted alone or in pairs. Hatchlings probably stayed with their parents until they were old enough to hunt small prey themselves. {@i Velociraptor}'s wings may have been used for communication, with swift flicks similar to modern crows, and perhaps also used to mantle kills (extending them over a carcass while feeding to hide it from other predators).

We suggest {@i Velociraptor} be played as an alert predator, actively monitoring its territory. It may stalk intruding parties for a while before determining whether to attack and should not necessarily be scared off by humanoids' presence alone. Large groups may be found scavenging corpses but {@i Velociraptor} should not hunt in a pack. Instead, each individual or pair should function as their own unit, similar to modern birds of prey.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Velociraptor} was a dromaeosaurid, a very well-known family of generally small to medium sized theropods that occurred on every continent and are commonly referred to as "raptors". Within Dromaeosauridae, {@i Velociraptor} is part of the Velociraptorinae sub-family, which are mostly small dromaeosaurs with elongate skulls.

entries.name: The Price of Fame
entries: {@i Velociraptor} rose to fame in the late 80s and early 90s through its prominent role in the {@i Jurassic Park} franchise, based on Michael Crichton's books. While dramatic and popular, it was inaccurately portrayed in the franchise. This was, in part, due to science at the time considering {@i Velociraptor} a potential synonym of the larger {@i Deinonychus}, which Crichton incorporated into his writing. This resulted in {@i Velociraptor} being misrepresented in media as a large hyper-intelligent pack hunting animal for decades. While recent studies have suggested some large predatory dinosaurs may well have been much more intelligent than previously assumed, {@i Velociraptor} is not believed to have been particularly smart or prone to pack hunting. Today, incorrect depictions of animals like {@i Velociraptor} in the media have led to an increasingly vocal movement to find a balance between scientific accuracy and engaging science fiction – exactly what we are attempting in this book!

We pushed through thick undergrowth that reeked of rotting meat, the sickly smell fillin' me nostrils. The half-devoured carcasses of various herbivores lit'ered the area, decayin' slowly. "This is rex territory" I whispered to the rest of the party.
"But tis OK, we'll hear 'em comin' long befo-". My words were split by the sudden crash of bushes and trees bein'
crushed beneath the thunderin' charge of a dinosaur. Far smaller than expected, but also far faster, a young Tyrannosaurus rex was barin' down on us somethin' fierce.

{@i Tyrannosaurus} is inarguably the most famous fossil animal and was the heaviest land carnivore known. Much of {@i Tyrannosaurus}' ecology and morphology has been studied extensively, and one area of particular interest is the stages of growth that {@i Tyrannosaurus} underwent. Several immature fossils of {@i Tyrannosaurus} demonstrate that it underwent dramatic changes throughout its life that not only altered its size and general appearance, but also its niche within an ecosystem.

entries.name: Ontogeny
entries: Ontogeny is the study of how an animal changes through life, from the fertilisation of its egg to it maturing into an adult and beyond. In addition to increasing in size, the young of many animals undergo dramatic changes as they mature. The classic extreme example of this is the metamorphosis that a tadpole undergoes when becoming a frog.
In dinosaurs, ontogenetic changes include bones fusing together, jaws size ratios changing, developing horns or frills, growing elaborate feathers, changes in their teeth, and much more.

{@i Tyrannosaurus} has very interesting ontogeny, as juveniles were strikingly different from their parents. So different in fact that some juvenile skeletons have been described as new genera. The most famous example of this is a specimen that was initially assigned to the new genus '{@i Nanotyrannus'}. Young {@i Tyrannosaurus} was lightly built with long thin legs, making it a faster animal. Its skull was also much lighter and elongate, although still distinctly tyrannosaurian, reducing its bite strength to size ratio significantly. It retained this gracile morphology until it was at least 13 years old, at which point it underwent a rapid period of growth and bulking until the age of about 15-18 years, but continued to grow afterwards ({@b page 195}).

entries.name: Niche Partitioning
entries: We know that young {@i Tyrannosaurus} was at least semi-precocial (able to fend for itself somewhat) and probably hunted its own food. The smaller size and gracile build of juvenile {@i Tyrannosaurus} made it a fast predator, but one that" could not tackle large prey. It likely would have snuck within charging range, then run down prey smaller than itself. This means that the two life-stages occupied different niches, relying on different resources to avoid direct competition with one another.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: We recommend that young {@i Tyrannosaurus} be played as an ambush predator, quietly stalking prey until it is close enough to charge. It can be significantly more active than its adult counterparts, since it will require lots of food to fuel its growth. Young {@i Tyrannosaurus} may have been less territorial than other similarly sized predators, as it was likely operating within one of its parent's territories. When challenged, it could flee to a parent, prompting them to seek out whoever upset its offspring.

trait.name: Ankylosaur Osteoderms
entries: Zuul is resistant to non-magical bludgeoning, slashing, and piercing damage, has an AC of 20, a -10 modifier to Acrobatics, and a -8 modifier to Athletics (excluding for shove and grapple checks, all included above).

trait.name: Hulking Mass
entries: Zuul has disadvantage on all Dexterity saving throws, but advantage on all Constitution and Strength saving throws.

action.name: Clubbed Tail
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 7} to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}19 ({@damage 2d12 + 6}) bludgeoning damage.

A creature hit by this attack must succeed a {@dc 14} Strength saving throw or be knocked {@condition prone}. Any creature knocked {@condition prone} by this attack (or was already {@condition prone}) must then succeed a {@dc 14} Constitution saving throw or suffer a "shattering blow" and have their movement speed reduced by 10 ft.

A {@spell lesser restoration} spell, equivalent effect, or long rest is required to remove "shattering blow". Multiple "shattering blows" are cumulative, reducing a creature's movement speed by 10 ft. for each blow (to a minimum of 5 ft.).
{@i "ZOOL"} {@b (AFTER ZUUL FROM GHOSTBUSTERS)}

As we moved over the rollin' scrub, we came across somethin' remarkable. A lone dinosaur feeding on scrub, entirely oblivious to us. Few times in my life had I ever come across such an unyieldin' amount of muscle and armour. When I first saw this thing, I knew it was built for one thing and one thing only – defence. We studied it in detail. Armoured back, armoured limbs, even armoured eyelids. Unbelievable. It didn't even seem to mind us flittin' around it.

{@i Zuul} is an ankylosaur from the Late Cretaceous (75 million years ago) Judith River Formation of North America. A close relative of {@i Ankylosaurus} that takes its name from the Ghostbusters franchise, it has recently revealed behavioural interactions of ankylosaurs.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Zuul} was a medium sized ankylosaur that measured approximately 20 ft. long and may have weighed 2 tonnes. Its morphology is typical for the ankylosaurs, with short stout legs, a wide body, rows of spikey osteoderms (bones embedded in the skin) that form a layer of armour, a broad head, and a heavy club on the end of its tail. It had an enormous gut for its size, making it an extremely rotund animal.

{@i Zuul} was a low-grazing herbivore with broad, leaf-shaped teeth, and fed on a variety of ferns, shrubs, leaves, succulents, and fruits. It probably could not process hard woody plants like some other dinosaurs, although may have swallowed small stones (gastroliths) to help grind material in its stomach. It lived in coniferous forests among shade-dwelling plants, rather than in open fernland.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: For many years it was assumed that ankylosaurs used their clubs exclusively to fight off predators. However, recent studies of {@i Zuul}'s holotype have revealed that several healed injuries were likely the result of tail-club attacks from other {@i Zuul}. This indicates that it engaged in intraspecific combat, although its club was undoubtedly also used as a defensive weapon. Additionally, an exceptionally preserved larynx found in {@i Pinacosaurus}, a small Asian ankylosaur, showed much stronger similarities to modern birds than crocodiles or reptiles. This suggests that the group produced complex high-pitched sounds and were quite vocal, perhaps even melodic, animals.

We suggest that {@i Zuul} be a relatively sedate animal, lumbering through the undergrowth, perhaps in small herds of 4-5 animals. A party might hear the clash of clubs against armour or a chorus of calls long before they see {@i Zuul}. As long as the herd isn't disturbed, {@i Zuul} should be non-aggressive, instead focusing on feeding and socialising. When threatened, any {@i Zuul} should stand its ground, making intimidating motions by swinging its heavy tail.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Zuul} is a member of the Ankylosauria. This group of armoured dinosaurs is divided into several subgroups, and included the relatively small animal {@i Struthiosaurus} ({@b page 93}) and the larger well-known {@i Ankylosaurus}. Like {@i Ankylosaurus, Zuul} was an ankylosaurid and the two were closely related. Ankylosaurids seem to be restricted to Laurasia (North America, Europe, and Asia), but were very successful within that geographic range, appearing in the Early Cretaceous and surviving until the end-Cretaceous extinction.

entries: Zuul has disadvantage on all Dexterity saving throws, but advantage on all Constitution and Strength saving throws.

trait.name: Ectoplasmic Reach
entries: A ghoulish jelly like substance extends from Zuul's tail. Increase the reach of Zuul's Clubbed Tail attack to 15 ft. and change its damage type to necrotic.

entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 7} to hit, reach 15 ft., one target. {@h}19 ({@damage 2d12 + 6}) necrotic damage.

A creature hit by this attack must succeed a {@dc 14} Strength saving throw or be knocked {@condition prone}. Any creature knocked {@condition prone} by this attack (or was already {@condition prone}) must then succeed a {@dc 14} Constitution saving throw or suffer a "shattering blow" and have their movement speed reduced by 10 ft.

A {@spell lesser restoration} spell, equivalent effect, or long rest is required to remove "shattering blow". Multiple "shattering blows" are cumulative, reducing a creature's movement speed by 10 ft. for each blow (to a minimum of 5 ft.).

action.name: The Gatekeeper (1/day)
entries: As an action, Zuul can attempt to open an interdimensional portal directly in front of it that ejects malicious energies. Roll a {@dice 1d20}:
On a 1, Zuul detonates with malicious magical energies, dealing {@damage 8d8} necrotic damage to itself and {@damage 4d8} necrotic damage to each other creature within 25 ft.

On a 2-10, an unstable portal forms for 1 minute and pulses with malicious energy. Each creature (other than Zuul) within 25 ft. of it must succeed a {@dc 12} Constitution saving throw or take {@damage 1d8} necrotic damage. As a bonus action, Zuul can pulse the portal, forcing this save again.

On an 11-19, a metastable portal forms for 1 minute and crackles with malicious energy. Each creature (other than Zuul) within 25 ft. of it must succeed a {@dc 12} Constitution saving throw or take {@damage 1d8} necrotic damage and gain vulnerability to necrotic damage for 1 minute. As a bonus action, Zuul can pulse the portal, forcing this save again.

On a 20, a stable portal opens for 1 minute. Each creature (other than Zuul) that starts its turn within or moves within 25 ft. of the portal gains vulnerability to necrotic damage. At the start of their turn, any creature (other than Zuul) within 25 ft. of the portal suffers {@damage 1d8} necrotic damage.
If Zuul is slain, the portal it created either closes or stabilises to another plane of existence (DM's decision) for {@dice 1d20} minutes.

trait.name: Power Over Speed
entries: Ancient Tyrannosaurus Rex has advantage on all Strength checks and Strength saving throws, but disadvantage on all Dexterity checks and Dexterity saving throws.

trait.name: Territorial Titan
entries: Ancient Tyrannosaurus Rex has advantage on attacks with its Strongest Bite against creatures with a size category of Huge or Gargantuan.

trait.name: When Dinosaurs Ruled the Earth
entries: All non-Tyrannosaurus beasts are {@condition frightened} of Ancient Tyrannosaurus Rex.

Every minute while within line of sight of Ancient Tyrannosaurus Rex, or at the end of each of its turns in combat, a beast can make a {@dc 17} Wisdom saving throw to become immune to this ability for 24 hours. Succeeding this Wisdom saving throw does not make it immune to Ancient Tyrannosaurus Rex's Iconic Bellow.

trait.name: Legendary Resistance (2/day)
entries: If Ancient Tyrannosaurus Rex fails a saving throw, it may choose to succeed it instead.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Ancient Tyrannosaurus Rex chooses the attack action, it may make one Strongest Bite attack and one Crushing Tail Slam attack.

action.name: Strongest Bite
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 13} to hit, reach 10 ft., one target. {@h}23 ({@damage 3d12 + 4}) piercing damage plus 23 ({@damage 3d12 + 4}) force damage.

A creature hit by this attack is {@condition grappled} and {@condition restrained} (escape {@dc 21}). Until this grapple ends, Ancient Tyrannosaurus Rex can't Strongest Bite another target and has an additional +5 to hit the grappled creature with any Strongest Bite attack.

action.name: Crushing Tail Slam
entries: Each creature within 10 ft. of Ancient Tyrannosaurus Rex must succeed a {@dc 21} Dexterity saving throw or take 28 ({@damage 3d12 + 9}) bludgeoning damage and be knocked {@condition prone}. On a success they take half as much damage and are not knocked {@condition prone}.
A creature grappled by Strongest Bite is not affected by this attack.

action.name: Iconic Bellow
entries: Every non-Tyrannosaur creature within 200 ft. of Ancient Tyrannosaurus Rex that can hear it must succeed a {@dc 20} Wisdom saving throw or take 13 ({@damage 1d12 + 7}) psychic damage and be {@condition frightened} of Ancient Tyrannosaurus Rex for 1 minute. A creature can repeat this saving throw at the end of each of its turns, ending the effect on itself on a success. If a creature's saving throw is successful, the creature is immune to the {@condition frightened} condition from Ancient Tyrannosaurus Rex's Iconic Bellow for the next 24 hours.

legendary.name: Lunging Head Bash
entries: Ancient Tyrannosaurus Rex may move up to 10 ft., then make the following attack:
{@atk mw} {@hit 13} to hit, reach 10 ft., one target. {@h}20 ({@damage 2d10 + 9}) bludgeoning damage.
{@i "TIE-RAN-O-SORE-US"} {@b (TYRANT LIZARD KING)}

Chosen by Ross Grundler {@i For a week we had been restin' at a small settlement in the Southeast of the continent, eager to explore further South. Our gracious hosts warned us not to go traipsin' through the southern forests, as it was guarded by a fearsome beast. They just kept callin' it the "Blue Death" and told hyperbolic stories of a maw so great that'd swallow a full party whole and limbs so powerful that they couldn't be stopped. Nevertheless, our adventurin' drive was strong so we decided to push on with our plans, while takin' their warnin's to heart. We were cautious and travelled quietly. After a couple days walk, we were enterin' its territory. The first signs we got of its presence was a rumblin' that shook the very ground. A deep-bass bellow in the middle of a bright night, well-lit by a full moon. It shook our bedrolls and our campfire clanged as the pots fell from their hooks. We just had to see this thin' before we move on. We tracked its location over the course of a few weeks, the bellows stronger every night. Once we knew we were close, me and a few of the stealthier members of our party set out in the night to sneak up on it, keepin' to the moonlight shadows as much as possible. As we approached, the rumblin' was so intense that it was hard to stand. Crouchin' in the bushes, a clearin' ahead revealed an absolutely colossal deep blue, almost black, Tyrannosaurus rex. This thin' outsized any of our other records for rex size. We could immediately see why it was called the Blue Death and imagined that it could live up to that name. All big carnivores pick up a few scars, but the Blue Death had the most any of us had ever seen. Its face 'n' belly had been shredded in the past, probably failed attempts by other big predators to kill it. They'd healed in big archin' scars. There are even some scorch marks that were probably made by dragon's breath. We wondered how the other beasties might've looked after toillin' with this thin'.}

Its eyes were a piercin' as it raised its head and bellowed motionlessly in the moonlight. Our rogue asked whether it was a buck, callin' for a mate... but I'm not so sure. Truth be told, we usually rely on colour patternin' for this species, but the hyperpigmentation of this one put a stop to that and none of us was willin' to check the plumbin'. Whatever it was, I have no doubt that it sired most of the offspring in the region. The lack of rumblin' answers back suggested that it was the dominant predator for a hundred miles or so around and it'd probably be easier to list what it didn't eat, rather than what it did. Its territory encompassed grasslands, forests, lakes, and even a small mountain range. Our ventures over the followin' weeks saw evidence of Blue Death all over. It evidently patrolled its territory constantly and it seems that no settlements could safely be founded there. I feel remorse for the foolish ones who tried in the past.

entries.name: Size and Age Limits
entries: {@i Tyrannosaurus} long held the title of largest land carnivore at 40 ft. long and weighing up to 8 tonnes. However, since the 1990s newly discovered or re-examined species like {@i Giganotosaurus}, {@i Carcharodontosaurus} ({@b page 69}) and {@i Spinosaurus} ({@b page 75}) have shown that many giant predators stalked the Mesozoic (though none were probably as heavy as {@i Tyrannosaurus}). This prompted the question: "{@i What really was the largest size these animals could reach?}".

It's been suggested that the largest theropod dinosaurs couldn't get much bigger than 40-50 ft. long, due to limitations in their body plan and metabolic rate. However, a 2023 presentation highlighted that only a tiny fraction of life is preserved in the fossil record, meaning that we will never find the largest individuals of any given species. Research using statistical modelling demonstrated that the largest {@i Tyrannosaurus} could have probably reached over 13 tonnes in weight, over 50% bigger than our largest specimen. These models also highlighted that, statistically, over 500 specimens would need to be found before we were likely to find an individual over 10 tonnes, which could take another century.

Further evidence suggests that the {@i Tyrannosaurus} specimens we previously considered to be adults are in fact subadults, with more growing to do. We previously calculated that it had a maximum lifespan of 28 years, but a recently discovered carcharodontosaurid named {@i Meraxes} has brought that into question. It died somewhere between the ages of 38 to 50, demonstrating that large predators could live for much longer than we anticipated. All of this highlights that {@i Tyrannosaurus} almost certainly lived for decades longer than we previously thought and reached sizes far larger than any specimen found so far. Ultimately, palaeontology is an ever-developing science and even an animal as well-studied as {@i Tyrannosaurus} can yield new dramatic discoveries.

monster.name: Ancient Tyrannosaurus Rex (Magical Variant)
languages: Archosauric
understands one other language (usually Common)

trait.name: Power Over Speed
entries: Ancient Tyrannosaurus Rex has advantage on all Strength checks and Strength saving throws, but disadvantage on all Dexterity checks and Dexterity saving throws.

trait.name: Territorial Titan
entries: Ancient Tyrannosaurus Rex has advantage on attacks with its Strongest Bite against creatures with a size category of Huge or Gargantuan.

trait.name: When Dinosaurs Ruled the Earth
entries: All non-Tyrannosaurus beasts are {@condition frightened} of Ancient Tyrannosaurus Rex.

Every minute while within line of sight of Ancient Tyrannosaurus Rex, or at the end of each of its turns in combat, a beast can make a {@dc 17} Wisdom saving throw to become immune to this ability for 24 hours. Succeeding this Wisdom saving throw does not make it immune to Ancient Tyrannosaurus Rex's Iconic Bellow.

trait.name: Legendary Resistance (2/day)
entries: If Ancient Tyrannosaurus Rex fails a saving throw, it may choose to succeed it instead.

trait.name: Imparted Speech
entries: Ancient Tyrannosaurus Rex can understand Archosauric and another language of your choosing (usually Common). It can speak Archosauric, albeit slowly. Its Intelligence score is increased to 8.

trait.name: Wise Old Beast
entries: Ancient Tyrannosaurus Rex has advantage on Wisdom saving throws.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Ancient Tyrannosaurus Rex chooses the attack action, it may make one Strongest Bite attack and one Crushing Tail Slam attack.

action.name: Strongest Bite
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 13} to hit, reach 10 ft., one target. {@h}23 ({@damage 3d12 + 4}) piercing damage plus 23 ({@damage 3d12 + 4}) force damage.

A creature hit by this attack is {@condition grappled} and {@condition restrained} (escape {@dc 21}). Until this grapple ends, Ancient Tyrannosaurus Rex can't Strongest Bite another target and has an additional +5 to hit the grappled creature with any Strongest Bite attack.

action.name: Crushing Tail Slam
entries: Each creature within 10 ft. of Ancient Tyrannosaurus Rex must succeed a {@dc 21} Dexterity saving throw or take 28 ({@damage 3d12 + 9}) bludgeoning damage and be knocked {@condition prone}. On a success they take half as much damage and are not knocked {@condition prone}.
A creature grappled by Strongest Bite is not affected by this attack.

action.name: Iconic Bellow
entries: Every non-Tyrannosaur creature within 200 ft. of Ancient Tyrannosaurus Rex that can hear it must succeed a {@dc 20} Wisdom saving throw or take 13 ({@damage 1d12 + 7}) psychic damage and be {@condition frightened} of Ancient Tyrannosaurus Rex for 1 minute. A creature can repeat this saving throw at the end of each of its turns, ending the effect on itself on a success. If a creature's saving throw is successful, the creature is immune to the {@condition frightened} condition from Ancient Tyrannosaurus Rex's Iconic Bellow for the next 24 hours.

legendary.name: Lunging Head Bash
entries: Ancient Tyrannosaurus Rex may move up to 10 ft., then make the following attack:
{@atk mw} {@hit 13} to hit, reach 10 ft., one target. {@h}20 ({@damage 2d10 + 9}) bludgeoning damage.

trait.name: Steady Healing
entries: At the end of Big Al's turn, she recovers 8 hit points. Big Al is resistant to necrotic damage (included above).

trait.name: Clumsy
entries: Whenever Big Al begins moving, roll a {@dice 1d20}. On the roll of a 1, Big Al instead stumbles and trips directly forward 10 ft., is knocked {@condition prone}, suffers {@damage 1d4} bludgeoning damage, and cannot move for the rest of her turn.
If Big Al is below 10 hit points, she stumbles on a roll of 1-10, rather than just 1.

trait.name: Subadult
entries: Big Al's Wisdom stat is reduced to 6 (included above) and she cannot gain advantage on any Wisdom checks or Wisdom saving throws.

trait.name: Stalker
entries: The first time each day that Big Al fails a Stealth check, she may instead choose to succeed it.

trait.name: Starving
entries: The first time an Animal Handling check is made against Big Al each day, if that check utilises food suitable for a carnivore, it automatically succeeds.
If Big Al is fed, she'll periodically return to whoever fed her of her own accord for more food.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Big Al chooses the attack action, she may make one Big Al's Maw attack and one Big Al's Claws attack.

action.name: Big Al's Maw
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 7} to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}10 ({@damage 1d8 + 6}) piercing damage.

action.name: Big Al's Claws
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 7} to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}13 ({@damage 2d6 + 6}) slashing damage.
Chosen by Lucian T. Moreman ALLOSAURUS {@i "AH-LOW-SORE-US"} {@b (DIFFERENT LIZARD)}

More than once we came across a young injured Allosaurus. The rest of the party kept callin' it "Big Al". No idea why the name stuck, but it did. It seemed to walk with a wobbly gait, like it had hurt its toe, but still pushed on. Poor thin' never had the stomach to really attack us... it kinda just followed our group for a while, fed on scraps, left, then returned every now 'n' again. I imagine it would have given it a go if our group had been fewer in number though.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Allosaurus} was a large predatory theropod dinosaur from the Late Jurassic (155-145 million years ago) of North America and Western Europe. It was a strong and robust animal with powerful limbs and was up to 28 ft. long. "Big Al" is the name given to a near-complete female sub-adult specimen from Wyoming that was approximately 22 ft. long.

entries.name: Palaeopathology
entries: Pathology is the science of disease and injury, and palaeopathology is the interpretation of pathology in fossils. We can use this information to identify predator/ prey relationships, environmental hazards, (rarely) diseases present, and the life history of individual animals, including their susceptibilities and rates of recovery.

Big Al is the most famous case study of palaeopathology in dinosaurs, with at least 19 broken or injured bones. These include broken and damaged chest ribs, broken gastralia (belly ribs), injured vertebrae, an infected illium (hip bone), a broken vertebral arch, a punctured shoulder blade, a badly mangled right arm, and numerous injuries and infections on both feet. Many had healed, but not very well and had clear signs of infection, meaning Big Al was in a sorry state towards the end of her life. This animal was likely in pain for many years but persisted perhaps in part due to a localised immune system that prevented serious infections from spreading around the body.

In fact, despite her grievous injuries, we think that Big Al was still able to reproduce, as new evidence indicates that she likely laid eggs just before her death. We know this because of the presence of medullary bone, which is a type of bone laid down by female egg-laying animals as a calcium store for eggshell production. Not only does this identify Big Al as female, but also provides a major insight into the extent of trauma these animals could endure while still following their reproductive instincts. Nevertheless, Big Al's injuries to her feet and arm prevented her from hunting, and she ultimately died from emaciation.

trait.name: Big Al's Ballad
entries: When Big Al awakens at dawn each day or is in combat, dramatic orchestral music plays loudly centred over her location and all of Big Al's choices, thoughts, and actions are also narrated by a disembodied, stoic British voice. This music and voice can only be heard by player characters.

trait.name: Story Set in Stone
entries: Big Al cannot be killed by normal means. If Big Al is reduced to 0 hit points or suffers an effect that would kill her, she instead falls to 1 hit point, cannot attack, loses her Steady Healing ability, and will flee from combat.

She can only take lethal damage from her Clumsy ability. If she does not trip while fleeing, she will wander for 24 hours, then die emaciated on the nearest riverbank. However, if Big Al is healed during this 24 hour period (excluding from a short/long rest), she regains her Steady Healing ability, is able to attack again, and may behave normally.

trait.name: Olfactory Enlargement
entries: Carnotaurus has a +10 bonus to any Perception check that involves smell. If its sense of smell is hindered or lost, it instead has a -10 modifier and disadvantage on any Perception check that involves smell.

trait.name: Explosive Ambush!
entries: In the first round of combat, Carnotaurus may dash as a bonus action.

trait.name: Scent of Prey
entries: Carnotaurus has advantage on Survival checks to pursue prey.

trait.name: Possible Pack Mentality
entries: All Carnotaurus treat other Carnotaurus as allies.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Carnotaurus chooses the attack action, it may make two Slashing Bite attacks and one Brow Horn Gore attack.

action.name: Slashing Bite
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 4} to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}6 ({@damage 1d6 + 3}) piercing damage plus 5 ({@damage 1d4 + 3}) slashing damage.

action.name: Brow Horn Gore
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 6} to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}11 ({@damage 1d10 + 6}) bludgeoning damage.
A creature hit by this attack must make a {@dc 11} Strength saving throw or be knocked {@condition prone}.
Chosen by Ahappypsycho {@i "CAR-NO-TORE-US"} {@b (MEAT-EATING BULL)}

Some predatory dinosaurs hunt largely by smell and carno was one such beastie. It pursued us for four days, followin' the scent trail we left. Thankfully, we were able to out manoeuvre it. More than once we crossed a river, and circled round to observe it. We watched it lose, then re-pick up our trail several times. Must have been very hungry to chase us for so long.
I guess it picked up the trail of somethin' easier to track when it stopped followin' us though.

{@i Carnotaurus} is the most famous member of the unusual Abelisauridae, a group of medium-sized theropods. {@i Carnotaurus} is known from the La Colonia Formation (71-69 million years ago) and has distinctive brow horns, giving it a bull-like appearance.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Carnotaurus} was medium-sized for an abelisaurid, at 26 ft. long and weighing approximately 1.5-2 tonnes. It had relatively long and strong legs which would have allowed for short bursts of sprinting. It also had highly reduced arms, so much so that the elbow joint no longer worked. Its arms could be rotated at the shoulder but couldn't bend like other theropods, and it also had 4 tiny fingers which may have lacked claws. Its head was boxy, with a tall and narrow skull but shallow lower jaw, and topped with a pair of prominent keratin-covered brow horns that protruded sideways.

{@i Carnotaurus} was built for short, explosive bursts of speed, making it an excellent pursuit hunter, running down prey. It was also able to bite rapidly, allowing it to quickly snap at escaping victims. {@i Carnotaurus} likely hunted prey smaller than itself, but it may also have predated upon medium-sized (juvenile) sauropods, bringing them down through rapid slashing bites. It is thought to have been a woodland or open plains predator.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Carnotaurus} would likely have stalked prey by getting within sprinting distance and then charging. It had an exceptional sense of smell, with a large olfactory lobe, but relatively low frequency hearing. It may also have hunted in pairs or small groups, meaning that prey would be charged by multiple {@i Carnotaurus}. Its horns were likely primarily used for intraspecific (same species) competition, displaying to, and even fighting with, other {@i Carnotaurus.}

We recommend that {@i Carnotaurus} be played as an ambush and pursuit hunter. It should track prey with its powerful sense of smell, sneak up as close as possible, then charge and pursue if the prey flees. It can be present in small groups (2 or 3 animals), socialising with each other. Like most large carnivores, {@i Carnotaurus} would have spent much of its time resting, so it would not be uncommon to encounter a small group sleeping together for most of the day.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: Abelisaurs were an unusual group of theropods, with boxy skulls adorned with horns or bosses, and highly reduced arms. {@i Carnotaurus} was therefore fairly typical for the group. They first appeared in the Jurassic and were reasonably successful, surviving until the end-Cretaceous extinction.
They are mostly known from the Southern Hemisphere in Africa, South America, India, and Madagascar, although there is some evidence that they may have been present in Europe too.
