entries.name: Domestic Animals
entries: Some animal lineages undergo a process known as domestication. Domesticated animals are those that have been made more amenable for handling and are generally less dangerous to humanoids. This process takes generations – potentially hundreds or thousands of years depending on reproductive speed. Most, if not all, civilisations domesticate animals. These are rarely large predators, although that is not unheard of. In the real world, common domestic animals include companion animals (dogs, cats, bearded dragons, etc.), farm animals (cows, sheep, goats, etc.), and animals used for transport/racing (horses, camels, pigeons, etc.). We tended to domesticate animals for food, companionship, pest control, transport, assistance with hunting, warfare, or entertainment. In your fantasy world(s), different groups of people may have domesticated animals for one or all of the same reasons.

Most animals that are domesticated are done so through selective breeding, a process whereby humanoids select which animals breed to accumulate desirable traits in their offspring. In general, these are traits that make them more docile and/or reduce their capacity to cause harm, as well as traits that fit the desired role.

We also think that some animal lineages, such as domestic cats, initially underwent domestication without direct selection by humans – that is, they were instead subject to selection pressures caused by living adjacent to humans that ultimately also domesticated them.

entries.name: Domestic Animals in Your Game World
entries: Including domesticated animals in your world makes for a much more immersive setting. In this book, you can select animals of appropriate sizes and diets that can replace existing modern animals. For example, {@creature Microraptor|DrDhrolinsDictionaryofDinosaurs} (page 50) might be used by townsfolk for ratting their grain stores in the same way that cats and small dogs are, or {@creature Paralititan|DrDhrolinsDictionaryofDinosaurs} (page 71) might be a huge mount used for war in the same manner as an elephant. When including a domesticated animal, we recommend applying the following changes:

items.name: Make them visually distinct:
items.entry: Most domesticated animals have reduced offensive capabilities – narrower jaws, shorter claws/talons, and smaller or blunter horns. We recommend also changing their colour, plumage, and/or patterning to denote that they are different from wild forms.

items.name: Change their damage:
items.entry: We suggest that you half all of the damage caused by animals that aren't used for combat. Those that are used for combat can be kept the same or even increased!

items.name: Make them behaviourally docile:
items.entry: Do not use the behaviour tables presented on pages 214-217 for domesticated animals. It doesn't make sense for domesticated small carnivores to be overly frightened of humanoids, nor for large herbivores to be overly aggressive. We suggest picking a known real-world animal and making their behaviour somewhat similar.

items.name: Keep animal handling checks simple:
items.entry: A single roll should be sufficient to control the animal and, if it is well-trained, the roll can be made at advantage. A particularly well-trained animal should require no check at all.

variantrule.name: Howdahs
entries: Howdahs are ornate carriages that were historically mounted on elephants or camels. They originated in the "East Indies" (a colonial term encompassing the Indo-Australian archipelago, India, and surrounding areas) but are associated with the range of {@i Elephas maximus}, the Asian elephant.

Generally, they were designed to be comfortable and lavish modes of transport that convey wealth and social status, commonly fitted with a canopy and adorned with expensive materials. However, armoured variants were also implemented as mobile bastions.

It is exciting to imagine the sorts of howdahs and carriages that would be constructed to fit dinosaurs. The titanic sauropods in particular offer evocative mounts that could become living fortresses.

Below is a set of loose rules to assist you in designing howdahs for Mesozoic reptiles. Generally, we envision these functioning as mobile bases of operations, allowing party members to rest while on the move and store items in a relatively safe place. The specifics of cost and how long it takes to acquire and fit a howdah will depend on your campaign's pace and economy. We've outlined some rough guidance, but feel free to alter it however you desire.

entries.name: Large/Huge/Gargantuan Howdah
entries: A standard large howdah has a maximum capacity of five humanoids and includes two hammocks with space for two bedrolls underneath, accompanied by two storage chests, and finally a saddle with reins for controlling the mount. A creature equipped by a Howdah has its speed reduced by 5 ft., to a minimum of 5 ft.

Huge and gargantuan howdahs have the same basic set-up, but can also be augmented with additional amenities. We recommend that a huge howdah have up to two additional amenities, and a gargantuan howdah have three or four, although you may want to allow more on the largest creatures in your campaign.

To construct a Howdah, you will generally require a team of people, including a carpenter, blacksmith, and general labourers. Alternatively, specialist components can be purchased and assembled by just general labourers (or the party). The table below outlines the recommended costs and build times. In some settings, howdahs may be commonplace and significantly cheaper.

We have also included amenities that you can augment your howdah with. Several have restrictions on the types of dinosaurs that may use them, but there should be few (or no) restrictions for their use with non-dinosaur creatures.

entries.caption: Howdah Amenities
rows: A collection of lockable crates and chests that can store a large volume and weight of items/materials. The players are issued with keys for them, and we recommend that picking the locks has a {@dc 20} or that the locks are otherwise magically protected.

A full set of {@item smith's tools|PHB|blacksmith's equipment}, including an anvil, sharpening wheel, and a small forge. It allows for the forging and repair of equipment. If attached to a huge howdah, this reduces the mount's speed by an additional 5 ft. (to a minimum of 5 ft.)

A series of brewing pots, glass vials, pestles and mortars, and a case of common catalytic ingredients with instructions. These allow for the brewing of potions and poisons from harvested resources with relative ease and non-expert knowledge.

A place of worship that can be dedicated to any single entity or pantheon. If a creature communes at the shrine with something they worship for 10 minutes, they gain the effects of the {@spell Bless} spell for 1 hour. A creature can only be affected by one instance of bless from any shrine at a time.
This area acts as a roost for up to 2 small/medium (or 1 large) flying creatures. It comes with a feeding trough and bedding straw, as well as storage for saddles.

Another set of two hammocks with space for two bedrolls underneath them, accompanied by two storage chests. These effectively increase the transport capacity of the howdah, allowing four additional humanoids.
{@i Sauropods only.} A seat on the head of this sauropod allows a medium or smaller humanoid to see much further (many miles) than if they were sat anywhere else on the Howdah.

entries: {@i Non-ceratopsians only.} Allows the mount to make an additional tail attack using its bonus action:
{@b Tailblade.} {@atk mw} reach 10 ft., to hit: Dexterity modifier (+ proficiency bonus if the creature already has a tail attack). {@h}{@dice 2d6} + Strength modifier slashing damage.

Alternatively, you can simply increase the damage of the creature's innate tail attack by {@dice 2d6} + Strength modifier slashing damage. This may be attached to a large howdah in addition to other sizes.
A humanoid manning the Harpoon Launcher can take the following actions/bonus actions:
{@b Action}

{@b Harpoon Launch.} {@atk rw} range 200 ft., +(Dexterity modifier) to hit, one target. {@h}({@dice 2d10} + Dexterity modifier) piercing damage. You may add your proficiency bonus to the hit and damage rolls of this attack if you are proficient with crossbows and firearms. Once fired, the Harpoon must be reloaded before it can be fired again.

An optional rope may be attached to the harpoon to snag a hit creature. If a creature hit by at least one of these attacks attempts to move out of range of the Harpoon Launcher, it must make a Strength saving throw with a DC of (16 + (2 × number of ropes attached)). On a failed save, its speed is reduced to 0 for 2 turns and it is knocked {@condition prone}. On a successful save, all ropes break, freeing the creature.
{@b Bonus Actions}
{@b Reload Harpoon Launcher.} The harpoon is reloaded and ready to fire again.

{@b Reel In.} Any harpoons fired with ropes attached begin to automatically reel in at 40 ft. per round, reducing the distance in which this Strength save is triggered and dragging a prone creature closer. No further harpoons can be fired with ropes attached until this process is complete.

Allows players to communicate in the same manner as the {@spell Sending} spell an unlimited number of times from this location, so long as the target has a {@item sending stones|DMG|sending stone} (or similar device) to receive the message.

Once per day, a portal to another portal nexus (usually located in big cities or other Howdahs) may be temporarily opened. We recommend that it requires an {@item Evolunite Shard|DrDhrolinsDictionaryofDinosaurs} (page 298) or similar resource of at least 250 gp in value and that only up to 8 humanoids are able to use the portal before it closes.

rows: {@i Theropods only.} Sheets of jagged metal form a tough helmet and provide a vicious steel edge to jaw and head attacks. The mount's AC is increased by 2 and any bite or head-bash attack deals an additional {@damage 2d6} piercing damage. This may be attached to a large howdah in addition to other sizes.

{@i Ankylosaurs, Nodosaurs, and Ceratopsians only.} Heavy armour covers this creature's flanks. Its AC is improved by 4, but its speed is reduced by a further 5 ft. (to a minimum of 5 ft.). This may be attached to a large howdah in addition to other sizes.

language.name: Archosauric
entries: Archosauric (or Archosauran) is the official/state language of the sapient archosaur races and may be selected as one of your player character's languages. It is envisioned as the root language of fantasy dragon and bird languages, despite those languages' great differences. As such, it functionally sounds like a hybrid of the two, sharing features of both.

Archosauric combines high-pitched clicks and whistles with deep guttural growls and rolling harsh syllables. The frequency and abundance of these two starkly different tones within the language are typically a result of the formality of the conversation. That is, higher pitched clicks and squawks are usually casual slang, whereas deeper tones are more formal, although there is certainly intermingling between the two in many conversations.

entries.name: Physical description
entries: The Pluvenn are a society of raptorfolk, made from a collection of different species of raptors (evolved from {@i Saurornitholestes langstoni, Sinornithosaurus millenii, Deinonychus antirrhopus}, etc.). This gives them a very diverse appearance, varying greatly in size, colour, A Pluvenn Druid taking a long rest on an adventure.

plumage, and robustness. On the whole, they are lightly built and gracile bipeds, covered by a thick coat of fluffy feathers. The feathers on their forelimbs are long and sturdy, and they have long flowing feathers on their tails. Their plumage can be vivid, drab, patterned, or even camouflaged. They have long, snouted heads and a row of extremely sharp teeth. All Pluvenn have scaled bird-like feet with a large, recurved claw on the inside toe.

entries.name: Background
entries: The name Pluvenn comes from the Cornish word for feather and is a fitting reference to rural English society, which the Pluvenn are inspired by. Most raptorfolk in fiction are portrayed as a savage and vicious jungle-dwelling race. We have taken a very different approach and instead envision them as a peaceful society of townsfolk that fit into the idealistic Beatrix Potter-esque rural life. They live in quiet towns and villages, busying themselves with gardening, tea drinking, cooking, artistry, and socialising. Despite this humble appearance, the Pluvenn have other characteristics that some races find disturbing, most notably their vicious, predatory nature. They are obligate carnivores and so do not bother with agriculture (other than growing herbs and spices to season their meat). They instead rear livestock and partake in gory festival hunts.

entries.name: Courtship and Reproduction
entries: Pluvenn undertake a prolonged period of courtship when seeking a mate. This usually begins as simple conversations, followed by long (sometimes chaperoned) walks, then joint attendance of social events. During this time, they will exchange gifts of wild flowers, hand-crafted trinkets, and specialist foods. Public displays of affection rarely exceed handholding. Eventually, they will ceremonially pair to publicise their relationship and this commitment is for life.

Pluvenn are an egg-laying race and lay eggs in clutches of 3-4. Incubation is carried out at home by both parents, but hatchlings are cared for in a dedicated community nursery during the day and only return home to sleep. These nurseries are run by particularly gentle and well-spoken members of the Pluvenn community and hatchlings remain there until they are about 6 months old. After this, they enter a strict schooling system where they attend almost every day and are schooled by dedicated educational staff.

entries.name: Bristlebush Vale
entries: Hidden amongst the strife and hardship of the ancient world lies Bristlebush Vale. This idyllic region is famed for its long bright summers, drizzly autumns, spring meadows full of life, and twinkling icicle winters. Aside from the hunting activities of the Pluvenn themselves, Bristlebush Vale is a peaceful and quiet setting. Between gnarled, misty forests and rolling hills lie secluded villages and hamlets. In these settlements, the Pluvenn play out their pleasant lives of socialising, gardening, farming livestock, and hunting.

Pluvenn hunts are a combination of whimsy and horror. One-to-two times a month, the Pluvenn will undertake ritualistic group hunts at dusk. Donned in their finest garb, they venture into the surrounding forests, setting traps and positioning in the shadows to ambush game. They prefer to kill ensnared prey with their jaws and claws, letting their otherwise docile nature drop away in that gory moment. In a single night, dozens of creatures are slaughtered in a bloodbath that leaves many non-Pluvenn horrified.

Slain prey are returned to the village for a night-time festival of roaring fire barbecues and butchery. Bunting and stalls decorate the village, with each stand boasting their own cooking technique or particular spices. These are considered bonding experiences and family units will often hunt together and share their stories around the firelight. In the morning, the remaining meat is prepared for consumption in later weeks. It may be stored in cool underground buildings or spiced and cured in great smoking barns. Some Pluvenn favour making specialist gravy-like meat teas that are brewed from jerky mixed with spices.

entries.name: History and Religion
entries: The Pluvenn of Bristlebush Vale have a relatively simple history of village life. Their ancestors arrived in the region centuries ago as several disparate travelling tribes, composed of different species of raptorfolk. Over time, these intermingled until a single cohesive culture was formed. Since then, they have had a docile history with no major conflicts beyond the repelling of unwanted bandits. These invaders are sometimes ritualistically devoured in a grand post-battle feast (called a "gool").

Pluvenn religion revolves largely around ancestor worship. Their dead are buried with precious trinkets and sentimental items in sacred burial mounds and small catacombs hidden deep within nearby forests. These places are sacred to the Pluvenn and are, unfortunately, usually the targets of any intruding raids. Pluvenn may travel to these sites to ask their forebearers for guidance during the rare times of hardship or social strife.

entries.name: Names
entries: The Pluvenn favour high-pitched squawky names spoken in their ancient Archosauric tongue, such as Skree, Kek, Kareese, or Pip. They also sometimes have names spoken in Common, such as William, Hermione, Richard, or Audrey. Typically, the naming convention of an individual village will be similar among its populace, either all having Archosauric names or all having Common names.

entries.name: Physical description
entries: The Manyhorn is a name given to the array of ceratopsian humanoids (evolved from {@i Styracosaurus albertensis, Diabloceratops eatoni, Sinoceratops zhuchengensis, Protoceratops andrewsi} etc.) that have formed a cohesive society of multiple guilds. They vary greatly in size and horn shape/number, but otherwise look quite similar. They are bulky dull-coloured scaly-skinned humanoids with short, stout limbs, large, bony head crests, a beaked mouth, and horns. A handful of Manyhorn (i.e. those evolved from {@i Protoceratops}) do not actually possess horns, but are still considered Manyhorn nonetheless. Most Manyhorn are generally dull greens, reds, and browns in colour, but brighter variants exist.

Manyhorn prefer to dress formally, with well-fitted suits and multi-layered robes or tabards. They invariably display their guild sigil prominently on their clothing, but sometimes also have it painted or tattooed onto their crest. When armoured, their armour usually is accompanied by tabards displaying their guild's colours.

entries.name: Background
entries: We have constructed Manyhorn society to primarily operate as a series of guilds that can exist within any regional setting. The guilds protect and employ each of their members, who in turn help the guild prosper. Each guild consists of members of every species of Manyhorn who are extremely loyal to their guild. Each guild can (and does) function entirely independently of other guilds, but each guild also typically focuses on mastering a specific aspect of society. These may be tied to philosophical ideals, commercial aspirations, or political conquest of a region. The number of guilds within a region may vary, but typically range from 3 to 6.

It is exceedingly rare for a Manyhorn to leave their guild and swapping guilds is almost unheard of. Those without a guild are branded socially as 'guildless', a considerable insult within Manyhorn society.

entries.name: Reproduction
entries: Manyhorn undertake ceremonial marriages that must occur with a different guild. It is not acceptable for any Manyhorn to marry or reproduce internally within a guild as this has historically led to reduced gene pools within each guild. Members who breach this rule risk expulsion from their guild.

Manyhorn tend not to be attentive parents, and females lay between 3 and 10 eggs in a clutch (depending on species) that are then raised by communal "hatchwatchers". Offspring are cared for in large groups of 20 or more hatchlings. All eggs are the centre of a fierce custody battle between the different guilds of each parent. Even before they hatch, both guilds vie for the "right of adoption" to bolster their own numbers. Some guilds will amicably divide the eggs, others will issue a winner-takes-all challenge.

entries.name: The guilds of Un Grazook
entries: Once a small fishing port, Un Grazook was utterly transformed by the prosperity brought by the Manyhorn guilds over several centuries. The city now boasts a vast population with inhabitants from every conceivable species and every corner of the world. A metropolis of trade and culture, founded on the competing principals of five different guilds, each specialised in different areas of society:

items: The Alorah – The guild of stonemasonry and land lordship, whose colours are green and gold and whose sigil is a sapling with deep roots.
The Janth – The guild of shipbuilding and commerce, whose colours are red and black and whose sigil is a sailboat on stormy waters.
The Orb'eth – The guild of politics and negotiation, whose colours are yellow and purple and whose sigil is a fired arrow with a ribbon attached.
The Umalai – The guild of arts and entertainment, whose colours are orange and royal blue and whose sigil is a four-winged bird (or {@i Microraptor}).
The Thyrothe – The guild of education and science, whose colours are pale blue and white and whose sigil is a torch held aloft within a circle.

entries: The guilds compete openly for political power, but also engage in espionage to undermine each other's influence. Every year, one high-ranking member of each guild is selected as a representative to form a council that makes city-wide decisions and guides the overall rule of the region.

City districts are predominantly run by a single guild and may range from peaceful areas of reason and enlightenment to crime-ridden hubs of corruption, the former being more likely due to the self-respect of most guilds.

entries.name: History and Religion
entries: The history of Un Grazook is one wrought with strife, violence, and ultimately prosperity. When the Manyhorn first arrived at the small port, they were a disparate people of many different cultures pressed together by circumstance. Species prejudice gave rise to clans that fought in gang warfare for generations before the fallout of their battles brought the city to near destruction. This turning point caused younger members of each clan to overthrow their elders, toppling the philosophy of division. Eventually, the clans were entirely disbanded and their members distributed between ten guilds dedicated to specific tasks to restore the city both physically and culturally. Within a matter of years, the bubbling tension between different ceratopsian species was ejected entirely from their society. However, philosophical differences developed between each guild, ultimately producing a new kind of tension. Thankfully, this largely manifested as a competitive and industrious economic battle, rather than a bloody one. The five lost guilds were not slain in gory battles, but were rather slowly absorbed by larger and/or more successful guilds.

Religious worship varies dramatically between guilds. Some guilds have a strictly enforced single religion, others allow their members to worship whoever or whatever they please, and others still outlaw religion entirely, seeing it as a distraction from loyalty to the guild. In the more restrictive guilds, most Manyhorn keep their religious beliefs private and simply project the status quo.

entries.name: Names
entries: A name is not given to a Manyhorn until its "right of adoption" has been completed. Names are then issued by a guild elder and each elder may follow a different naming convention. Some examples of different guild names are as follows:

items: The Alorah – Hard guttural Archosauric names:

entries: Grulgrug, Arough-Roth, or Barr.

items: The Janth – Double-barrelled names in Archosauric:

entries: Hur-Kreck, Uy-Gungg, or Farenk-Aron.

items: The Orb'eth – Sharp and relatively high-pitched Archosauric names: Kreenk, Flarek, or Brekbrek.
The Umalai – All names begin with the prefix "Un-" to honour their cultural heritage: Un-Krof, Un-Tharalla, or Un-Palapa.
The Thyrothe – Are given names that are intended as guidance for their future careers or area of research:

entries: Astroquoth, Minerag, or Chemokruln.

entries.name: Physical description
entries: The Jeholrak are small-statured, weedy creatures with a short, stout tail and three-clawed hands. They have a stout, beaked snout and a row of fan-shaped teeth. Their bodies are covered by soft, downy feathers that look superficially like a short layer of fur. Their feathers are typically dull greys and browns, although colourful variants do exist.

entries.name: Background
entries: The Jeholrak are based on {@i Jeholosaurus}, a small herbivorous ornithopod dinosaur from the Early Cretaceous Jehol biota that had a downy layer of feathers. We envision the Jeholrak as small humanoids who love to supplement their drab natural colours with spectacular dyed robes and feathers from various bird and dinosaur species. We also imagine that the Jeholrak have overcome their weak stature with specialised pheromone glands that allow them to subdue other species. This gives the Jeholrak a faint sweet aroma. The Jeholrak have several large kingdoms, spread across the multiverse. The largest city (imagined here to be from the Jehol Formation) is built into the side of a large mountain, Mount Karao'kr. Below, the society of the city of Mount Karao'kr is described.

entries.name: Reproduction and Gender
entries: The Jeholrak are an egg-laying species and typically construct a nursery within their homes. This is often an elaborate and colourfully decorated room in which hatchlings spend their first few years. Jeholrak rarely have a single offspring and will instead lay clutches of eggs, raising 3 to 5 hatchlings at a time every five years or so. Caring for hatchlings is typically undertaken by females and this is largely a pragmatic response to resource investment, as it is quite taxing to produce several eggs. Once the hatchlings are 5-6 years old and venture out of the nursery, males will assist in their care. Outside of offspring care, gender roles vary greatly among different Jeholrak societies. Some only allow one gender to be the ruling class or military force, while others have no restrictions whatsoever.

entries.name: The Jeholrak of Mount Karao'kr
entries: Mount Karao'kr is both the name of the mountain and the name of the extravagant city carved into its side. It is a mighty metropolis of stone, with grand spires piercing the sky. It houses tens of thousands of individuals of many races, but the Jeholrak make up the vast majority of its population. The city itself is patrolled by large dinosaur cavalry, kept domesticated by the intoxicating pheromones of their Jeholrak riders.

The Jeholrak of Mount Karao'kr may be small, but they have big personalities. Despite their docile, herbivorous ancestry, they have developed a complex political society of backstabbing and blackmail, with each Jeholrak trying to claw their way to the top. The hierarchy of the city is built entirely on personal gain by any means. Political sabotage, backstabbing, and bribery are commonplace and considered the norm within the city. This city is ruled by a single dictator (or occasionally a 'monarch'), usually for a very short period of time, and has a strictly tiered class system based on personal wealth. Class mobility is exceptionally high between these tiers, with individuals able to purchase or swindle their hierarchical position, often trading places with another. As mentioned above, Jeholrak typically have large numbers of offspring, so inherited wealth is quickly divided among large families. The naturally reclusive nature of the Jeholrak has allowed them to thrive within this society, although it by no means attests to the personal beliefs of every Jeholrak within the city.

Most of these Jeholrak prefer the finer things in life, and they are decadent herbivores, though they do partake in meat occasionally. They have a rich, artistic culture and produce fantastic sculptures, poems, and music. Despite their drab natural colours, the Jeholrak of Mount Karao'kr value beauty highly and they decorate themselves with brightly coloured robes, jewellery, and vivid feathers from other species. They see the value of education, and their societies house great libraries and schools, giving rise to remarkable scholarly pursuits.

entries.name: Religion and ideals
entries: A variety of religions permeate Jeholrak culture, with no one religion being permanently dominant. In Mount Karao'kr, all manner of deity-worship, cults, and churches have risen and fallen throughout the city's existence. Religions are followed passionately, and so the only uniting factor is that their Jeholrak members tend to be aggressive fanatics. It is no surprise that vast conflicts have been fought in the names of various deities, although usually by paid mercenaries, rather than by the Jeholrak themselves.

entries.name: Names
entries: Within Mount Karao'kr, a hatching Jeholrak is typically given a simple name. However, once coming of age, Jeholrak begin to bestow upon themselves ever more extravagant names with reference to (supposedly) heroic deeds they have achieved. As such, the older or more influential a Jeholrak is, the longer and more ludicrous their name becomes. Below are some examples:
{@b Hatchling names} Rassolax; Zilfor; Perfrill; Blukkar.
{@b Adolescent names} Mighty Herebra; Urgine the Quick; Jabara Blade-Touched.
{@b Adult names} Tribe-Herald Wurranii the Impeccable; Warrider Runolox, Jewel-Eater of the Throne.
A Jeholrak Wizard ponders her orb.
{@b Official names} Grand-Leader Taltor, Bringer of Dawn and Ender of Revolutions; Battlemaster Scarb the Bloodied Maw of Venomspire's Bane.
{@b Example Elder name} Arch Councillor Kukuok Blade Mind, Herald of the Five Banners, Grand Monarch of Karao'kr, Magister of the Golden Ring, Throne-taker, Slayer of Giants, Bastion of Wisdom.

entries.name: Physical description
entries: The Ankylier are a race of heavily armoured, herbivorous humanoids. They have a large and broad appearance, with thick, bony osteoderms covering their back, flanks, limbs, and head which are, in turn, covered in tough scutes. They are so heavily armoured that even their eyelids are reinforced. Their skin is thick, scaly, and gives them a leathery appearance. Ankylier have low brows, large, muscular limbs, bulging stomachs, and a thick tail that ends in a heavy, bony club.

entries.name: Background
entries: The Ankylier are, of course, based on the well-known dinosaur {@i Ankylosaurus}. They emulate its impressive bulk and defences, and play as a relatively slow and extremely durable race. We envision them as industrious, expansionist, and aggressive relative to most herbivorous creatures. This aggression stems from their inability to outrun foes, forcing them to stand and fight. The Ankylier described below are but one group of this race, and your own character could deviate from these characteristics significantly, perhaps even portraying a peaceful, gentle race.

entries.name: Reproduction
entries: Ankylier familial bonds are strong. Pairs mate for life and eggs are laid individually several years apart, with offspring cared for up until maturity before the next egg is laid. Eggs are usually carried in threaded wire baskets lined with dried plants to create a portable nest. Hatchlings and young children form close attachments with their parents, usually following in their footsteps, figuratively and literally. Children are incorporated into Ankylier society as fast as possible, working as apprentices as soon as they are able. Some other races see this attitude as akin to child labour, but the Ankylier value the safety and contribution of their children very much. While parents offer harsh criticism, they also provide great praise when deserved.

entries.name: Bladestone Gully
entries: The most well-known Ankylier society is that of Blazestone Gully. Blazestone Gully incorporates a huge expanse of land – originally a series of riverways that crossed a wide-open, hilly plane. Over centuries, shallow gorges were carved by rivers, steep valleys in an otherwise open region. These once lush ravines were ravaged by a drying climate, creating a relatively barren and rocky scrubland, quenched only by trickling waterways. These environmental conditions are important, as they shaped Ankylier society.

The erosion exposed rich iron deposits in the rusty-coloured sandy rocks that allowed the Ankylier to forge their existence. Decades of mining and smithing have produced huge, industrial iron-clad towns of punished metal where the Ankylier forge all manner of industrial goods. Their society is constructed around this commerce, relying entirely on their craft to trade for other essential goods. This lifestyle has made most Ankylier natural smiths and master metalworkers, often hammering iron with their own tails.

Their brutal appearance is conveyed in their overall culture. Although individuals vary dramatically, softer-spoken Ankylier exist in the shadows of their aggressive kin. Most are quick to anger, but value discipline and reign in their tempers just as fast. They take great pride in their own constitution, and regularly engage in tests of endurance. Competitions to see who can stomach the toughest foliage or forge the hottest steel with just their tail are common.

entries.name: History and Religion
entries: The Ankylier of Blazestone Gully have a long history of conflict and warfare. Their stern attitudes and aggressiveness often land them in hot water with other races, and their politics are no different. Harsh words and bruised egos tend to cause a backlash in smithing pricing, and if another city backs out of a large contract, the Ankylier armies will be sent to recover costs by force. Given Blazestone Gully's monopoly over the region, such conflicts are commonplace.

Blazestone Gully has an official policy on religion whereby any deity that favours honour, strength, or war should be worshiped openly, and other deities are generally not accepted. That being said, the joint worship of additional deities that embody the attributes of commerce, wisdom, honesty, philosophy, valour, or discipline are tolerated publicly. The worship of any remaining deities is considered socially taboo and akin to weakness.
An Ankylier Fighter surveys the battlefield.

entries.name: Names
entries: The Ankylier invariably give their offspring names that convey strength or power by combining two words, and are usually in their native tongue Archosauric. Names are nether gender- or sex-specific. Common names include: Boulderfist, Ruggedhide, Ironguts, and Booming-Chest. If their names are in Archosauric, to a non-speaker they would sound like: Karko-ragh, Gurrgu, Oo-tarm-ma, and Vro-fath.

entries.name: Physical description
entries: The Limukin are a small, lean reptilian species of humanoids. They are remarkably gracile, and what they lack in strength and size, they make up for with speed. Their thin, scaly skin comes in a variety of hues, but is typically earthy in colour (greens, browns, and deep yellows). These can be mottled with dark or vivid spots, stripes, and other forms of camouflage. They have relatively short forelimbs.

entries.name: Background
entries: The Limukin are based on {@i Limusaurus inextricabilis}, a small Jurassic dinosaur that was an early member of Ceratosauria (the same group that contains the large predatory {@i Ceratosaurus}). This species' name translates to "Mud Lizard" and they underwent unusual morphological changes as they developed into adulthood, transitioning from toothed omnivores to beaked herbivores. We envision the Limukin as a race of river-, forest-, and jungle-dwelling dinosaurian creatures. They are among the most ancient of the dinosaurian races and inhabit many regions, although the bulk of them are found along the Shisux River. A description of the largest population of Limukin is given below, but many other populations exist scattered across the multiverse that differ in significant ways.

entries.name: Reproduction and Gender
entries: The Limukin are an egg laying species and will either hide their eggs in chambers within their dwellings, or carry one or two eggs in slings, pressed close to their body. Offspring are typically cared for communally and an individual Limukin will not notably recognise two others as it's parents.

In general, Limukin society typically has no definitive gender identities or roles. Individuals court and may decide to pair as a couple for several years. When two individuals of the same sex couple up and choose to reproduce, one of them may opt to change sex over a period of several weeks. Also, an opposite sex couple may choose to swap sexes if it would be preferential for the male to egg-lay at any given point and they may do this many times throughout their relationship. Limukin offspring are omnivorous and will actively hunt small prey such as insects and small mammals, learning the basics of stealth, trapping, and fishing. As they mature, they eventually transition into a more herbivorous diet before becoming entirely herbivorous as adults.

entries.name: The Shisux River Limukin
entries: The Limukin of the Shisux Riverways typically form small-to-medium societies (kinlins) of dozens to a few hundred individuals that live in the root hollows of trees, small cave systems, or otherwise create burrows near running water. Larger kinlins are composed of multiple such dwellings over a large area, usually spread across the Shisux delta or along a large portion of the river's length.

The Limukin of the Shisux Riverways choose to pursue a fisher-gatherer society, and do not typically pursue technology. They instead try to stay in-tune with the ebb and flow of nature; fishing and foraging, supplemented with limited seasonal agriculture. This Limukin society has a hierarchical leadership, with the elder-most members guiding the younger ones. They typically have a council of elders, rather than a single ruling individual. Decision-making is slow, as simple topics may be debated for days or weeks before a consensus can be reached.

The Shisux River kinlins prefer to defend themselves using silent ranged weapons, such as slingshots and bows. They also fashion melee weapons such as daggers, spears, and short swords from the bones and teeth of larger creatures. This, combined with their naturally dextrous nature, makes them formidable guerrilla fighters, able to strike and disappear into the undergrowth. Some Limukin are able to secrete toxins that they coat their weapons with.

entries.name: Religion and ideals
entries: The Shisux River Limukin have a very close relationship to nature, which can take many forms. Some venerate great beasts, admiring their vicious, predatory behaviour, while others see the tranquillity of the forest as a divine gift that must be nurtured. In all cases, the natural world forms the basis of the Shisux River religions. The Limukin make great celebrations of harvests, building small shrines within their burrows for each event. These Limukin also see themselves as part of nature, and so celebrate their own achievements in a form of ancestry worship. For example, they will honour both a predated great Limukin as well as the beast that hunted them. Hunter and hunted are equally respected. The Shisux River Limukin have no formal religious texts and instead use a simplistic pictographic form of Archosauric to paint on the walls of their dwellings.

entries.name: Names
entries: Limukin typically have short names with two, three, and (rarely) four syllables. Their names, and language in general, include many hard 'K', 'N', and 'I' sounds. Typical names include: Piphi, Torsek, Nuek, Nanzaahn, Gerumal, Jam'reer, Liph'ko, Neararu.

entries.name: Physical description
entries: The Children of Seth are tall humanoids with long arms, short legs, and membranous wings connecting from an elongate finger to their lean bodies. They have a soft, downy fuzz, long pointed beaks, and a large, vividly-coloured crest atop their very large head.

entries.name: Background
entries: The Children of Seth, also known as the Dromeus, are based on {@i Thalassodromeus sethi}, a medium-to-large sized pterosaur from the Early Cretaceous of South America. The species name {@i sethi} is taken from the Egyptian god Seth. We envision them as tall, nomadic humanoids that have no definitive racial homeland. There are many different clans or tribes of the Dromeus, each with its own subtle differences. The Children of Seth described below are but one tribe, and your design could deviate from these substantially.

entries.name: Reproduction and Gender
entries: The Children of Seth birth live young after a 3-year gestation period. Their offspring are precocial, meaning that they are able to walk and fly shortly after birth, albeit slowly. This is a trait shared among many pterosaurs, and means that infants require significantly less care compared to other species. However, due to their nomadic lifestyle, the Children of Seth adopt the social traditions of whichever society they spend the most time in, including parental care approaches. Over time, these traditions will change as they move between societies. Sometimes, older members of the Children of Seth instead pick and choose their preferred traditions from different societies that they've encountered.

entries.name: Tribe: Children of Seth
entries: The Children of Seth are nomadic traders and adventurers who seek to share in the experiences of other peoples across the multiverse. They usually travel in small groups of 4-5 individuals, or on their own. Most tend to travel very light, favouring lightweight, high-value goods to trade, such as precious stones, fine silks, and magical trinkets. Those lucky enough to obtain one or more bags of holding may ferry many times their normal flight weight with them.

The Children of Seth have remarkable memories and are able to recall specific details of their long lives with ease. This aptitude for memory is one of the reasons they seek out different cultures and societies. They value experiences and knowledge above personal possessions, and greatly enjoy sharing what they know. Every few decades a clan or tribe will have a grand gathering, where each member shares stories of their travels or adventures over magnificent feasts. These are culturally significant celebrations that may last weeks or months, and are often the only opportunity for the Children of Seth to form mated pairs before departing again.

entries.name: History and Religion
entries: Due to their remarkable memories, the Children of Seth have no written records. Despite this, most can read and write multiple languages. As they do not record their own history, they have no sacred texts or religious scriptures. Instead, their religions and ideals are composed of a series of fables and tales that have, naturally, changed over time. Some contain deep truths about their society and nature, while others are now little more than children's stories. This has led to a wide range of beliefs and religions among the Children of Seth, as they are often greatly influenced by the varied places they visit and the myriad societies they encounter.

entries.name: Names
entries: The Children of Seth names are influenced by the societies they interact with. A parent may choose to name their offspring with a human or elven name if they have spent a considerable amount of time with these societies. As such, they have a wide variety of names. Examples include: Borra, Chavazin, Guzzleguts, Vargrelly, Teaneethyn, Thricestrike or Tim.
