entries.name: The Bahariya Formation
entries: We had sailed down that river for three days, but eventually found ourselves unable to continue. The waterways fanned out into an expansive delta, stretchin' as far as the eye could see. Lush vegetation and mangroves filled the area, along with the silhouettes of some pretty big dinos in the mornin' sun. The stretchin' of the river made it pretty shallow and the mangroves encroached on almost all of the waterways. They were far too shallow and narrow for our boat to get through quickly, and we knew that the ship off the coast would only wait for us a few more days. There wasn't time to carry the boat around, and the smoke on the horizon suggested that it ain't safe anyway. So, we had only one option: ditch the boat, wade through the delta, and flag down the ship with a fire from the coast. I knew this was gunna be a dangerous few days.

entries.name: Background
entries: The Bahariya Formation is located in the Western Desert of Egypt and is Early Cretaceous, specifically Cenomanian (93.5-99 million years ago), in age. Its sedimentology and stratigraphy are well-studied, in part due to the region's rich iron deposits making it a focal point of geological research. The Bahariya Formation itself was deposited over a period of 3 to 6 million years and forms a consistent succession of rock between 295 and 330 ft. thick.

Early excavations of the Bahariya Formation were undertaken by German palaeontologist Ernst Freiherr Stromer von Reichenbach (1871-1952) and his expedition team. They discovered the first {@i Spinosaurus} fossils, along with many other animals from the Bahariya Formation. Unfortunately, the vast majority of their collection was destroyed in the bombing of Munich Museum in 1944 during World War II.

entries.name: Description
entries: The lowermost part of Bahariya Formation yields most of its dinosaur fossils. This portion of the formation was deposited in a fluviatile-deltaic (river-delta) setting, which was a major component of the Bahariya palaeoenvironment. Plant fossils indicate that Bahariya was a colossal mangrove swamp (sometimes called the Bahariya Bight), possibly up to 115 mi2 and is hypothesised to be similar to the "Ten Thousand Islands" in modern Florida, USA.

The Bahariya Formation had regular dry and monsoonal seasons. The monsoons were likely violent and devastating during the wet season, whereas the dry season would have been very hot and calm, leading to low-energy waters for most of the year and the retention of nutrients within the sediments. This made the mangroves among the most productive non-marine biomes from the Mesozoic (measured in tonnes of carbon produced by photosynthesis per unit area), meaning abundant plant growth within organic and nutrient-rich sediments that were not washed away by high-energy waters for most of the year. This provided a lush and nourishing environment. Rare traces of charcoal indicate that wildfires ripped through the surrounding arid scrub during the hottest periods.

entries.name: Geology
entries: The Bahariya Formation is an excellent example of a complete stratigraphic sequence. It has unconformities at its base and top, which means that there was a period of erosion before it was deposited, and deposition stopped after it (but it wasn't eroded entirely away). This means that the Bahariya Formation provides a single snapshot of one basin that we can be sure represents continuous deposition over 3-6 million years. This, in turn, allows us to understand how environments in a single location change over time. For Bahariya, the lowermost rocks were deposited in river and delta settings, which then transitioned to costal, shoreface, shelf, and finally outer shelf in the uppermost rocks. This shows that the environment changed from river, to coastal, then to open sea as the basin level changed.

The rocks themselves consist of interbedded siltstones and sandstones, followed by cross-bedded amalgamated sandstones, then dark coloured ferruginous (iron-rich) sandstones in the uppermost unit. The different stages of the environmental change correspond to different rock types and colours.

entries.name: Fossils
entries: The formation yields a mixture of aquatic and terrestrial animals, with lots of molluscs (specifically oysters and clams), crabs, and fish, as well as turtles, sea snakes, plesiosaurs, crocodiles, and pterosaurs. Dinosaurs are not uncommon but, despite the abundance of lush plant-life, the fossils indicate that herbivores were relatively under-represented within the formation, generally restricted to gigantic titanosaurian sauropods (with lots of offspring, but few large adults). On the other hand, carnivores were present in their normal numbers and were probably sustained by the abundant fish and crustaceans that thrived in the nutrient-rich waters. This would have led to an environment that is substantially more carnivore-dominated than other Cretaceous settings. In the following pages, we have included the rules for the Bahariyan Polycotylid, {@i Carcharodontosaurus, Paralititan, Spinosaurus}, and {@i Stomatosuchus.}

entries.name: As a Roleplaying Environment
entries: The Bahariya delta is a region of extremes. In the dry season, the weather should be beautifully calm and sunny with overwhelmingly lush mangroves and waters abundant with life. Giant dinosaurs should roam the sandbanks, most of which are predators, making it a treacherous place for humanoids. Players can be directed into the mangroves by fires in the surrounding scrub, pushing all manner of creatures into the confines of the waterways for safety.

In the monsoon season, the region should be battered by heavy rains, strong winds, and blackened skies. Many of the animals will persist in the region, but may be seeking shelter within the densest mangroves, or fleeing rising waters by moving into the soaked scrubland.

{@b Predatory Population} Players have an increased chance of encountering carnivores. If you roll on a table to determine encounters for the party, the first time you roll, re-roll any result that isn't a carnivore (do not re-roll a second time). If you do not use an encounter table, the first time the party encounters a large carnivore, they instead encounter two fighting in a titanic battle.
{@b Over-productivity} When foraging for food, you can find triple the amount of food that you would normally be able to find in the same amount of time (particularly fish, fruits, and shellfish).
{@b Soupy Sediment} Any creature that takes the dash action while moving across the mangrove sediment (touching the ground) must roll a {@dice d6} and consult the table below.

entries.caption: Soupy Sediment
rows: Its speed becomes 0 until its next turn. It may use a bonus action to make a Strength or Intelligence check with a DC of 14. On a success, it is instead considered to be moving through difficult terrain until its next turn.
It treats the ground as difficult terrain.

entries.name: Bahariya Formation Flora
entries: The Bahariya forest was fundamentally a mangrove forest with mixed salinity waters. However, muddy banks and margins would have allowed other plants to flourish as well. Further upstream from the delta's mouth, the fresh waters would have fed more diverse forests.

entries.name: Weichselia reticulata
entries: {@i Weichselia reticulata} was a tree fern that formed much of the Bahariya mangrove forest. Its long, slender, and light trunks would have been useful for simple raft building, but lacked the structural integrity to be used in larger constructions. Their leaves may have contained an irritant, and caused mild rashes when touched, however the submerged part of the stem would likely have been edible, although not very tasty and difficult to harvest.

entries.name: Congestant
entries: The thick stem of this plant causes a creature's sinuses and ear canals to swell if chewed, dulling their hearing. A creature that chews this stem gains resistance to thunder damage for 24 hours, but also has disadvantage on {@skill Perception} checks that involve sound for 24 hours.

entries.name: Mild Irritant
entries: If a humanoid creature touches the leaves of this plant, they break out in a mild rash. This causes no damage and does not affect any of their abilities, but is itchy and uncomfortable.

entries.name: Marsilea sp.
entries: {@i Marsilea} sp. was a small aquatic fern with clover-like leaves. These leaves would have floated on the surface of shallow water around the Bahariya delta. Both the leaves and sporocarps (small growths at the base of the leaf) would have been edible. In fact, the sporocarps could have been ground into flour if enough were harvested. However, other components of the plant would have been highly toxic and modern relatives of this genus are known to cause brain damage to livestock that eat it.

entries.name: Optional Magical Rules
Neurotoxic Stimulant
entries: The leaves of this plant are a powerful stimulant. They can be crushed to create a potion that, if consumed, gives advantage on Dexterity saving throws for 24 hours. However, if the wrong parts of the plant are included in the potion, it also inflicts {@dice 2d4} psychic damage when consumed. When harvesting the plant as an ingredient, a {@dc 14} {@skill Nature} check is required to ensure that only the correct parts are harvested.

{@i Cladophlebis} was a genus of fern that grew in clusters within moist ground. It grew along the margins and sandy banks of the Bahariya delta as a low-lying plant. Despite its generic appearance, some components of this plant would have been edible. Young fiddleheads (the curled up developing leaves) could have been cooked and eaten, and the rhizome (underground stem) could have been processed to make a butter-like substance.

entries.name: Agathis sp.
entries: The use of "sp." indicates" that the specimen belongs to a species within that genus, but the scientists describing it cannot determine which one.
{@i Agathis} sp. was an exceptionally tall evergreen coniferous tree that stood more than twice the height of the tallest sauropods.
This genus persists today and its trees (sometimes called Kauri or Dammara trees)

can be found in Southeast Asia, Australia, and many of the surrounding island regions. The hard wood and wide trunks of this tree make it an exceptional building material and Polynesian cultures have historically used it in ship construction. The trees themselves can live for a very long time, reportedly well over a thousand years.

entries.name: Ancient Soul
entries: Certain trees of this species harbour an old druidic soul (DM's choice). A humanoid who knows the spell Speak with Plants feels a strange spiritual connection to this tree when they first come within 30 ft. of one possessing such a soul. They instinctively know that they can commune with it in a 10 minute meditation ritual. If they do so, they gain advantage on all saving throws for the next 24 hours.

entries.name: Optional Magical Rules
Flammable Oils
entries: The oils in this plant's rhizome ignite and detonate when compressed rapidly. If a Medium or larger creature falls onto or steps on this plant, it suffers {@dice 1d4} bludgeoning damage and {@dice 1d4} fire damage as the plant detonates. The plant is destroyed by this process.
Alternatively, the rhizome can be carefully extracted with a {@dc 10} {@skill Sleight of Hand} check and then may function like a grenade:

entries.name: Rhizome grenade
entries: As an action, a humanoid creature can throw the grenade (20/60 ft.). Any creature within 5 ft. of where it lands must succeed a {@dc 12} Dexterity saving throw, or take {@dice 1d4} bludgeoning damage and {@dice 1d4} fire damage.

entries.name: Nelumbites
entries: {@i Nelumbites} was a small aquatic lotus that grew in still water. The close modern relative {@i Nelumbo} (lotuses) is grown as a food crop, as it produces nutritious tubers buried in the wet sediment. Unusually, this plant is also able to generate its own heat through a thermoregulatory alternative oxidase pathway (AOX). It is probable that {@i Nelumbites} also produced such edible structures, and would have been an excellent source of food, and may have even had the same heat-generating properties as {@i Nelumbo}. Lotus flowers also carry cultural significance as symbols of beauty, purity, faithfulness, and spirituality.

entries.name: Optional Magical Rules
Daucunoid-like Tuber
entries: Each plant yields a thick tuber that can provide one day's ration and grants a darkvision of 60 ft. for 24 hours when consumed.

entries.name: Spiritual Warmth
entries: Rarely, this plant will produce a single large magical flower. This flower radiates warming spiritual energies and can be carefully harvested by completing a {@dc 15} {@skill Nature} check. On a success, the harvested plant becomes the magical item described below. On a failure, it instead crumbles to ash.
{@b {@i Pure Lotus Broach/Barrette}} {@i Wondrous Item, RARE, requires attunement. Appearance: A large perfectly formed lotus flower, coloured with soft pink and white petals.}
Rules: This flower hardens into a durable porcelain form and can be attached to clothing or hair. While attuned to this item, you gain resistance to cold damage and advantage on Wisdom saving throws.

Coturel, E.P., Bodnar, J., Morel, E.M., Ganuza, D.G., Sagasti, A.J., and Beltrán, M. 2018. New species of osmundaceous fertile leaves from the upper Triassic of Argentina. {@i Acta Palaeobotanica}, {@b 58(2)}, 107-119.

We'd been told of a mysterious island 30 miles off the coast that was, apparently, filled with all manner of strange creatures. After a few hours of sailin', we arrived. This island was quite large, covered in dense forest and jungle. The tales were indeed true, as it was largely populated by miniature dinosaurs – a remarkable sight to behold. I had read about such a phenomenon, called "insular dwarfism" in the literature. A term I found interestin' as a dwarf meself. Several other adventuring parties had also warned us not to go though, sayin' it was unsafe. Looked perfectly fine when we arrived and most of the lil' beasts posed no threat at all. However, we soon found out that the warnin's were to be heeded.

entries.name: Background
entries: Hațeg Island isn't a single geological formation, but rather a landmass that we can determine existed by the characteristics of the sediments that were deposited in its surrounding basins. Located in modern day Romania, Hațeg Island was a landmass that persisted for a very long time, but the sediments that we study to learn about it are of Late Cretaceous age.

Hațeg Island first drew the attention of palaeontologists in the early 1900s, after the discovery of dinosaur bones in the region. It quickly became apparent that many of the examples found appeared to be adult specimens, but were significantly smaller than their close relatives found elsewhere. It soon became apparent that Hațeg Island was the first example of insular dwarfism in the fossil record. This is a process whereby large animal communities isolated on islands for thousands or millions of years adapt to the limited resources by significantly reducing their body size over many generations.

entries.name: Description
entries: Hațeg Island was either a single island, archipelago, or (at the very least) an isolated spit of land. Current data suggests that it was most likely a very large island (30,000 mi2), with the nearest mainland over 125 mi away, and had at least one volcano.

It was in the warm sub-tropical part of the Tethys Sea, about 27° North of the equator. This gave it a hot climate with a mean annual temperature of 20 – 25 °C (68 – 77 °F), as the Cretaceous was warmer than the world today. This climate supported a sub-tropical flora, with a mix of ferns and flowering plants.

entries.name: Geology
entries: As there are many geological formations that allow us to reconstruct Hațeg Island, describing the combined geology of all of these strata is rather complex. Nevertheless, the two main Late Cretaceous successions are the Densuş– Ciula and Sânpetru formations. These are generally molasse-type deposits, which in geology means a combination of sandstones, shales, and conglomerates (rounded coarse-grains cemented together) deposited in non-marine aquatic settings, such as lakes, rivers, and streams. Deposits of volcanic tuffs, tuffities, and volcanic agglomerates indicate infrequent periods of volcanic activity from at least one volcano on the island. Most of the fossils are preserved in these molasse-type deposits, but our information about Hațeg Island is also supplemented by an array of shallow marine basin deposits that were formed in the surrounding Tethys Sea.

entries.name: Fossils
entries: Hațeg Island has been described as having a diversity so large that it must have been from a large island (>30,000 mi2). These encompass a wide variety of animals, including fish, frogs, turtles, and crocodiles in the island's waterways and coastal waters, as well as lizards, snakes, pterosaurs, dinosaurs, and mammals throughout the island. This fauna is generally reflective of the typical Euramerican Early Cretaceous fauna. As mentioned above, the flora was dominated by ferns and angiosperms (flowering plants), forming a hot dry sub-tropical woodland setting.

entries.name: As a Roleplaying Environment
entries: Hațeg Island can be run one of two ways: either as a giant mysterious island, or as dozens of small islands, each populated with their own unique creatures. In either case, the creatures found on Hațeg should be visually distinct from their mainland relatives, displaying unusual colours and patterns in addition to their reduced size.

Hațeg borderlines on a tropical island setting (albeit a bit cooler) and can be populated by lush forests and jungles. The isolation of the island(s) makes it a great setting for forgotten temples and lost civilisations, and including Hațeg as a 'lost island' in a nautical-themed setting can add a sense of realism to this standard fantasy trope. In the following pages, we have provided stats for {@i Balaur, Hatzegopteryx, Magyarosaurus, Struthiosaurus,} and {@i Zalmoxes.}

{@b Insular dwarfism} Any creature (excluding {@i Hatzegopteryx, Balaur, Zalmoxes, Magyarosaurus,} and {@i Struthiosaurus}) that makes landfall on Hațeg Island is affected by {@b Insular Dwarfism}. If the affected creature remains on the island, it will shrink by one size category after its next long rest. A creature can only ever be reduced by one size category from this effect. The affect dissipates after 24 hours if the creature leaves Hațeg Island within the next two days. If it does not, the affect becomes permanent and can only be removed by a Greater Restoration spell or effect.
{@b Island Isolation} Non-humanoid creatures on this island do not see humanoids as a threat and are instead highly curious of them. These creatures may still see humanoids as prey.

entries.name: References
entries: Benton, M.J., Csiki, Z., Grigorescu, D., Redelstorff, R., Sander, P.M., Stein, K., and Weishampel, D.B. 2010. Dinosaurs and the island rule: The dwarfed dinosaurs from Haţeg Island. {@i Palaeogeography, Palaeoclimatology, Palaeoecology,} {@b 293(3-4)}, 438-454.

entries.name: Designers' Note
entries: We ran an adventure to Hațeg Island with a level 4 party and it worked exceptionally well. In this, we had Hatzegopteryx be a looming deadly presence that the party had to avoid, rather than fight. They travelled throughout the island, encountering other dinosaurs and the ruins of a civilisation that worshipped Hatzegopteryx. This was interspersed with chase scenes through narrow forests and caves, fleeing from Hatzegopteryx itself.

Stein, K., Csiki, Z., Rogers, K.C., Weishampel, D.B., Redelstorff, R., Carballido, J.L., and Sander, P.M. 2010. Small body size and extreme cortical bone remodeling indicate phyletic dwarfism in {@i Magyarosaurus dacus} (Sauropoda: Titanosauria). {@i Proceedings of the National Academy of Science}s, {@b 107(20)}, 9258-9263.

Although Hațeg island was in the sub-tropical part of the Tethys Sea, the warmer Cretaceous temperatures meant that its flora would have been comparable to a modern tropical island, rather than a modern sub-tropical one. This means that most of the island was covered by lush forest and jungle.

entries.name: Phyllites sp.
entries: {@i Phyllites} sp. was a small undergrowth fern that would have grown around the bases of trees and in other shaded areas. It favoured damp soils and in summer would have likely developed rows of orange-brown or yellow sori (clusters of spore-making structures) along the underside of its leaves. {@i Phyllites} sp. would not have been edible, and may even have been an irritant or poisonous to humans.

entries.name: Phototoxic
entries: A viscous milky fluid runs through this plant's stem. If the plant is damaged, it oozes out. Any creature that comes into contact with this fluid gains vulnerability to radiant damage for 24 hours. This affliction can be removed with a lesser restoration spell or effect.

entries.name: Pandanites trinervis
entries: {@i Pandanites trinervis} was a branching shrub with root supports at its base and rosettes of strap-like spiky leaves at the ends of branches that would have been sharp enough to cut skin. These leaves were also highly fibrous and could have been weaved into baskets or used to make thread or rope. Interestingly, modern relatives of this plant ({@i Pandanus}) are a key ingredient in many curries, and it is likely that {@i Pandanites trinervis}' leaves could have also been dried and used as a curry spice. The plant also produced fragrant flowers that could have been used as a perfume or to flavour drinks. Upon pollination, these would have developed into pineapple or cone-like fruits that were edible and yellow or orange in colour.

entries.name: High Scoville Pungency
entries: This plant is exceptionally spicy. If a creature consumes this plant's fruit, it takes {@dice 1d6} fire damage, but gains the following ability for 24 hours:

entries.name: Flamin' Breath
entries: This ability has a number of charges equal to your proficiency bonus. As an action, you can exhale a cone of flaming breath. Each creature within a 15 ft. cone in front of you must succeed a DC (8 + Constitution bonus) Dexterity saving throw, or take {@dice 1d6} + PB fire damage.

entries.name: Araliaephyllum sp.
entries: {@i Araliaephyllum} sp. was a small to medium sized lauraceous bush with multiple thin stems or trunks and a bushy canopy. This canopy was made up of narrow three-lobed leaves that had the silhouette of a bird's foot. Little is known about this plant, but its modern affinities suggest that it may have developed small inedible black fruits and possibly had medicinal uses.

entries.name: Theropod-footed Healing Balm
entries: This plant's bird-foot-shaped leaves can be crushed into a paste and applied to a wound to help it heal. If this balm is applied to a creature during a short rest, that creature heals {@dice 1d6 + 2} hit points and its walking speed is increased by 10 ft. for the next 24 hours.

entries.name: Sabalites longirhachis
entries: {@i Sabalites longirhachis} was a tall, thin, large-leaved palm tree that reached up to 45 ft. in height. It possibly produced bunches of small dry berry-like fruits, but these would have been extremely difficult to reach, given the tree's height, and were probably inedible to humans. The large leaves and long, straight trunks of this tree would have made it an ideal resource for building structures.

entries.name: Synaptic Regulator
entries: The small dry fruits that this plant produces have a bitter taste and cause a creature to feel nauseous for a few minutes if consumed. However, they also stimulate the nervous system and provide that creature advantage on Intelligence saving throws for the next 24 hours.

entries.name: Ettingshausenia onomasta
entries: {@i Ettingshausenia onomasta} was a large plane-like tree with broad three-lobed leaves that favoured moist soils, growing near water. Its bark would have had a knobbly and mottled appearance, with a camouflage-like pattern. Its wood would have been highly resistant to splitting and therefore useful for making sturdy wooden objects (e.g. a butcher's block), but would have been hard to carve. Modern relatives of this plant produce hair-like new growth that can become a respiratory irritant when the wood is cut.

entries.name: Optional Magical Rules
Polymorphic Fibres
entries: {@i When this plant is cut down, pale pink hair-like fibres erupt from its central trunk, causing creatures within 10 ft. to cough and splutter. When this happens, the closest creature must succeed a DC 12 Wisdom saving throw or be polymorphed into a non-magical Sharovipteryx (see} {@b {@i page 175}}{@i ) for 10 minutes. If that creature takes damage, the effect ends.}

Marmi, J., Gomez, B., Martín-Closas, C., and Villalba-Breva, S. 2010. A reconstruction of the fossil palm {@i Sabalites longirhachis} (Unger) J. Kvaček et Herman from the Maastrichtian of Pyrenees. {@i Review of Palaeobotany and Palynology}, {@b 163(1-2)}, 73-83.
Popa, M.E., Kvaček, J., Vasile, S., and Csiki-Sava, Z. 2016. Maastrichtian dicotyledons of the Rusca Montană and Haţeg basins, South Carpathians, Romania. {@i Cretaceous Research}, {@b 57}, 699-712.

entries.name: References
entries: Herman, A.B., and Kvaček, J. 2007. Early Campanian Grünbach flora of Austria. {@i Paleontological Journal}, {@b 41}, 1068-1076.

Herman, A.B., Golovneva, L.B., Shczepetov, S.V., and Grabovsky, A.A. 2016. The late Cretaceous Arman flora of Magadan oblast, Northeastern Russia. {@i Stratigraphy and Geological Correlation}, {@b 24}, 651-760.

entries.name: The Crato Formation
entries: When our ship arrived at the coast, we were greeted by the most beautiful lagoon I'd ever seen. The pale creams and oranges of the sun-baked sand were stunnin'ly contrasted with the milky-blue water and deep-green tropical plants. This felt like a lil'

paradise in a dry desert. Once we made landfall, one of the crew set to restock their water. They scooped up a mouthful and in delight it was fresh! Well, at least the first gulp was. The second scoop their faces scrunched, and they spat it out. Seems there was only a sliver of fresh water on the top. Told 'em that the milky colour shows they shouldn't drink it. "Noted", said the crewman.

entries.name: Background
entries: The Crato Formation of north-eastern Brazil is a series of strata that boasts arguably some of the best-preserved fossils ever found. A unique combination of environmental, geochemical, sedimentological, and geological events caused fossils from this locality to be preserved with unbelievably high fidelity. It is approximately 120 million years old and was deposited near the equator during the hot Early Cretaceous.

There is a lot of controversy around the Crato Formation (and the nearby Santana Formation). Fossils from these locations have been routinely illegally exported for decades and can be found in almost every fossil shop around the world. While this has allowed exceptional Crato material to be widely studied, it has also impacted domestic Brazilian palaeontology and science tourism, as well as perpetuated colonial attitudes. We here at PalaeoGames Ltd. support the repatriation of illegally acquired fossils to their home country.

entries.name: Description
entries: There is still conjecture about the exact environmental setting of the Crato Formation, with some scientists arguing that it was an ancient lake/lagoon, and others that it was a semi-arid wetland. Regardless, the entomofauna (insects) and flora (plants) show a combination of species that are from harsh arid scrublands and lush freshwater environments. This, combined with the high salinity, geological data, and reduced fish fauna, indicates that the Crato Formation was a body of lush water in an otherwise arid region, but that that water was stratified – with fresh water on top and salty, oxygen-poor water at the bottom. Regardless of the exact parameters of its deposition, the Crato Formation was an oasis of beauty in an otherwise barren landscape. This desolate weather was intermittently broken by huge storm events that flooded the surrounding landscape, flushing many small ground-dwelling invertebrates into the water.

entries.name: Geology
entries: The Crato Formation is a sequence of rock about 200 ft. thick and is composed of a variety of rock types. The strata of interest (called the Nova Olinda Member) is a buff-coloured creamy rock made of 99% calcium carbonate. This mineral was precipitated in water by algae as they photosynthesised, causing a milky haze in the water that drifted down as tiny crystals. Over time, the accumulation and cementation of these crystals formed the rock that entombed any carcasses that sank to the bottom of the water body.

entries.name: Fossils
entries: The Crato Formation yields truly astonishing fossils. Some of them preserve details that most people would not believe is possible. A single insect fossil can be preserved entirely intact with every joint fully articulated, with every body segment complete, each covered in cuticular scales, with hair-like setae still attached to those scales, with each of those hairs retaining microscopic surface details (such as ridges and grooves), and with fossilised bacteria sat between those grooves. This sub-cellular level of preservation absolutely shatters the previous understanding of the limitations of fossilisation. Furthermore, some fossils not only retain their external-most features, but volatile internal tissues that usually degrade within hours of death can also be preserved. We do not exaggerate when we say that the Crato Formation may yield the best-preserved fossils in the world.

Interestingly, there are no skeletal records of large terrestrial vertebrates, like big dinosaurs, or large logs (although some amber has been found) in the Crato Formation. This suggests that there is a mechanism that prevents larger fossils from being preserved. That could either be environmental, with the harsh environment not sustaining bigger organisms, or (much more likely) a filtering mechanism that has prevented them from being preserved or us from finding them. The latter is favoured by scientists, as they believe that smaller fossils may have been blown/ washed into a large body of water, then concentrated by gyres, and finally deposited in the middle of the water body. In the following pages, we have provided stats for {@i Cratoavis, Ludodactylus, Tetrapodophis}, {@i Tupandactylus,} and "Ubirajara".

entries.name: As a Roleplaying Environment
entries: The Crato lake/lagoon should be an oasis of life among an otherwise hot and harsh scrubland. Lush green plants teeming with vividly coloured insects, birds, and pterosaurs should provide a chorus of colour piercing the scorching yellows and browns of the surrounding scrublands. Temporary waterways are filled with tiny invertebrates that thrive after an annual wet season. This location makes an ideal rest stop on a long journey for both players and migrating animals, which can lead to conflict.

Small streams drain into a single massive waterbody, similar to an inland sea. The main waterbody itself persists all year around and has little-to-no drainage, so concentrates salts similar to (but not as extreme as) the dead sea. The water is not drinkable and should have a milky-white appearance with green-tinted algae-rich areas. It is populated by millions of tiny fish (1.5 - 2 inches long), but little else.

Rarely, a huge storm should roll in from distant mountains, bringing with it heavy thumping rainfall accompanied by a torrent of water that washes small creatures and objects into the water in a tropical storm event.
{@b Stratified waters.} Water appears fresh and the first sip always is.... However, further drinking or filling up of water supplies only provides salt water.
{@b Perfect Preservation.} {@i Through the murky water, you can see fossilised creatures resting on the bottom}.
Any creature that touches the bottom of the Crato palaeolake/lagoon while more than 20 ft. from the shoreline must succeed a {@dc 18} Constitution saving throw or be {@condition petrified}.

entries.name: Weather Effects:
entries: {@b Blistering sun.} If players travel for more than 8 hours without seeking shelter from the sun, they gain one level of exhaustion. This effect is inactive during a Rainstorm Event.

{@b Rainstorm Event.} After {@dice 1d4} days in this environment, the players are met with a sudden drastic change in weather. Over the course of an hour or less, the skies darken and a heavy storm rolls over the landscape. Hammering rain makes travel difficult. The rain lasts for 1 hour. Shortly after the rain ends, there is a distant rumbling sound followed by a torrent of knee-high flash flood water. Creatures have one round to escape the oncoming flood (i.e. climbing a tree or flying away), then must succeed a {@dc 13} Strength saving throw to avoid being washed away. A creature washed away moves at 40 ft. per round in the direction of the flowing water. A creature that succeeds on this Strength saving throw may wade through the water, treating it as difficult terrain if they move against the flow.

entries.name: References
entries: Barling, N.T., Martill, D.M., Heads, S.W. and Gallien, F. 2015. High fidelity preservation of fossil insects from the Crato Formation (Lower Cretaceous) of Brazil. {@i Cretaceous Research}, {@b 52}, 605-622.

Barling, N.T., Martill, D.M., and Heads, S.W. 2020. A geochemical model for the preservation of insects in the Crato Formation (Early Cretaceous) of Brazil. {@i Cretaceous Research}, {@b 116}, 104608.

entries.name: Crato Formation Flora
entries: The Crato Formation was an environment of extremes, with scorching dry heat and intermittent tremendous downpours. Its waters had fluctuating salinities and most plants had to be particularly hardy to survive in these dynamic conditions.

entries.name: Klitzschophyllites flabellatus Optional Magical Rules
entries: {@i Klitzschophyllites flabellatus} was an aquatic plant that grew in small clusters in shallow water. As no close modern relatives of this plant persist today, little is known about its biology beyond its overall morphology. It had roundish, leathery, gland-covered leaves with spikey edges and a thick root. These glands suggest that {@i Klitzschophyllites flabellatus} may have been able to tolerate intermittently hypersaline water.

entries.name: Babel Leaves
entries: If a single leaf is plucked from this plant and placed under the tongue of a creature with an Intelligence score of 8 or more, it is able to speak and comprehend any language for 1 minute. Once the effect wears off, the leaf shrivels and cannot be used again.

entries.name: Equisetum sp.
entries: {@i Equisetum} sp. (horsetails) grew in and around the edges of ponds, marshes, and other quiet fresh-water, as well as in consistently moist ground. They have a distinctive banding and long thin leaves, that can give them a feather-like appearance in some species. They grew close together, forming 3-4 ft. tall dense reeds, but had relatively weak stems and could have been pushed through with ease. Adult plants were poisonous, but young stems were paler, succulent, and edible if cooked. When crushed, these plants could also be used to make green or pale-yellow dyes.

entries.name: Toxic Maturity
entries: Fresh shoots of this plant are non-toxic and can be brewed into a simple, but delicious, potion that heals {@dice 1d4+1} hit points when consumed. However, mature plants are highly toxic and any creature that consumes them (or a derivative of them) is {@condition poisoned} for 24 hours. A successful {@dc 10} {@skill Nature} check is required to determine which shoots are safe to consume.

entries.name: Jaguariba wiersemaniania
entries: {@i Jaguariba wiersemaniania} was a small aquatic plant that grew in the shallow waters of ponds and lakes. Its leaves floated on the surface and it occasionally produced flowers, in the same manner as a modern waterlily. It produced a rhizome (an underground stem), similar to a potato, which would have been edible (albeit quite soggy). The flowers it produced were likely a psychodysleptic narcotic (similar to a hallucinogenic).

entries.name: Delicious
entries: The root of this plant is edible and can provide one days' ration. However, it is also particularly delicious to herbivores/omnivores. If you offer this food to a herbivorous/omnivorous beast while performing an {@skill Animal Handling} check, you gain advantage on that check.

entries.name: Psychodysleptic
entries: If a creature consumes the flowers of this plant, it must succeed a {@dc 14} Constitution saving throw or be {@condition stunned} for {@dice 1d4} minutes. On a successful save, it is instead {@condition frightened} of all other creatures for {@dice 1d4} minutes. Whenever that creature takes damage while under either effect, it may make another {@dc 14} Constitution saving throw, ending the effect on a success.

entries.name: Welwitschiophyllum brasiliense
entries: {@i Welwitschiophyllum brasiliense} was a desert-dwelling plant with long, pointed, strap-like leaves, and clusters of cones at the end of long thin stems. The fibrous leaves came to a sharp point, with edges sharp enough to cut skin. Dead, dropped leaves could have been used to make fibres for twine or as kindling for a fire. The thick central stem would have been edible, probably tasting similar to an onion.

entries.name: Razor-leaves
entries: The leaves of this plant are rigid and come to a sharp point. If a Large, Medium, or Small creature falls onto, runs through, or is pushed into this plant, it takes {@dice 1d4} piercing damage.

entries.name: Edible
entries: This plant's stem can be carefully harvested by succeeding a {@dc 10} {@skill Survival} check, providing four days' worth of rations for a single humanoid. Failing this check results in {@dice 1d4} piercing damage and a nasty cut.

entries.name: Ruffordia goeppertii
entries: {@i Ruffordia goeppertii} was a drought-tolerant fern that grew as small clusters of plants in shaded areas. If crushed, it would have produced a balsam aroma similar to pine needles. Modern relatives of this plant contain essential oils that, once extracted, can be used as an antiseptic or to treat burns. In some traditional medicines (particularly in South Africa), these plants are used to prevent children's nightmares.

entries.name: Optional Magical Rules
Antiseptic
entries: The roots of this plant have a horribly bitter taste, but also have medicinal properties. Eating them grants resistance to poison damage and immunity to the {@condition poisoned} condition for 24 hours.

entries.name: Sound Sleeping
entries: If a creature completes a long rest within 24 hours of consuming the roots of this plant, they gain temporary hit points equal to their proficiency bonus.

Dilcher, D.L., Bernardes-De-Oliveira, M.E., Pons, D., and Lott, T.A. 2005. {@i Welwitschiaceae} from the Lower Cretaceous of Northeastern Brazil. {@i American Journal of Botany}, {@b 92(8)}, 1294-1310.
Martill, D.M., Bechly, G., and Loveridge, R.F. 2007. {@i The Crato Fossil Beds of Brazil: Window into an Ancient World}. Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, pp 625.

Mohr, B., Bernardes-de-Oliveira, M.E.C., Loveridge, R., Pons, D., Sucerquia, P.A., and Castro-Fernandes, M.C. 2015. {@i Ruffordia goeppertii} (Schizaeales, Anemiaceae) – A common fern from the Lower Cretaceous Crato Formation of northeast Brazil. {@i Cretaceous Research}, {@b 54(3)}, 17-26.

Mohr, B., Bernardes-de-Oliveira, M.E.C., Barale, G., and Ouaja, M. 2006. Palaeogeographic distribution and ecology of {@i Klitzschophyllites}, an early Cretaceous angiosperm in southern Laurasia and northern Gondwana. {@i Cretaceous Research}, {@b 27(3)}, 464-472.

entries.name: References
entries: Coiffard, C., Mohr, B., and Bernardes-de-Oliveira, M.E.C. 2013. {@i Jaguariba wiersemana} gen. nov. et sp. nov., an Early Cretaceous member of crown group Nymphaeales (Nymphaeaceae) from northern Gondwana. {@i Palaeobotany}, {@b 62(1)}, 141-151.

data.name: Sapient Species and Societies
entries: This section presents six races/species that you can use in your games as player characters (PCs) and non-player characters (NPCs). For each race, we've provided a description of an example society in which they live, along with some ideas for you to add your own flair. We have worked hard to make these races interesting and unique, and we hope you have fun using them in your games. These races are fictional, but we used a process called speculative biology to design them as if they were real. It's worth noting that humanoid-dinosaur creatures have been a topic of discussion for many years.

entries.name: Humanoid Dinosaurs
entries: Since we first learned of the creatures that existed before us, we have asked the questions "{@i What if the [non-avian] dinosaurs hadn't died out?}", "{@i What would they have evolved into?}", and "{@i What if dinosaurs became humanoids?}". Many people tried to imagine intelligent bipedal (walking on two legs), humanoid-like, scaly dinosaurs. This idea has persisted in human culture for centuries now, and there have been semi-serious attempts to predict what such creatures could look like. In 1982 the palaeontologist Dale Russell and artist/sculptor Ron Séguin produced a highly-detailed life-sized sculpture of their imaginary human-shaped theropod dinosaur called the Dinosauroid. This was a shocking sculpture at the time, as it drew elements from contemporary speculations of aliens. For many years, this sculpture was what came to mind for most people when discussing dinosaur humanoids. However, we now know that such a creature is highly unlikely to evolve. Reality is not so anthro-centric (centred around us). Simply put, the Dinosaroid was an inaccurate hypothesis that misunderstood many features of the dinosaurs it was exploring.
Children of Seth concept sketches.
Pluvenn concept sketches.

The truth is that dinosaurs {@i did} survive the end-Cretaceous extinction, {@i did} evolve bipedality, and {@i did} evolve high intelligence. These lineages exist today as ostriches & penguins (non-flying bipeds), and corvids (crows, magpies, and their kin with high intelligence and tool use) respectively. Nevertheless, it is a fun and important thought experiment to imagine what might cause a species to evolve similar intelligence to our own and what that might look like.

entries.name: Speculative Biology
entries: Modern science uses a process called speculative biology to help fill gaps in the fossil record, hypothesise possible evolutionary lineages, or predict what alien life might be like. This process relies on understanding selection pressures (see {@b pages 16-17}). In speculative biology, known life on Earth is the starting point. We base our speculation on the limitations of characteristics that an organism has already developed. What we mean by this is that some fundamental components of an organism are difficult (but not impossible) to modify without reducing survivability. One example of this would be a crab's exoskeleton. As this hard shell is used for protection and to anchor muscles for movement, it would be difficult for that to evolve into a soft skin-like characteristic without compromising the crab's ability to move.

We have designed the new races with speculative biology in mind. Understanding the skeletal mechanics of the organisms that these races are hypothesised to evolve from offers an interesting challenge. How would an organism with huge, winged forelimbs develop the ability to manipulate trinkets or hold a sword and shield? How could the hips of a low-stooping herbivore change to allow it to stand upright? We have attempted to address these challenges with the species here. Each is accompanied by artwork depicting these races as a scientific proposition (albeit with a little fantasy anthropomorphism thrown in too).
{@i Pachyrhinosaurus} muscle reconstruction.

entries.name: Custom Language
entries: Accompanying these races is an additional custom language. Archosauric (or Archosauran) is the official/ state language of the races described in this book and may be selected as one of your player character's languages. We envision it as the root language of fantasy dragon and bird languages, despite those languages' great differences. As such, it functionally sounds like a hybrid of the two, sharing features of both. Archosauric combines high-pitched clicks and whistles with deep guttural growls and rolling harsh syllables. The frequency and abundance of these two starkly different tones within the language are typically a result of the formality of the conversation. That is, higher pitched clicks and squarks are usually casual slang, whereas deeper tones are more formal, although there is certainly intermingling between the two in many conversations.
Reconstructing {@i Effigia}.

data.name: Player Character Customisation
entries: Many campaigns using this supplement may heavily focus on elements of deep-time or include a large number of encounters with huge beasts. To allow players to specialise their characters around these elements, we have included three custom sub-classes; one that utilises deep-time, one that harvests the remains of large creatures, and one that specialises in hunting large prey.

items: {@class Ranger|PHB|Big Game Hunter|Big Game Hunter|DrDhrolinsDictionaryofDinosaurs}
{@class Artificer|TCE|Bonesculptor|Bonesculptor|DrDhrolinsDictionaryofDinosaurs}
{@class Druid|PHB|Circle of Cycles|Cycles|DrDhrolinsDictionaryofDinosaurs}

entries.name: Backgrounds
entries: In this section we have provided three additional backgrounds that you can use in character creation. These are themed around time travel, geology, and palaeontology respectively. For each, we have also provided recommended first level feats and ability score improvements, in case you are generating those from your background.

entries.name: Feats
entries: In this section we have provided a handful of feats, largely designed around geology and palaeontology (although not exclusively so). With these, we have included a recommended level restriction (and provided feats for levels 1, 4, 8, and 12). If you do not wish for feats to be level restricted, feel free to have these available to everyone, but be aware that some are considerably more powerful than others.

entries.name: Special Thanks
entries: We are forever grateful to the thousands of people who supported our dream of creating this book and the continued support of those who purchased copies after the end of our Kickstarter. If you a reading this, thank you {@i sincerely} for changing all of our lives. Some of our supporters went the extra mile. They allowed us to add far more content to this book than we otherwise would have been able to, helping make it the best it can be. Their names are provided below.
